summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Check your change as rare Royal Mint 20p coin sells for 1,800 times face value
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: We are all being encouraged to check our change after a rare 20p coin sold for more than 1,800 times its face value this week. The 20p piece is a “mule” coin dating from 2008 and was minted without a date on the coin due to an error. The mistake means the coin is considered a collector’s item. A batch of coins was issued without dates in 2008 due to an error in the minting process. An example of a rare undated 20p mule coin  (Image: eBay/Getty/Vandervelden) Prior to November of that year, the date on 20p coins would be found on the tail side. However, the Royal Mint switched it so that the date would now be next to the Queen’s head. A mistake in 2008 led to the old format being used on the Queen’s side and the new format being used on tails side. As a result, the first batch of British coins with no date on them was released into circulation for the first time in more than 300 years. Around 250,000 20p coins minted in November 2008 are believed to have entered circulation with no date. And now one has sold on eBay, attracting a winning bid of £363, 1,815 times its face value. The 50 pence piece has become the most valued and collected coin in the UK, with many collectable designs appearing on its heptagonal canvas. Its 27.5mm diameter makes it the largest of any British coin, and allows space for decorative pictures. It has often been used to celebrate big events over the past 50 years of British history. The rarest coins tend to be of the greatest value, with the mintage (number of coins with each design made) being the fundamental attraction for collectors. Along with the design, other aspects of the coin which increase value are the condition of the coin and whether it has an error in its design. The way in which it is sold can also determine the coin’s value - while some coin collectors will bid vast amounts of money on eBay or at auction, others opt for more robust valuations by selling via a coin dealer.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Martin Lewis slams 'ridiculous' energy-saving advice as bills rocket this winter
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Martin Lewis has hit out at the “ridiculous” tips households are having to follow to keep warm and cut their energy bills, saying it is not the kind of society he wants to live in. The Money Saving Expert founder said people were being forced to rely on basic energy-saving measures and even USB-heated clothing to stay warm as the cost of heating their homes continues to put pressure on household budgets. Speaking to the BBC, Martin reluctantly said households should first look at ways to reduce energy use without affecting their quality of life. A post shared by BBC News (@bbcnews) He advised people to keep curtains closed when it is dark and open during daylight, make sure blinds face inwards and avoid hanging curtains over radiators. He also urged households to check their radiators are properly bled and, if they have a combi boiler, look at whether its flow temperature is set too high. But Martin said the fact people need this kind of advice in order to manage their heating costs was a sign of a much wider problem. “Again, I don't, you know, it's not because we want to live in that society, but we do live in that society. It's ridiculous,” he said. He also pointed to 1p an hour USB-heated clothing as another way people are trying to keep themselves warm without having to heat their entire home. “The USB heated gilet costs a penny an hour to run. It keeps you warm. It doesn't keep your house warm, but it'll keep you going,” he said. Martin added: “And we are in that situation, and that's not a society I want to live in, where we have to be giving out that type of information and advice. But it is there, and it is going to be happening.” Recommended reading : His comments underline the pressure facing households as they look for ways to keep energy costs down, with simple changes around the home being presented as ways to make heating go further.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire road compensation payouts double to £217,643 as MP demands action
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A rising compensation bill is piling pressure on Cambridgeshire County Council to improve the condition of its roads after payouts to motorists more than doubled in a year. North West Cambridgeshire MP Sam Carling has called for action after compensation payments reached £217,642.65 in 2025/26. The increase follows complaints about road conditions, particularly in northern Huntingdonshire and rural communities including Ramsey and Bury. Mr Carling said: “Residents deserve roads that are safe, repairs that last, and a council that takes responsibility. Read more Plans for nurse-led care home in Hunts village Face of thief jailed after stealing televisions and champagne Confirmation that 'debacle' car park scheme will not progress welcomed 10 Cambridgeshire criminals who were jailed in November “People are fed up with potholes damaging their vehicles, dangerous road surfaces and repairs that seem to fall apart almost as soon as they have been carried out.” He said taxpayers were effectively paying twice when inadequate repairs resulted in subsequent compensation claims and also questioned how contractors were being held accountable. The council extended its M Group highways contract in July and introduced performance-related penalties, although the new contract was not signed until October. Mr Carling said the council could outsource repairs but “cannot outsource its responsibility for proper scrutiny, quality control and accountability”. He called on the authority to explain what was being done to ensure repairs lasted and urged it to make effective use of increased Government funding for tackling potholes. Cambridgeshire County Council defended its record, saying it was making its biggest highways investment in more than a decade. A council spokesperson said: “We know how important our roads are, which is why we identify defects and repair them as quickly as we can. “Over the past two years, the council has made the biggest investment in the highways network in over a decade. We’re spending more than £78 million on highways maintenance; this includes delivering improvements which both repair and prevent potholes.” The council said motorists could submit claims if highway defects caused personal injury or vehicle damage, but each claim was assessed individually because public money was involved. It added that the authority would generally be liable for compensation where it had failed to meet its duties under the Highways Act relating to maintenance of the public highway.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Co-op 'do not eat' warning issued as product recalled over health concerns
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Co-op is recalling king prawns after packs were labelled with the wrong use-by dates. The Food Standards Agency (FSA) said the affected prawns are unsafe to eat after their correct dates in November, despite the labels showing dates in December. The recall affects 140g packs of Co-op King Prawns in a Chilli & Coriander Marinade with printed use-by dates of December 27 and December 30. Packs marked December 27 should have a use-by date of November 27, while those marked December 30 should say November 30. Wednesday 25 November - Co-op recalls Co-op King Prawns in a Chilli & Coriander Marinade because of incorrect use by dates #FoodAlert https://t.co/4CSbgpyRMR https://t.co/msTp00x8su — Food Standards Agency (@foodgov) November 25, 2026 The FSA said customers should not eat the product after the correct use-by date and can return it to a Co-op store for a refund or replacement, subject to availability. Co-op's customer notice separately tells shoppers to dispose of the product. In the notice, Co-op said: "For a refund or replacement (subject to availability) please visit your local store. "If purchased online, you can receive a refund by calling 0330 041 7737. "You can contact our Customer Careline on 0800 0686 727 or email via Product issues or returns - Co-op ( coop.co.uk ). "We apologise for any inconvenience caused." The FSA said notices explaining the recall and what customers should do will be displayed in stores selling the product. If a food product should not be sold because of a problem, it may be withdrawn from shelves or recalled, meaning customers are asked to return it. The FSA issues product recall information notices to inform consumers and local authorities about problems with food. In some cases, it issues a food alert for action, giving local authorities details of action to take on behalf of consumers.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: £17.3m transport row erupts between Cambridgeshire leaders over spending plans
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A row has erupted over how an extra £17.3 million in government funding should be spent on transport improvements across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough. Regional leaders are fighting over which transport schemes should get priority for the money. Cambridgeshire and Peterborough mayor Paul Bristow has accused Liberal Democrat councillors on the Combined Authority Board of "playing politics" after they blocked his proposals during a recent meeting. Mr Bristow said: "At my board the county council Lib Dems have a veto and used it to block a whole series of transport improvements in our region. Read more The 'hidden gem' garden centre in Cambridgeshire with 'fun for all the family' CQC recognises significant improvements across East of England Ambulance Service Hunts man accused of possessing 'extreme pornographic' video of cow Confirmation that 'debacle' car park scheme will not progress welcomed 10 Cambridgeshire criminals who were jailed in November "Despite being the elected mayor they have this veto – no other Mayoral Authority has these veto rules." The government funding will pay for improvements to roads, buildings and other transport infrastructure over the next three years. Mr Bristow’s projects included upgrades to the A141, Whittlesea railway station and the A10 BP roundabout, plus transport schemes in March and improvements to the A16 at Norwood and Fengate access. He said an independent assessment identified the schemes as the most developed and likely to have the biggest impact, rather than politically chosen. Mr Bristow said: "But I am not taking this lying down – this report is valuable and these schemes are the right ones to deliver now. "So as mayor – I shall use the funds we have to prioritise these schemes – and bring to board." He said other projects recommended in the report could be developed for delivery in future years. However, Liberal Democrat councillors argue that while large infrastructure projects are important, some of the funding should be set aside for smaller-scale improvements that could deliver immediate benefits to communities. They suggest this could include road safety measures outside schools and upgrades to dangerous junctions, such as Humphries Way. The group said it was willing to compromise by supporting the larger schemes, provided that other areas of Cambridgeshire also received targeted investment from the additional funding. Cambridgeshire County Council leader Cllr Lucy Nethsingha said: "I am genuinely sad that we could not reach an agreement. "We were ready to meet the mayor halfway, and I hoped right up to the meeting that he would do the same. "This was never about opposing the big projects. It was about fairness. "Families in our towns and villages pay their taxes too, and they deserve safer roads to school and safer junctions on their doorstep. "A small share of this money could have delivered that. "I will keep making the case for the whole of Cambridgeshire, and I hope the Mayor will now work with us to find a fairer way forward." Mr Bristow said he would keep pushing the proposals, arguing that Liberal Democrat members would have to veto each scheme individually to stop them going ahead. He said: "It's time to stop playing politics – my only interest is to improve the lives of local people. "It's time to get Cambridgeshire and Peterborough moving." Both sides agree investment is needed; they are fighting over how to spend the money. Mr Bristow believes the funding should be focused on major projects that are already developed and ready to deliver, while Liberal Democrat councillors want to see some of the money directed toward smaller, community-focused schemes across the Combined Authority area. The Combined Authority, which was established in 2017 as the area's transport authority, is led by the elected mayor and oversees a £20 million annual budget.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Timeline of events after knifeman guilty of attempted murder on Huntingdon train
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An LNER service travelling from Doncaster to London King's Cross had just departed from Peterborough at around 7.30pm on November 1, 2025, when an unprecedented disaster struck. Emergency calls began flooding in to police, with passengers claiming a knife attack was taking place on board. Just 15 minutes after it left Peterborough, the train made an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon station after the driver took action and moved it onto the slower line. Anthony Williams, 33, was arrested at the scene and later charged with 14 counts of attempted murder, ten of which relate to the incident on the train. He pleaded guilty to wounding with intent and a handful of other offences including affray and common assault, but denied attempted murder. At Cambridge Crown Court on November 26, 2026, a jury of nine men and three women found him guilty of all 14 counts after a month-long trial. Below is a timeline of the events leading up to and during the attack, as set out by prosecutors during the trial. Around 7pm: Williams stabs a 14-year-old boy on a footbridge over the River Nene in Peterborough. The boy and his friend manage to escape. Minutes later: Williams encounters Dawid Taborski, 26, on the same bridge and attempts to stab him, but he flees. Soon after he encounters William Ogelby, 22, in the Rail World car park and his jacket is cut. Around 7.20pm: Williams arrives at Ritzy Barbers in Peterborough. He is caught on CCTV brandishing a knife and shouting, before leaving in a taxi. Williams in the Ritzy Barbers shop (Image: PA) 8.17pm: Williams arrives at Peterborough train station and boards a train to London. A passenger sends a text message to British Transport Police soon after informing them a man is acting suspiciously. Officers stop the train at Stevenage but cannot locate the man. 10.30pm: Williams is caught on CCTV stealing a set of kitchen knives from an Asda store in Stevenage. Soon after he boards another train to London. 11.30pm: Williams arrives at Farringdon station. 12.43am: Williams stabs 17-year-old Isaiah Idris on a DLR train heading to Pontoon Dock station. He gets off at Pontoon Dock before travelling around London on the Tube network and getting a train back to Stevenage. Williams on the DLR train (Image: BTP/Press Association) Around 6am: Williams steals alcohol from the same Stevenage Asda store. He then boards another train and gets off at Hitchin. Williams boarding a Thameslink train at Stevenage (Image: BTP/Press Association) 7.51am: Williams boards a train to Peterborough. On this service, he spits at passenger Jordan Morley, who gets off at Biggleswade. 9.30am: Williams arrives at his home address in Peterborough. He spends around nine hours here and makes a call to his bank. 7.26pm: Williams boards the LNER service to London King's cross which departs a few minutes later. 7.38pm: Police receive the first calls about a knife attack on board the train. Ten men were stabbed: LNER staff member Samir Zitouni, 48, and passengers Jonathan Gjoshe, 22, Sachin Balakrishnan, 29, David Presland, 73, Scott Bletcher, 50, Scott Green, 52, Kevin Deely, 58, Stephen Crean, 61, Raza Aslam, 44, and Michael Paffett, 34. Williams brandishing a knife on the LNER service (Image: BTP/Press Association) 7.44pm: The service makes an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon station. Armed police attend and Williams is arrested minutes later. 9.42pm: Williams arrives at Parkside Police Station in Cambridge. 3.27am: Williams punches police constable James Farrell on the nose while in custody.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A quayside pub in Cambridgeshire has been described as a "hidden gem" and serves "amazing" meals, according to happy visitors. Its become a favourite of both locals and visitors for its fresh, seasonal menu and warm, friendly service. On Trip Advisor, the Cambridgeshire pub has more than 150 'excellent'-rated reviews, earning praise for its service and value. Elsewhere, on Google Reviews, The Oliver Cromwell has a score of 4.5 out of 5 from more than 600 reviews. The Oliver Cromwell, renowned for its excellent food, was forced to close its kitchen in July 2024, but soon reopened. It was taken over by Tom Blestoe who transformed it into a "traditional English pub", creating an environment where "where everyone can feel welcome". summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire woman’s weekly home help leads to lasting friendship
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A helping hand at home has led to a lasting friendship for one Cambridgeshire resident. Louise, who lives in Cambridgeshire, was recovering from a fall down the stairs in March while already managing arthritis and fatigue from her medication. She was unable to manage daily tasks and became isolated during her recovery, with her sons out at work and college during the day and limited mobility keeping her indoors. Louise said: "I was very lonely after the accident. "There was somebody that would come in regularly once a week, just to do even the lightest bit of housework. "It just made such a difference because I couldn't do anything." On a friend’s recommendation, she contacted Care Network Cambridgeshire and was matched with volunteer Sandra through the charity’s Help at Home service. Sandra visited weekly for approximately two months, helping with light household tasks, benefits paperwork, and personal difficulties, while also offering reassurance and practical guidance. The support soon grew into a friendship, and the two remain in touch even after formal support ended. Louise said: "I ended up with one of the ladies who, even after I was discharged from Care Network, has now become a firm friend. "It was just so lovely knowing that there was somebody there who cared about us." Lynda Phillips, CEO of Care Network Cambridgeshire, said: "Louise's story shows that sometimes it's the simplest things that make the biggest difference. "Having someone come into your home, help with everyday tasks and take the time to listen can mean so much when you're feeling isolated or struggling." The charity, which marked its 40th anniversary in October 2026, is encouraging more people to volunteer or support its work to help others facing similar challenges. For more information on volunteering, accessing support, or making a donation, visit www.care-network.org.uk.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Huntingdon bed factory’s £1m relaunch keeps British craftsmanship alive
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A bed factory that has been making mattresses for more than 60 years is keeping traditional craftsmanship alive. Generations of families have worked at Bensons for Beds’ Huntingdon site, where craftsmen still use hand side-stitching and tufting every day. The factory, which opened in 1962, is now playing a key role in the relaunch of heritage bed brand Staples & Co, first established in 1895. One of the team at work in the factory. (Image: Rosie Pratt) Nick Collard, chief executive officer of Bensons for Beds, said: "What makes our Huntingdon factory special isn't just what we make here. "It's the people, the pride they take in their work and the knowledge that has been built up over decades. "There are families whose connections to bedmaking in Huntingdon stretch back generations. "That's an extraordinary legacy, and one we have a responsibility to protect." the skilled craftspeople at Bensons for Beds' Cambridgeshire manufacturing facility are playing a central role in the relaunch of Staples & Co, a historic British bed brand founded in 1895, following an investment of more than £1 million.  (Image: Rosie Pratt) The relaunch follows an investment of more than £1 million by Bensons for Beds and aims to combine modern manufacturing with traditional British craftsmanship. The refreshed Staples & Co collection features contemporary designs and high-quality natural materials, including regeneratively farmed British wool. The Huntingdon team, which includes employees with more than 40 years of experience, is now training a new generation of apprentices to carry the skills forward. Inspecting the quality of a mattress. (Image: Rosie Pratt) Mr Collard said: "At the same time, we want to create opportunities for young people to build rewarding careers in manufacturing. "The future of British bedmaking depends on passing that expertise on, while giving the next generation the opportunity to develop skills of their own." Bensons for Beds supports apprenticeships and specialist training programmes at the site, aiming to secure the long-term future of the craft. One of the team tape edging a mattress in the Staples factory. (Image: Rosie Pratt) The Huntingdon factory is central to the company’s UK operations, combining traditional methods with innovation and large-scale production. It also holds the Furniture Makers' Manufacturing Guild Mark and BSI Kitemark, reflecting its production standards. Bensons for Beds owned brands director Emma Forbes said: "There's something remarkable about watching a skilled bedmaker at work. One of the team tape edging a mattress in the Staples factory. (Image: Rosie Pratt) "Techniques such as hand side-stitching take time to master, and you can see the care and precision that goes into every stage. "When we developed the new Staples & Co collection, we wanted to create products that genuinely benefit from that expertise. "It's about the details you may not immediately see, but which make a real difference to how a mattress feels and performs." One of the team at work in the factory. (Image: Rosie Pratt) "Being able to draw on the skills and experience of our Huntingdon team is a real strength for the brand." She said the Huntingdon team’s experience and skill are a "real strength" for the brand. The Staples & Co relaunch is part of Bensons’ wider growth plan, which includes investing in its brands and UK manufacturing. One of the team tape edging a mattress. (Image: Rosie Pratt) The new collection will go on sale in Bensons stores nationwide from November. The Huntingdon site has employed several generations of the same families, underlining its deep community roots. It makes Bensons for Beds mattresses, including Staples & Co ranges, using specialist techniques and natural materials. The skilled craftspeople at Bensons for Beds' Cambridgeshire manufacturing facility are playing a central role in the relaunch of Staples & Co, a historic British bed brand founded in 1895, following an investment of more than £1 million.  (Image: Rosie Pratt) The factory also supports apprenticeships and ongoing training to build its skilled workforce. Staples & Co is a heritage brand founded in 1895 and now owned by Bensons for Beds. Backed by an investment of more than £1 million, the relaunch combines traditional craft with modern design across three mattress ranges – Artisan, Signature and Iconic – plus matching divan bases and headboards. One of the team at work in the factory. (Image: Rosie Pratt) Selected collections use regeneratively farmed British wool sourced from a network of approximately 50 to 60 farmers. Bensons for Beds calls itself the UK’s leading sleep specialist, with more than 175 stores and a focus on personalised service and quality products. The factory in Huntingdon. (Image: Rosie Pratt) The company employs over 1,700 people across its retail, manufacturing and distribution operations.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A drug dealer has been jailed for running a crack cocaine and heroin supply operation in Cambridgshire. Curtis Reeve, 27, was arrested on January 6 after police executed a warrant at his home on Cobden Avenue in Millfield, Peterborough. Officers found a mobile phone linked to a drug line and several wraps of crack cocaine. A police investigation uncovered hundreds of calls and messages with other dealers, including texts detailing drug quantities and evidence of topped-up phones connected to the operation. Reeve was also found with more than £2,000 in cash and evidence he had purchased designer goods worth £1,600, despite being unemployed and claiming benefits. The items included a pair of Dolce and Gabbana trainers worth £579 and a Moncler coat costing £659. He purchased a pair of Dolce and Gabbana trainers worth £579 (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) He purchased a Moncler coat costing £659 (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Other suspected dealers arrested with large amounts of class A drugs were also found to have links to Reeve through their mobile phones. He admitted being concerned in the supply of crack cocaine and heroin, as well as possessing criminal property. On November 24, he was sentenced to 47 months in prison at Cambridge Crown Court. Curtis Reeve was jailed for 47 months (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Detective Constable James Campbell said: "This investigation showed Reeve was a significant member of an organised crime group supplying crack cocaine and heroin. "He tried to distance himself from the operation by getting others to hold most of the drugs and complete the dealing, but the evidence of his involvement was clear. "Class A drug dealers trade in human misery – whether that be those exploited as part of the operation or those trapped in addiction. "We will continue to do all we can to identify people involved in supplying drugs in Cambridgeshire and bring them before the courts." summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Undercover female officers run county's streets in crackdown on harassment
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Police are targeting parts of Cambridgeshire after more than three-quarters of women in a survey said they had felt unsafe while running. Cambridgeshire Constabulary’s Operation Vexa is focused on preventing harassment and other offending in public spaces, with activity being directed towards locations where women reported experiencing problems. The first undercover operation was held in Huntingdon on Monday night when a group of female officers ran a circuit around the town, including Hinchingbrooke Park, which was one of the areas highlighted in the survey. Det Supt Dave Taylor gives his team a briefing before the first night of action in Huntingdon as part of Operation Vexa aimed at improving women's safety. (Image: Sarah Cliss) They were backed up by male officers in uniform in vehicles ready to act if the need arose during the hour-long exercise. The women completed their run without incident, but runner Det Supt Denise Harper said many women do not enjoy the same freedom. "When I was asked about this operation, I volunteered to do it straight away. I feel very passionately about keeping women and girls safe," she said. "It's not right that women and girls have to put certain measures in place, and think about their personal safety when they are trying to go about normal activities like exercising and running." Before the women took to their heels on the 3.2 mile circuitous run, they and their male colleagues were given a pre-operation briefing by Det Supt Dave Taylor, who is the leading officer responsible for protecting vulnerable people for Cambridgeshire. He explained to the team, alongside representatives from the media, the importance of Operation Vexa, which this week will see two further exercises in Cambridge and Peterborough. He said the operation aimed to prevent and tackle offending by identifying perpetrators before their behaviour escalates. Two of the female officers who ran the streets of Huntingdon in the first of three nights of action as part of Operation Vexa. (Image: Sarah Cliss) He said 2,149 women had responded to a public survey conducted in August with more than three-quarters saying they felt unsafe while running. Only three per cent had reported their concerns to police, he said. Det Supt Taylor said: "That means just because it is not being reported, it is not happening. I am hoping this operation will increase women's confidence reporting offences to the police." More than half, 54 per cent of those who took part in the survey, said they had experienced harassment and 64 per cent said they had been cat-called. Det Supt Denise Harper was among the women runners. She said she felt passionately about trying to improve the safety of women and girls on Cambridgeshire's streets. (Image: Sarah Cliss) The team will carry out a similar operation along Cambridge’s riverside corridor on Wednesday before moving to Peterborough on Friday. Det Supt Taylor said early evening and the hours after dark were key deployment times. But he warned that harassment can happen in daylight and that a lack of recorded incidents does not mean there is no risk. Det Supt Taylor said women’s experiences had shaped the operation. He said: “We are listening to runners’ experiences and using them for targeted prevention activity. “These operations are being carried out in areas where women who responded to the survey told us they have experienced problems. “Through this operation we want to target poor behaviour and criminal offences to enable women to be and feel safer in public spaces.” He described Operation Vexa as a “perpetrator-focused prevention and enforcement activity in public spaces”. The operation aims to prevent harm, deter harassment, identify repeat or escalating behaviour and intervene when offences or risks require police action. Officers will also use the deployments to build intelligence about concerning behaviour, people, vehicles, locations and times, while Det Supt Taylor emphasised the force takes women's safety seriously, and wants to increase their confidence that reports of harassment and sexualised behaviour will be taken seriously. The briefing listed possible incidents, including sexualised comments, gestures or approaches, being followed on foot, by bicycle, e-scooter or vehicle, stalking, assault and threatened violence. The plain-clothes officers were to report concerning behaviour, locations and risks while following agreed routes and staying in contact with colleagues throughout the run. Uniformed male officers were there to intervene if needed to safeguard people, make an arrest or preserve evidence. The force said its aim is to make Cambridgeshire’s public spaces safer by preventing harm where women have reported harassment or fear. Det Supt Taylor said women should not have to change where, when or how they exercise because they fear harassment. The operation also draws on the Angiolini Inquiry, which found that women routinely change their routes, plans and behaviour because of safety fears. The briefing said offences and concerning behaviour in public spaces can go unreported and unrecorded. It says non-contact and early-stage sexual behaviour should be taken seriously because it may be part of a pattern that repeats or escalates. Operation Vexa is part of the constabulary’s wider response to violence against women and girls. It aims to prevent offending and change perpetrators’ behaviour instead of asking women to change their routines.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Martin Lewis says £100 energy payment 'won't cover' January bill increase
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Martin Lewis has warned households to prepare for a huge jump in energy bills after Ofgem confirmed today (November 25) that the price cap will rise by 26% in January. The Money Saving Expert founder discussed the looming increase on his television show last night, warning that households could face an extra £160 to £170 in energy costs over just three months. His forecast proved remarkably close to the figure confirmed by regulator Ofgem this morning, with the new price cap set at £2,166 a year for a typical household using gas and electricity and paying by Direct Debit. This is an increase of £443 compared with the current annualised figure of £1,723, and will affect around 20 million households on variable tariffs. The confirmed increase means the price cap will reach its highest level in almost four years , putting further pressure on households already struggling with the cost of living. Martin also warned that the headline 26% increase would not affect every household in the same way, with gas users potentially facing a much bigger jump than electricity-only households. He explained that the increase was being driven primarily by the amount people pay for each unit of energy, rather than standing charges. Speaking on his show, he said: "But this is the really big thing to look at: standing charges not up that much. The unit rates, the amount you pay for each unit of gas and electricity, that is where the big rise is going to come from. "Electricity up 24%, gas up 37%." Tomorrow morning, Ofgem will announce the Jan-March energy price cap. It's likely to go up 26% but what after that? And does this mean you should fix? A clip from my Martin Lewis Money Show energy special tonight. Watch the full thing for far more help: https://t.co/Vcrj5Jywiw https://t.co/yR2mlzgyBw — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) November 24, 2026 The warning also comes after Chancellor John Healey announced a one-off £100 Household Energy Payment for around 20 million households in council tax bands A to D. The money is expected to start reaching eligible households in January 2027, but Martin warned it would not be enough to offset the increase in energy costs for most people. He said: "That is a rise of £160 to £170 just from January to the end of March, not 2027. Just January to the end of March. "The government energy support of £100 is paid in January for those in council tax bands A to D, it will not cover the rise for most households." The Government's £100 payment will therefore provide some help, but households could still face a significant shortfall. Martin also used last night's programme to examine whether households should consider moving away from their current variable energy tariff and locking into a fixed deal - but explained that every situation is different. He warned that energy prices could remain substantially higher throughout 2027, although he stressed that forecasts further into the year were much less certain. He said: "If those predictions are right, and this is pretty certain, it is going to be substantially higher throughout 2027 than it is now." Martin then highlighted the cheapest two-year fixed deal available at the time of his programme, which was around 2% more expensive than the existing price cap. That means customers choosing the deal would initially pay slightly more over the remaining weeks of the current price cap period. However, if the January forecasts proved correct, he said they could save more than 20% between January and March, with potentially further savings over the following year - but while it is good to consider options, circumstances will vary. Recommended reading : He was careful not to guarantee that switching would save money, saying: "I cannot tell you that fixing will save you money because I would need a crystal ball, but I can tell you the vast balance of probabilities means it will save you money over the next year." He added: "And if you are risk averse and want to avoid those January price hikes, fixing is the sensible option if you are on the price cap." As always, households should compare available tariffs against their own energy usage and check any exit fees before switching, as the cheapest deal will vary depending on where they live and how much energy they use.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP Winter Fuel Payment warning as pensioners say they have to wrap up in blankets
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Pensioners fear they will be forced to sit in freezing homes and wrap themselves in blankets this winter as household energy bills are set to jump by 26% in January. Charities have warned the price rise could leave older people struggling to afford to heat their homes - despite DWP winter fuel payments - while terminally ill people face the added worry of keeping vital medical equipment running and maintaining a warm environment. Age UK and palliative care charity Sue Ryder have both called for targeted energy support for those most at risk as the cost of keeping warm rises. One in five pensioner households in Great Britain are likely to be in “fuel stress” this winter, Age UK explained of its analysis. This means they will spend more than 10% of their after-tax household income on energy bills. Among the poorest households – those in the bottom 20% of the income distribution – almost half are expected to be in this position. The charity estimates the average pensioner household will spend £1 in every £14 of its income on gas and electricity at the forecast prices. Caroline Abrahams, charity director at Age UK, said the latest increase “will be deeply worrying for many older people who are already anxious about how they will afford to keep warm this winter”. While welcoming the Government's £100 energy payment for households from January, and winter fuel payments more broadly, she warned it was “simply not enough”. She added: “Another increase in energy bills risks pushing more households into hardship at a time when keeping warm is not a luxury, but an essential part of protecting their health. “Our recent analysis suggests that this winter is set to be extremely challenging for pensioners who are struggling to afford the energy they need. That’s why we believe ministers should introduce an emergency energy support package targeted at those households most at risk of cold homes, financial hardship and worsening health this winter.” Three pensioners in their 80s have spoken about the difficult choices they fear they will face as bills rise. Roger, who did not give his surname, described the 26% increase as “unbelievable” and said it “will lead to utter despair” for many older people. He works in a care home and said he can still “balance the books”, but added: “It worries me what might happen if I’m unable to work one day”. Sheila, who also did not give her surname, said she had not used her central heating for years and instead relied on a couple of electric heaters in whichever room she was in. She said that on particularly cold nights she was “often left sitting in a cold house, wrapping myself up in blankets”. A post shared by Martin Lewis (@martinlewismse) Age UK is encouraging older people on low incomes who are struggling with their bills to contact its free advice line on 0800 169 65 65 or visit www.ageuk.org.uk/money . The rise in energy costs could also have serious consequences for people living with terminal illnesses, Sue Ryder warned. Dr Paul Perkins, the charity's chief medical director, said the increase could “darken the precious time they have left”. Recommended reading: He said: “It may make them anxious and afraid, wondering how they’re going to keep themselves warm and keep their medical equipment going when they should be spending time making memories with loved ones. “Many rely on higher levels of heating to stop symptoms worsening, while others depend on vital electrical medical equipment, which in some cases is keeping them alive. All this leaves them with significantly increased costs. “Targeted help with energy costs would remove a substantial burden and allow people to make the most of the time they have left, not spending it watching their bank balance. Everyone deserves to live well and with dignity until the very end.” Tomorrow morning, Ofgem will announce the Jan-March energy price cap. It's likely to go up 26% but what after that? And does this mean you should fix? A clip from my Martin Lewis Money Show energy special tonight. Watch the full thing for far more help: https://t.co/Vcrj5Jywiw https://t.co/yR2mlzgyBw — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) November 24, 2026 Becca Stacey, from end-of-life care charity Marie Curie, said: “No energy support scheme specifically targets people living with terminal illness, despite extensive evidence of higher bills and significant financial hardship at the end of life.” She said support available through the £100 household energy payment, £150 Warm Home Discount and £300 Winter Fuel Payment “covers just a quarter of an average household’s energy bills”. Marie Curie is calling for a 50% energy social tariff for people living with a terminal illness. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 10 commonly misunderstood UK road signs - how many can you recognise?
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A blank red-ringed road sign bans vehicles, including bicycles unless they are being pushed. It is one of several signs whose meaning might not be immediately obvious to drivers. The Department for Transport groups traffic signs into three basic types: those that give orders, warn road users or provide information. Here are ten signs and what they mean, using guidance from the Highway Code and sign maker Hirst Signs. This board tells drivers that another sign is not currently in use, according to Hirst Signs. The company says it may cover a temporary speed limit, a roadworks warning or a diversion that is no longer in place. A sign showing a vehicle and an explosion means vehicles carrying explosives are prohibited. It is a restriction on what the vehicle is carrying, rather than a warning that other cars might explode. This triangular warning sign means slow-moving military vehicles are likely to be in or crossing the road ahead. Hirst Signs says the sign may appear near military bases. A red-bordered sign showing a horse-drawn vehicle means those vehicles are prohibited. It is different from a warning sign telling drivers that horse-drawn vehicles may be on the road. A warning sign with a lightning-shaped symbol alerts road users to an overhead electric cable. The Highway Code says an accompanying plate indicates the maximum height of vehicles that can pass safely. A white circle with a red border means no vehicles, rather than just no motor vehicles. The Highway Code says bicycles can pass if they are being pushed, but not ridden. Check any accompanying plate, which may give times or other qualifications to a restriction. A triangular sign featuring a toad warns drivers of a migratory toad crossing ahead. Hirst Signs says the warning is used where toads cross the road, particularly during breeding season. A triangular sign bearing the word “Ford” warns that the road crosses a stream or river. Water levels can rise in poor weather, so a crossing that is normally shallow may become hazardous. A blue circle with a red border and red cross means no stopping on a clearway. The restriction applies to the main carriageway at any time. A blue circular sign with two white arrows means vehicles may pass on either side to reach the same destination. Unlike a keep-left sign, it allows a choice of which side to use.

Plans have been submitted to expand a community hub in a Huntingdonshire village into a nurse-led care home. A retrospective application to Huntingdonshire District Council (HDC) seeks to change the use of the property at 41 Station Road in Catworth from a home to a small residential care home and day centre, known as Little Orchard. The care home would provide permanent accommodation for six residents, each with their own room, and communal areas, with nursing staff on duty 24 hours a day. The previous use of the property was a 7-bedroom dwelling with associated parking and garage (class C3), but the plans would see the use change to class C2. The planning statement submitted with the application, from operator Golden Community, said the facility would offer companionship, activities, nutritional support, and nurse-led wellbeing oversight. All parking associated with the development would be accommodated within the site, which has nine parking spaces, including four staff spaces, three visitor spaces, one accessible space, and a dedicated ambulance bay. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: CQC recognises significant improvements across East of England Ambulance Service
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An ambulance service has been rated “good” after inspectors found major improvements in staffing and patient access. The East of England Ambulance Service NHS Trust (EEAST) welcomed the Care Quality Commission’s (CQC) latest findings on its Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) and Urgent and Emergency Care (UEC) services. Inspectors rated the trust’s EOC “Good” overall and in all five areas assessed: safe, effective, caring, responsive and well-led. Urgent and Emergency Care was also rated “Good” in all five areas, with the CQC praising improvements in safety, responsiveness and leadership. The findings represent a turnaround from the regulator's previous inspection in November 2024, when concerns were raised about staffing levels and how quickly patients could access services. Following that inspection, the CQC served a Section 29A Warning Notice after finding the trust in breach of regulations relating to staffing and safe care and treatment. Read more 10 pubs in Cambridgeshire you have to visit at least once Martin Lewis on cheapest fixes available now as energy bills to rocket in January Cold Weather Payment of £25 a week to help thousands with winter heating bills Prominence regime risks your right to choose your news Undercover female officers run county's streets in crackdown on harassment Inspectors said the service lacked enough staff with the right skills, qualifications and experience, while call waiting times fell below national standards. During the latest inspection, however, the regulator found improvements had been made to call handling and dispatch times and that the EOC was no longer in breach of those regulations. The CQC also found faster ambulance responses in Urgent and Emergency Care and said the service had met the warning notice’s requirements. Inspectors praised progress in staffing, mandatory training, appraisals, safeguarding, call handling, dispatch and ambulance response times. The CQC inspected the trust’s three Emergency Operations Centres in Bedford, Norwich and Chelmsford and spoke to call handlers, dispatchers, clinical co-ordinators and managers. Inspectors also examined six ambulance bases and held seven focus groups as part of their assessment of Urgent and Emergency Care, speaking to around 105 members of staff. They also accompanied ambulance crews responding to urgent calls and reviewed policies and procedures. EEAST provides emergency ambulance services 24 hours a day across Bedfordshire, Hertfordshire, Essex, Norfolk, Suffolk, Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, covering around 7,500 square miles and a population of more than 6.2 million people. The CQC did not speak directly to patients because its Emergency Operations Centre inspection had no patient-facing element. Inspectors praised improvements in workforce capacity and performance, including the trust’s Cardiac Arrest Desk initiative. Neill Moloney, chief executive of EEAST, said: "These findings recognise the enormous amount of work colleagues across EEAST have put into improving our services for patients. "The progress reflected in these reports is a testament to their professionalism, commitment and determination to deliver high-quality care every day. "We are proud that the CQC has recognised these improvements." Mr Moloney admitted more work was needed, particularly to make leadership and management consistently effective across Urgent and Emergency Care. He added: "We also recognise the areas of continued focus identified by the CQC, particularly around ensuring leadership and management arrangements are consistently effective across all parts of our Urgent and Emergency Care service, and we remain committed to building on the progress we have made." The earlier Section 29A notice also covered failures in investigating and mitigating controlled-drug incidents, service culture and using staff feedback to improve services.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Low-quality CCTV' delayed identification of Hunts train stabber by 18 hours
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Police took 18 hours to identify Anthony Williams as a suspect in a knife attack because of “low-quality” CCTV, an officer said. British Transport Police defended their handling of the attack on Isaiah Idris, now 18, who Williams knifed on a Docklands Light Railway train approaching Pontoon Dock in London. Williams asked the teenager “are you beefing with the devil?” before slashing his face at about 12.43am on November 1, 2025. CCTV of Williams on the DLR (Image: BTP/Press Association) Williams, 33, was identified as a suspect at 2.52pm, 14 hours later. Officers found he was registered to two addresses. Four hours later, officers reached Waltham Cross in Hertfordshire but found they had gone to the wrong address. By the time officers reached Waltham Cross, Williams had left his Peterborough address and was less than an hour from attacking a packed LNER train. Detective Superintendent Sam Blackburn, of British Transport Police’s Major, Serious and Organised Crime Unit, would not say whether police missed chances to stop Williams before the LNER attack. He said “low-quality CCTV” had hampered efforts to identify the knifeman who stabbed Mr Idris. “The insufficient quality of the CCTV on board that (DLR) train and at Pontoon Dock meant we couldn’t identify Anthony Williams maybe as quickly as we’d like,” said Mr Blackburn. (Image: PA) He said officers began planning Williams’s arrest once they identified him as the suspect. “There were two addresses we could have gone to,” Mr Blackburn said. “Those two addresses were Waltham Cross (in Hertfordshire) and Peterborough (in Cambridgeshire). “Intelligence supported our attendance first at the Waltham Cross address because it’s closer to Pontoon Dock, which is a factor. “But also the intelligence supported us through financial checks on Anthony Williams which linked him to that Waltham Cross address.” He said officers reached the Waltham Cross address at about 6.45pm on November 1, 2025. Mr Blackburn said it was “important to note” Williams had “left his home address in Peterborough” at 6.15pm that evening. “So even if we’d gone to a Peterborough address, we chose the Waltham Cross address, either address Mr Williams wouldn’t have been present,” he said. The officer continued: “By the time we’ve carried out our inquiry at the Waltham Cross address the Huntingdon attack has already happened.” The LNER train left Peterborough at about 7.29pm and made an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon at 7.44pm after Williams attacked. Mr Blackburn said Williams had boarded a DLR service at West Silvertown in London before the attack on Mr Idris. “On boarding that service the doors have shut and Mr Williams has almost immediately attacked a 17-year-old boy called Isaiah Idris,” he said. “Isaiah was seriously injured. “It’s not violence we normally see on the network and so we responded accordingly. “We responded within 10 minutes, us and other emergency services partners, to that incident and we began that serious investigation of trying to obtain evidence that was available to us.” An officer has explained why police took 18 hours to identify the train stabbing suspect (Image: PA) Mr Blackburn said the initial “CCTV harvesting wasn’t successful”. “But we looked at widening that search within those early hours, extending that search to other stations utilising our partners within TfL (Transport for London) and eventually we managed to obtain an image of the individual at Poplar, a completely different station to where the offence took place,” he said. “It was using that image that we then managed to identify Anthony Williams.” He described the response to Mr Idris’s attack as “proportionate and professional”. “We did everything we could to identify Williams as soon as we possibly could with the information that we had, with the CCTV that was available to us,” Mr Blackburn said. “It is difficult and I don’t want to speculate, but low-quality CCTV does limit us then in our ability to be able to identify individuals. “When we see the high-quality CCTV as we have seen on the LNER service itself and at other stations in London the process of identification becomes a lot easier.” On October 31, 2025, British Transport Police received a text report about a man “acting erratically and intoxicated” on a train travelling from Peterborough to Stevenage. The man was Williams, though this was not known at the time. Mr Blackburn said British Transport Police officers went to Stevenage station and “noticed the male who was on the tracks”. CCTV footage issued by British Transport Police showing Anthony Williams boarding a Thameslink train at Stevenage station (Image: BTP/Press Association) “Those were live tracks,” he said. “The officers have to consider their own safety and the safety of others. “They removed the power from the tracks and then conducted a full search to try and find that individual, a male we didn’t know at that stage was Anthony Williams. “Following that search it was a negative result but we did what we could in that instance in relation to responding to the information we were given.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Huntingdon train stabbing: Audio of call between driver and signaller released
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The driver of a train on which 10 people were stabbed told a signaller he had “a report of a person with a knife on board” in newly released audio of a call between the two staff. Driver Andrew Johnson previously told jurors at Cambridge Crown Court that someone activated an alarm on the London-bound service and he heard “someone screaming ‘there’s a knifeman stabbing people’” over an intercom. Nine passengers and one member of on-board staff, Samir Zitouni, were stabbed by Anthony Williams during the attack on the high-speed service on November 1 last year. The LNER train, which had departed Peterborough at 7.29pm, was next scheduled to stop at Stevenage, with the journey due to take 30 minutes. Mr Johnson said in evidence that he decided to stop the service sooner at Huntingdon and “it just came instinctively, I never really thought about it”. The train made its unscheduled stop at Huntingdon at 7.44pm. He earlier told the trial that the service was travelling at 122mph around Abbots Ripton when an alarm went off “which indicated someone was trying to open one of the passenger doors”. He contacted a signaller after he heard over an intercom that there was a knifeman attacking people, and he heard a scream he described as “terrifying”. In newly released audio, Mr Johnson tells signaller Rob Pape: “Hello signaller… I’ve got an egress happened. I’ve got a report of a person with a knife on board. “I’m going to stop at Huntingdon.” The signaller tells Mr Johnson he will “get you in on the slow” line as the pair work to bring the train in safely. Mr Johnson asks Mr Pape: “Can you also inform police immediately?” The signaller replies: “Yes – so you’ve got a report of a passenger with a knife on board.” The driver says: “Yes, please”. The signaller says: “There’s a train in platform two at the moment, as soon as that departs, I’ll get you into platform two”. Mr Johnson replies: “Yes, and inform police immediately, thank you very much.” The driver said, in his evidence at trial: “My mind was completely focused on one thing and that was getting the train to Huntingdon.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Ryanair quietly makes major change to seating policy affecting all passengers
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A major change to Ryanair's booking system means passengers will now be assigned free seats just three hours before departure. Previously, travellers using the 'free' seat option could see their assigned seat 24 hours before their flight. The low-cost carrier confirmed that the update quietly took effect at the end of October. A Ryanair spokesperson said: "The timing of the allocation of free random seats is determined at all times by the airline. "We moved this allocation from 24 hours to over three hours (prior to departure) when we cut across to our winter schedule at the end of Oct last. "The reason for this time change is to allow those passengers who wish to select their preferred seat more time to do so. "We had a number of complaints this summer that passengers could not book their preferred seat on the day of travel as it had been already randomly allocated as a free seat up to 24 hours prior to departure. "Passengers who choose a free of charge random seat clearly don’t mind where they sit, and their digital boarding pass is automatically updated between three to four hours prior to departure, which is well before they arrive at either their departure airport or their boarding gate." Read More Under the previous system, passengers were given the chance to upgrade, which would involve paying for a seat of their choice. Now, passengers wanting to guarantee a seat choice—such as an aisle or window—must pay to select it, or take their chances with a randomly assigned seat closer to departure. The change means those who opt not to pay will only find out where they are seated a few hours before their flight, instead of the day before. What do you think of the policy change? If you live alone, or nobody else in your household qualifies for the Winter Fuel Payment, you will receive: If you live with someone else who also qualifies and neither of you receives certain means-tested benefits, the payment is: If you and your partner jointly claim Pension Credit, Universal Credit or income-related ESA, one of you will receive: If you receive one of these benefits but are not part of a joint claim, you will receive £200 or £300 depending on your date of birth. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Confirmation that 'debacle' car park scheme will not progress welcomed
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Confirmation that a 'shambolic' scheme to build housing developments on car parks will not be progressed has been welcomed in Huntingdonshire. Proposals to transform Tebbutts Road car park in St Neots, Princes Street car park in Huntingdon and the old cattle market in St Ives into developments with up to 80 homes were first unveiled to the public in August. The plans were put forward by property developer Capital & Centric in partnership with Huntingdonshire District Council (HDC). The news sparked fury among residents concerned over the potential loss of parking spaces in the town centres. After a series of public consultations and around 90% of residents who were asked opposing the scheme, it was revealed that the developments were "highly unlikely" to go ahead. The St Neots public consultation in August (Image: Emily Stevens) At an extraordinary cabinet meeting of HDC at Pathfinder House on November 24, councillors assured the public that they will no be progressing the regeneration projects in their current form beyond Gateway 1. Cllr Ross Martin was first to speak, calling the scheme a "debacle" and "shambolic". He also called for a clear decision to be made that evening to reassure residents, despite it not technically being needed. The way the council operates means the scheme naturally comes to a close after Gateway 1 and a decision is needed to progress to Gateway 2, as there is no automatic commitment to do so. Cllr Liam Dewey-Beckett said: "We are not going any further with these schemes." Council leader Cllr Sarah Conboy also assured the public the project would not be moving forward. An independent review on the funding for the Capital & Centric projects will continue to be conducted, as HDC voted to review the funds after £1m was spent. The news that the plans will not progress has been welcomed by the Huntingdon Business Improvement District (BID). Paul Sweeney, chief executive officer of BID Huntingdon First, said: "The last few months have been incredibly difficult to navigate both personally as a resident of Huntingdon and professionally as the CEO of the Business Improvement District representing 300 businesses in Huntingdon town centre. "However last night’s decision at the cabinet meeting, which I attended in person, puts a welcome end to months of uncertainty for many."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A UK greeting card and party supplies company has entered administration after 42 years in business. Tiger Feet began as Budget Greeting Cards in 1984, offering greeting cards, partyware, balloons, stationery, and toys (before being rebranded in 2024). The company has since developed into a major UK wholesaler supplying more than 20,000 products to independent retailers across the UK and Ireland. A post shared by Tiger Feet | UK Wholesale Balloons, Cards, Party & More.. (@tigerfeetltd) Tiger Feet operates online and from seven cash and carry sites located across the UK and Ireland: Now, after 42 years in business, Tiger Feet has entered administration. Anthony Collier and Richard Goodall of FRP Advisory Trading Limited were appointed joint administrators on November 17. In a statement published by Business Sale Report (BSR), the administrators said: "Tiger Feet has an established position in the wholesale market and a long history of supplying independent retailers across the UK and Ireland. "Our priority is to maintain trading while we continue to explore options available for the business, we would encourage any interested parties to contact us as soon as possible." A notice on the Tiger Feet website confirms it is in administration and continues to trade under the management of the joint administrators. A post shared by Tiger Feet | UK Wholesale Balloons, Cards, Party & More.. (@tigerfeetltd) The statement reads: "Tiger Feet Ltd UK (01798438) entered Administration on 17 November 2026. "The affairs, business and property of the Company are being managed by the appointed Joint Administrators Anthony Collier and Richard Goodall both of FRP Advisory Trading Limited. "The business is continuing to trade. "The Joint Administrators act as agents of the Company and without personal liability." Tiger Feet has warned customers it is no longer offering refunds or returns, stating that "all sales are final." Customers have been advised to check goods carefully before purchase at cash and carry branches, as all items are sold "as seen and as available." For online orders, customers are instructed to report missing or damaged items within two days of receipt. The company added: "Tiger Feet Limited does not provide refunds, returns, exchanges, credit notes, warranty claims, repair or replacement services." It has been a tough year for the UK high street, with several retailers entering administration or liquidation and others announcing widespread store closures. Poundland has filed a notice to appoint administrators, putting the future of its 150 stores and 11,000 employees at risk. TG Jones and the British Heart Foundation will also be closing around 150 stores each across the UK. Wynsors World of Shoes is shutting 17 stores across the UK, with closing down sales already underway at several affected branches. UK entertainment retailer Zavvi has ceased trading after nearly 20 years, having collapsed into administration for a second time. Australian stationery retailer Typo is also set to pull out of the UK in 2027, closing all its stores and ending online trading. Other retailers have been forced to close stores this year, including: Several UK travel companies have ceased trading or entered administration in 2026, including: Wayfairer Travel Limited has also suspended all services "until further notice" as it looks to appoint an administrator. Meanwhile, five UK airlines have fallen into administration or liquidation: UK delivery company Yodel was phased out completely in July after being acquired by InPost. Iconic fashion brand Nasty Gal has also shut down its website after being sold by Debenhams in a deal worth around £12 million (US$16 million). summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Can you be sure he intended to kill?' judge asks jurors in train attack trial
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The judge in the trial of a knifeman accused of attempted murder on a train in Cambridgeshire has told the jury to consider whether they can be sure he intended to kill. Several people were injured on an LNER train from Doncaster to London King's Cross on November 1, 2025, which was forced to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon. Anthony Williams, 33, denies 14 counts of attempted murder: ten of them in relation to the LNER train, three said to have happened in Peterborough and one at Pontoon Dock DLR station in London. Anthony Williams is accused of 14 counts of attempted murder (Image: British Transport) The judge, Mr Justice Calver, began his summing up of the case at Cambridge Crown Court on November 23. In the case of count one, Williams is accused of attempting to murder a 14-year-old boy, who legally cannot be named, by a footbridge near Henry Penn Walk in Peterborough on October 31, 2025. The boy, who was walking there with a friend, was treated in hospital for a single stab wound two to three centimetres to the left of his breastbone. Mr Justice Calver told the jury that while the prosecution relies on the force and location of the stab wound showing intent to kill, the defence suggests a single stab wound does not show intention to kill. In the case of count two, Williams is accused of attempting to murder Dawid Taborski in the same area of Henry Penn Walk. Mr Justice Calver told the jury Mr Taborski said "I literally ran for my life", adding that prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC suggests this showed clear intent to kill as it was only because the victim was young, fit and ran for his life that he was not struck. He said that defence barrister Gillian Jones relies on the fact there was no physical contact, he did not attempt to run after Mr Taborski and his friend and the incident was consistent with Williams' psychotic state. In the case of count three, Williams is accused of attempting to murder William Ogelby in the Rail World car park in Peterborough. Mr Justice Calver told the jury that Mr Ogelby said: "I thought he was going to kill me" and added that the defendant tried to go for his chest. He said the defence suggests the victim's perception that he was going to be killed "should be considered with caution" as this does not show what was going on in the defendant's mind, and that the jury cannot be sure he intended to kill. The court heard that Williams arrived at Ritzy Barbers in Peterborough, which is around a ten minute walk away, at 7.20pm. Mr Justice Calver said the court has heard that Williams was waving a knife around inside the shop and the incident is captured on CCTV. Williams has pleaded guilty to affray regarding this incident. CCTV footage shows Anthony Williams brandishing a knife inside the Ritzy Barbers in Peterborough (Image: BTP/Press Association) CCTV footage issued by British Transport Police showing Anthony Williams brandishing a knife inside the Ritzy Barbers in Peterborough (Image: BTP/Press Association) The court heard that Williams then got a taxi back to his home address and threw the knife into his back garden, before travelling to Peterborough train station at 8.17pm and catching a southbound train to Stevenage. He stole knives from an Asda store in Stevenage before getting on another train to London and subsequent Underground services, jurors heard. CCTV footage shows Anthony Williams in the Asda store in Stevenage (Image: BTP/Press Association) In the case of count four, Williams is accused of attempting to murder 17-year-old Isaiah Idris on a DLR train at Pontoon Dock. The judge told the jury that the prosecution suggest Williams waited for the train doors to close and the striking of Isaiah's head shows intent to kill. However, Mr Justice Calver added, the defence dispute this, suggesting it was a quick slashing action and Williams was likely suffering from auditory hallucinations. CCTV footage dated issued by British Transport Police shows Anthony Williams with a knife on board a DLR train travelling towards Pontoon Dock in London (Image: BTP/Press Association) Continuing his summing up of the case, Mr Calver said the court heard Williams travelled back to Peterborough on trains, making stops at Stevenage and Hitchin, and returned to his home address before boarding the LNER service to London King's Cross at 7.26pm on November 1, 2025. Williams boarding a train at Stevenage (Image: BTP/Press Association) The remaining ten counts of attempted murder concern passengers on the train, namely Jonathan Gjoshe, Sachin Balakrishnan, David Presland, Scott Bletcher, Scott Green, Kevin Deely, Stephen Crean, Raza Aslam, Michael Paffett and Samir Zitouni. In each case, Mr Calver reminded jurors that they must prove intent to kill. Williams has already admitted to wounding with intent. Mr Calver asked jurors: "When he stabbed Mr Green three times with the knife, can you be sure he intended to kill him?" He told the court that prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC called the final three counts "one continuous attack with the intention to kill each of these victims." CCTV footage shows Anthony Williams brandishing a knife on an LNER Doncaster to London service (Image: BTP/Press Association) Dr Bernard Chin, a consultant forensic psychiatrist, diagnosed Williams with schizophrenia and said while he was likely suffering from "thought broadcast", where one experiences thoughts being said out loud to them, among other symptoms, he is not clinically insane. The jury of nine men and three women retired to consider their verdict at around 2.50pm on Monday, November 23. Mr Justice Calver told the jury: "What you must do is consider all of the evidence separately in relation to each count. "You must not speculate about what the evidence may tell you." Mr Calver said that jurors are under no time pressure and should take as much time as they need to come to a decision. The trial continues.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP Cold Weather Payments - Who gets the money and how does it work?
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: With temperatures set to plummet across Norfolk, the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) may soon be issuing Cold Weather Payments to eligible households. The payments are available to some people receiving certain benefits when the area where they live experiences a sustained period of freezing weather. But a brief cold snap or a single freezing night will not necessarily lead to a payment. Here is everything you need to know about Cold Weather Payments, including who qualifies, how they are triggered and when the money should arrive. Cold Weather Payments are intended to help eligible households with additional costs during sustained periods of very cold weather. A payment is triggered when the average temperature in a person’s area is recorded as, or forecast to be, 0C or below for seven consecutive days. The scheme runs between November 1 and March 31, 2027. It is important to note that the payment is based on the average temperature across a full seven-day period, rather than an individual cold day or night. Eligible recipients receive £25 for each qualifying seven-day period of very cold weather. This means someone could receive more than one payment during the winter if there are several qualifying periods. For example, one qualifying seven-day period would result in a £25 payment. Two qualifying periods would result in £50 and three qualifying periods would result in £75. Cold Weather Payments do not affect a person’s entitlement to other benefits. People may qualify if they receive one of the following: However, receiving one of these benefits does not automatically mean every claimant will qualify. The precise conditions depend on the benefit being received. People receiving Pension Credit will usually qualify for Cold Weather Payments. If a qualifying spell of cold weather is recorded in their area, the payment should be issued automatically. People will usually qualify if they receive income-related Employment and Support Allowance and are in either the work-related activity group or support group. Those who are not in either group may still qualify if they have: Universal Credit claimants will usually qualify if neither they nor their partner is employed or considered “gainfully self-employed”. They must also meet at least one of the following conditions: Someone is likely to be considered gainfully self-employed if self-employment is their main job, they work regularly and they expect to make a profit. Universal Credit claimants can also qualify if their award includes a disabled child amount. In this situation, it does not matter whether they or their partner are working, self-employed or unemployed.
