summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Wetherspoon rolls out change to policy in UK pubs after trial
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Wetherspoon is introducing a change across its UK pubs after a successful trial at 88 venues. The pub chain is changing how it maintains urinals, using a biological treatment called URIZAP, which is designed to tackle the build-up that can cause blockages and smells in men's toilets. The change covers its pubs in the UK and Ireland, and the company told the Mirror that the rollout was completed around July. It is a change to washroom maintenance rather than a new rule that customers must follow. The treatment comes from Thrive, a Lancashire-based company which began in a Lancaster University laboratory in 2019, according to Wetherspoon's magazine. Its scientists developed the product as an alternative to chemical cleaners used to deal with uric scale and blockages in urinals. The formulation works by digesting uric acid build-up and can be used in all types of urinals. Thrive says the treatment clears urinals and pipes at source instead of simply masking odours. Wetherspoon says the product is suited to busy washrooms and reduces the need for strong-smelling chemical cleaners traditionally used in such venues. In its winter and spring 2026/27 magazine, the chain said pubs using the treatment had reported a marked reduction in plumbing maintenance visits. The Mirror reported that staff at the 88 trial pubs noted improved odours, fewer maintenance issues and the removal of scale build-up from urinal pipework. Wetherspoon says the aim is to deal with problems before they arise, rather than waiting until a blockage needs attention. That matters during busy periods, when a urinal problem can pull employees away from serving customers or other work, according to the company. The chain says the treatment's continuous action can free staff to concentrate on other tasks and help avoid urinals being shut off at busy times. Wetherspoon also links the change to its sustainability ambitions, saying reduced reliance on chemical-based cleaners means fewer single-use plastic containers and lower volumes of chemicals entering wastewater. The company says the treatment allows it to make use of low-flush systems already installed in its washrooms to reduce water consumption. It has not given figures in the magazine for the amount of water, plastic or chemicals saved by the switch. Wetherspoon said: "Urinal issues generally demand attention at the worst-possible moments, pulling staff away from serving customers or other duties to deal with issues. URIZAP's continuous action frees staff to focus on other tasks." Vince Graham, chief executive of Thrive, said: "Wetherspoon leads the way on washroom standards. We're proud that one of Britain's best-known hospitality businesses has chosen URIZAP to take that standard even further, improving facilities for customers and staff." For customers, the intended result is fewer odours and fewer occasions when urinals need to be taken out of use for maintenance.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Center Parcs introduces new £5 rule for all guests at UK holiday parks
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Center Parcs has introduced a new rule at all of its UK holiday parks. Guests will now have to pay a deposit to reserve tables at resort restaurants. A new policy, which came into effect across all its resorts on November 16, requires guests to pay a £5 deposit per person when booking a restaurant. The change is designed to reduce no-shows and ensure that tables are kept full. A post shared by Center Parcs UK (@centerparcsuk) A statement on the Center Parcs website read: "To help us provide the best possible experience for our guests and make sure our restaurants are available for as many guests as possible, all restaurant bookings now require a deposit at the time of booking. "This will come into effect for all breaks starting from 16th November 2026 onwards. "If your plans change, you can cancel more than 48 hours before your reservation, and we’ll refund your deposit in full. "If you cancel within 48 hours of your reservation, the deposit is non-refundable. "Please note that restaurant bookings have their own cancellation terms, which are different from those for activity bookings." Affected venues include Huck’s American Bar & Grill (all sites), Rajinda Pradesh (all sites), The Pancake House (all sites) and Foresters’ Inn at Longleat and Elveden. The deposit is fully refundable if the booking is cancelled more than 48 hours in advance. Guests are still welcome to walk in without a reservation, but availability cannot be guaranteed. It is not the only change at Center Parcs sites in the UK in 2026, with its crèche services axed earlier this year. The price was around £30 a session and was for kids between three months and three years, for up to three hours. However, the service is no longer offered at any of its five UK resorts. A spokesperson for Center Parcs said at the time: "We’re always looking to review and evolve the guest experience. We have made the decision to remove the crèche activity from our breaks, to reflect guest feedback and limited demand for this particular activity. "Crèche sessions are one of more than 20 activities available within our Activity Den and our other activities will continue to run as normal." There are five Center Parcs holiday villages in the UK. The company's first village opened near to Sherwood Forest, Nottinghamshire, in 1987. Work has finally got underway to fix an “eyesore” gap in a town’s high street that has been filled with scaffolding for the past four years. Despite planning permission being granted, redevelopment of the former Barclays Bank in St Ives has faced delays, sparking action from the civic society. They demanded Huntingdonshire District Council take enforcement action to force the developer to start work on the scaffold-covered 11-12 The Pavement. But earlier this month the action group said scaffolders appeared at the site to fix the structure with the site owner confirming the issues delaying work had been resolved. A representative of the “Action for 11-12 The Pavement” campaign, which has now rebranded to “Action for St Ives” on Facebook said the development was “very positive”. He said: “We have had a response from the receivers who have confirmed that the difficulties they were facing have been resolved, and they expect to complete the project by August next year if they can. “The campaign is going to calm down now because we feel there’s not much to do now everything seems to be resolved. “It was a leap of faith for the civic society, who have generally worked behind the scenes, to use social media in this way – we thought this particular problem needed some action. “I would like to think we have focused attention from all those involved and managed to get work to restart, but we don’t know.” The barriers around the building have also since been painted with festive imagery in the run-up to Christmas – improving the appearance of the neglected site. A spokesperson for HDC said: “The developers continue to work towards recommencing construction on site. “We continue to monitor the site as part of an active investigation. The developers have advised that improvements are due to be made to the scaffolding imminently. “Information previously shared about anticipated works was provided by the site owner and was not a commitment made by Huntingdonshire District Council.” The Action for St Ives group said they will be redirecting their focus to other issues such as protecting heritage assets in the town. They said none of St Ives’ historic heritage assets are currently listed for protection and are asking the public to help nominate local landmarks.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Two men remain in custody after violent Peterborough jewellers robbery
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Two men arrested in connection with a violent robbery at a jewellers remain in custody as police continue their investigation. The robbery took place at Lala Jewellers on Gladstone Street, Peterborough, at around 11.50am on November 14. Six men entered the store, assaulted two employees, and emptied the shelves before fleeing in separate vehicles. A 50-year-old employee suffered serious injuries during the robbery and remains in hospital in a life-threatening condition. The other employee, a 30-year-old man, sustained minor injuries. Two men, aged 43 and 20, were arrested in Bradford on suspicion of robbery and transported to custody at Milton Police Station. Both men remain in custody. Detective Inspector Tracy Sawyer said: "This is a very concerning incident which has left one man seriously injured and we are carrying out extensive enquiries to identify those responsible. "We would like to hear from anyone who was in the Gladstone Street area at around the time of the robbery and saw anything suspicious either before or after the incident. "We would also urge anyone with CCTV, doorbell or dashcam footage from the area which may have captured something relevant to please get in touch." Officers are working closely with the community and increased patrols will be taking place in the area over the coming days and the weekend. They are particularly keen to speak to anyone who may have witnessed suspicious activity in or around Gladstone Street before or after the incident. Police are also appealing to the public to check any CCTV, doorbell, or dashcam footage that may have captured relevant activity. Anyone with information is urged to contact police online at www.cambs.police.uk or by calling 101 and quoting reference 35/88602/26. Information can also be provided anonymously through Crimestoppers by calling 0800 555111. Detectives said they are pursuing multiple lines of enquiry and remain committed to bringing those responsible to justice.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Do not eat' warning as high street chain recalls sweets containing pieces of metal
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Candy canes sold by Card Factory are being recalled because they may contain pieces of metal. The Food Standards Agency (FSA) has advised customers not to eat the affected red and white sweets and to return them for a full refund. The recall covers boxes of 12 Candy Canes, Red & White, with product code 2150010, batch code M01S06072601 and a best before date of June 6, 2028. Card Factory's customer notice says the item was on sale in stores between November 2 and November 6. Wednesday 18 November 2026 - Card Factory recalls Red and White Candy Canes because they may contain pieces of metal #FoodAlert https://t.co/OKxYZ6axt6 https://t.co/oresrSrE8C — Food Standards Agency (@foodgov) November 18, 2026 The FSA said the possible presence of pieces of metal made the product unsafe to eat. Shoppers who have bought the candy canes covered by the notice should return them to the store where they were bought, according to the agency. Card Factory said in its notice: "Card Factory are recalling the above product due to a risk that some products may contain metal." "Please stop using the item immediately and return the product to a Card Factory store, where you will be given a full refund." The retailer also apologised for any inconvenience caused and asked customers with further enquiries to contact customerservice@cardfactory.co.uk . The FSA said point-of-sale notices would be displayed in all retail stores selling the product, explaining the reason for the recall and what customers should do. The recall notice identifies the product as Candy Canes, Red & White, sold in a box of 12, rather than a recall of all candy canes. Customers can use the product code 2150010 and batch code M01S06072601, alongside the June 6, 2028 best before date, to identify the product listed by the FSA. The agency's advice is not to eat the product if you have bought it and instead to take it back for a full refund. Card Factory's own notice similarly tells customers to stop using the item immediately and return it to one of its stores. For further information about the recall, customers can contact the company's customer service team at customerservice@cardfactory.co.uk , the FSA said. If there is a problem with a food product that means it should not be sold, then it might be 'withdrawn' (taken off the shelves) or 'recalled' (when customers are asked to return the product). The FSA issues Product Withdrawal Information Notices and Product Recall Information Notices to let consumers and local authorities know about problems associated with food. In some cases, a 'Food Alert for Action' is issued. This provides local authorities with details of specific actions to be taken on behalf of consumers.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: HMRC has revealed how to spot scammers impersonating them after they received nearly 50,000 reports of attempts to dupe Brits last year. It states they received a total of 48,119 reports of scams where fraudsters impersonated the department in the past 12 months. How to spot if HMRC message is real or scam - as 50,000 cases reported (Image: Kennedy News/HMRC press release) They say those who file Self Assessment tax returns are 'often targeted' near the deadline and 1,704 scams relating to it were reported in the past year. HMRC say criminals often do this as Brits are more likely to expect communication such as emails and texts before the January 31 deadline. They listed three key actions that HMRC will never take to help Brits spot when scammers are impersonating them. They say they will never 'contact customers by email, text or phone call to tell them they are due a refund or ask them to claim one'. The other two are at they will never 'ask for personal or financial information by email or text message' or 'leave threatening voicemails about legal action or an arrest'. HMRC added that last year they received 900 reports about a single scam and it used email attachments to direct Brits to a fake government page. They were reportedly told they had unclaimed tax repayments and were told to verify their ID and payment details for fraudsters to use. Lucy Pike, HMRC’s chief security officer, said: "We know Self Assessment is a prime target for scammers who use fake tax refund offers to trick people into handing over personal and financial information. "You can check if contact from HMRC is genuine on GOV.UK before taking any action. "Reporting scams helps us shut them down and protect others."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Pension Credit to rise to £247.30 a week as 'poorest pensioners' get DWP income boost
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Millions of pensioners are set to receive a boost to their income from April, with the full new State Pension rising by around £490 a year and the basic State Pension increasing by approximately £375. Pension Credit - paid to the poorest pensioners - is also set to rise, with the Standard Minimum Guarantee increasing by the same 3.9% from April. The increases were confirmed by the Government as part of its annual benefits uprating, with both the basic and full new State Pension rates going up by 3.9%. The rise follows the Government's Triple Lock commitment, which means the State Pension increases each year by whichever is highest of inflation, average earnings growth or 2.5%. The 3.9% increase is based on growth in average weekly earnings in the year to May-July 2026. For single pensioners, this will take the weekly amount to £247.30, while couples will see their guarantee rise to £377.40 a week. The Government said the increase would help protect the incomes of the poorest pensioners. Pension Credit is a means-tested benefit for people who have reached State Pension age and live in England, Scotland or Wales. You can qualify if your weekly income is below the set threshold, although you may still be eligible if your income is higher and you have certain additional circumstances, such as a disability, caring responsibilities or housing costs. The current income thresholds are: These are the current rates, rather than the new April 2027 rates. If you have a partner You must include your partner on your application. You can qualify if both of you have reached State Pension age, or if one of you receives Housing Benefit for people over State Pension age. A partner means your husband, wife or civil partner if you live together, or someone you live with as a couple. What counts as income? The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) takes account of your income, including: Some benefits are not counted, including Attendance Allowance, Personal Independence Payment (PIP), Disability Living Allowance, Child Benefit, Housing Benefit and Winter Fuel Payments. What about savings? Having savings does not automatically rule you out of Pension Credit. For example, someone with £11,000 in savings has an additional £2 a week counted as income. You may still qualify if you have more than £10,000 in savings, but the amount you receive could be reduced. You can check whether you qualify using the Government's Pension Credit information and eligibility guidance. Recommended reading: The key increases confirmed for April are: Not all pension-related payments will rise by the same amount. Other State Pension and benefit rates covered by the Government's statutory review will increase by 3.5%, in line with the Consumer Prices Index (CPI) inflation rate in the year to September 2026. This includes Additional State Pension and the maximum amount of Pension Credit Savings Credit. The 3.5% increase also applies to most working-age benefits, benefits supporting people with additional needs arising from disability, and statutory payments such as Statutory Sick Pay and Statutory Maternity Pay.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cheapest supermarket for Christmas dinner 2026 revealed - with some half the price
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Families could pay almost double for their Christmas dinner depending on which supermarket they choose, with a new price comparison revealing a £21 difference between the cheapest and most expensive festive food shops. The 2026 Christmas Dinner Index from Raisin UK compared the cost of 10 festive staples across nine supermarkets, finding that Aldi and Lidl had the cheapest basket at £21.80 for four people. At the other end of the scale, shoppers buying the same basket at Waitrose would pay £42.90 – a difference of £21.10. That works out at £5.45 per person at Aldi and Lidl, compared with £10.73 at Waitrose. Asda was the next cheapest at £24.10, just £2.30 more than the lowest-priced basket, suggesting shoppers may not save much by making an extra trip to another supermarket. Kevin Mountford, personal savings expert and co-founder of Raisin UK, said shoppers should think carefully before travelling between several supermarkets in search of the lowest prices. He said: “A £21 difference is worth paying attention to, but you don’t need to visit three supermarkets to get a good deal. Asda was only £2.30 more than the cheapest basket in our check. If it’s the shop you already use, think about whether an extra trip would save you much once you factor in travel or delivery. “The turkey is the first price I’d compare. It accounted for around two-thirds of the gap between the cheapest and most expensive baskets we checked. Look at how many people it serves as well as the price. A bigger bird is only worth paying for if you need the extra portions or have a plan for the leftovers. “Before you shop, check what you already have in the cupboards or freezer, and make a list of what you actually need. Small changes, like swapping a more expensive side dish or cutting an unnecessary extra from the list, can make a bigger difference than chasing discounts on individual items.” Raisin UK's previous Christmas dinner comparisons suggest shoppers could save money by waiting until nearer Christmas to buy certain items. In 2024, Aldi's Christmas dinner basket for four fell by more than £5 between early and late December. In 2025, it dropped by more than £8. Turkey accounted for the biggest price reduction in 2025, while carrots, parsnips and Brussels sprouts together cost just over £2 less by the final check. Lidl has also announced a Christmas dinner promotion starting on December 19, offering a meal for eight for £11.11. However, this promotional basket contains fewer items than Raisin UK's 10-item comparison, so it was excluded from the rankings. The findings come as many households face pressure on their budgets. Raisin UK's Great British Savings Report 2026 found that almost two-thirds (64%) of savings account holders had dipped into their savings over the past year. Of those, more than two in five (42%) used the money for everyday costs such as groceries and bills.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire children offered free Christmas activities and healthy meals

Councillor Edna Murphy, chair of the children and young people committee at Cambridgeshire County Council, said: "We know that winter can bring extra pressures for many families, especially over the festive season. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Refreshed strategy to support Cambridgeshire's unpaid carers
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary:
A refreshed strategy from Cambridgeshire County Council aims to better support unpaid carers of all ages. They launched the updated All-Age Carers Strategy on November 19 to mark Carers Rights Day and renew its support for unpaid carers across the county. The strategy recognises people who care for ill, disabled or otherwise vulnerable family members, friends and neighbours. Councillor Graham Wilson, chair of the adults and health committee, said: "Unpaid carers make an enormous contribution to communities across Cambridgeshire, providing vital support to family members, friends and neighbours, often alongside work, education and other responsibilities. "We know that caring can be incredibly rewarding, but it can also have a significant impact on a person's health, wellbeing and finances. "Through this refreshed strategy, we want carers of all ages to feel recognised, valued and supported. "That includes young carers, young adult carers, parent carers and adult carers, each of whom may need different types of support at different stages of their lives." The strategy aims to improve wellbeing, strengthen families and help people live independently for longer. The 2021 Census recorded five million unpaid carers across England and Wales, while evidence suggests caring is becoming more intensive for people juggling work, education and family life. The updated strategy was developed in collaboration with unpaid carers, families, health partners, carer support organisations, and voluntary and community groups. Its seven priorities include better access to advice and support, improved emotional wellbeing, stronger health and social care links, and help for young, parent and vulnerable carers. Read more Campaigners celebrate as work begins on ‘eyesore’ gap in market town high street
    Huntingdon MP demands action after months of Thameslink delays and cancellations It also makes specific commitments to young carers, young adult carers, parent carers and adult carers. The strategy will focus on identifying and supporting young, young adult and parent carers so they can thrive while balancing their responsibilities. The launch comes as the council continues to invest in support for unpaid carers through partnerships with local organisations and services. The council’s Bridgit platform has reached more than 11,000 unpaid carers across Cambridgeshire, including people who did not previously see themselves as carers. Cllr Wilson said: "This includes ensuring young carers and young adult carers have the support they need to achieve their potential and get the best start in life, while making sure all carers can access the information, advice and practical help they need. "Carers Rights Day is an opportunity to recognise and thank unpaid carers for everything they do, while reminding them that they are not alone and that support is available whenever they need it." The council works with Caring Together, Centre 33, Pinpoint and Making Space to provide advice, emotional support, training, peer networks and practical help. The strategy will shape future carers’ services in Cambridgeshire and guide the recommissioning of the county’s All-Age Carers Service. It also supports the council’s goal of building a healthy, fair and sustainable Cambridgeshire. Anyone regularly caring for a family member, friend or neighbour can find support and read the refreshed strategy on the council’s website.

He then grabbed the handlebars of the scooter and made remarks suggesting he would try to steal that instead. The victim, a man in his 70s, managed to get away and Faragab was arrested by nearby police officers. On Monday (November 16) at Cambridge Crown Court, Faragab, of Thorpe Meadows, Peterborough, admitted attempted robbery. He was sentenced to 13 months in prison. DC Lisa Flatters said: "To target an elderly man on a mobility scooter like this really is shocking, and his reported behaviour towards other members of the public that day was also very concerning. "I’m pleased there were police officers nearby and Faragab was quickly apprehended so he could face justice for his actions. "The victim was understandably shaken by the experience but thankfully escaped unharmed." Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: We are all being urged to check our change for a rare 50p coin after one sold for more than 650 times its face value at auction this week. The coin, a Kew Gardens 250 th anniversary coin, sold for £330 on eBay. It is one of the Royal Mint’s rarest and most valuable coins, with just 210,000 copies entering circulation when it was released in 2009. As a result, it is one of the most sought-after coins by collectors in the UK. The coin features the Chinese Pagoda at the Royal Botanic Gardens on the tails side and a portrait of the Queen. After being listed on online auction site eBay, the 50p coin attracted 14 bids before selling for £330.01. The 50 pence piece has become the most valued and collected coin in the UK, with many collectable designs appearing on its heptagonal canvas. Its 27.5mm diameter makes it the largest of any British coin, and allows space for decorative pictures. It has often been used to celebrate big events over the past 50 years of British history. The rarest coins tend to be of the greatest value, with the mintage (number of coins with each design made) being the fundamental attraction for collectors. Along with the design, other aspects of the coin which increase value are the condition of the coin and whether it has an error in its design. The way in which it is sold can also determine the coin’s value - while some coin collectors will bid vast amounts of money on eBay or at auction, others opt for more robust valuations by selling via a coin dealer. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Passengers could be made to fold prams as Government reviews wheelchair access laws
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Wheelchair users could be given stronger legal protections when travelling by bus and coach, after the Government confirmed it is reviewing whether existing laws to safeguard spaces for disabled travellers need to change. The Department for Transport has responded to a petition calling for wheelchair users to have an enforceable right to designated spaces, regardless of the order in which passengers board. But, some passengers have said it is difficult for parents to fold up their prams on busy buses, so they also need to use wheelchair spaces. The petition, created by Isabel Canto, has attracted 13,496 signatures and can be signed until March 15, 2027. It calls for passengers without a competing disability-related or extenuating need to be required to move, share or fold their prams to make room for a wheelchair user. It also wants drivers to be required to enforce the rules, with penalties for passengers who refuse to comply. At present, wheelchair users can still be left unable to board if another passenger refuses to vacate the designated space. Responding on November 9, the Government acknowledged that, despite existing legal protections, wheelchair users can still face refusals and distressing confrontations when trying to travel. It said: "We recognise the petitioners' central concern that existing protections do not always provide wheelchair users with the certainty they need." The Government confirmed it has asked the Law Commission to review the existing legal framework for transport accessibility. Its findings will help Ministers consider whether legislation needs to change to better support disabled people travelling independently and with dignity. However, it stopped short of committing to the specific changes demanded by the petition. The response said any new rules would need to take account of other passengers who may also have access needs, including those whose disabilities or other protected characteristics mean they cannot easily move elsewhere on the vehicle. It added that any penalties would need to be practical and enforceable, while avoiding unsafe situations for drivers and passengers. The petition argues that access to wheelchair spaces should not depend on the goodwill of other passengers. Its wording states: "Passengers without a competing disability-related or extenuating need should be required to follow directions to move, share or fold belongings, with penalties for refusal." The Government said buses and coaches are an essential service for many disabled people, whose needs should be anticipated in the way services are designed and operated. Since 2000, the Public Service Vehicles Accessibility Regulations have required buses and coaches covered by the rules to include specific accessibility features, including at least one wheelchair space with accompanying signage. Drivers also have legal duties under separate regulations to facilitate access to a vacant wheelchair space and provide the required boarding assistance. The Equality Act 2010 additionally requires operators to make reasonable adjustments to avoid placing disabled people at a substantial disadvantage. The Government pointed to a 2017 Supreme Court ruling which clarified that reasonable adjustments can include a driver requiring passengers to move from a wheelchair space when it is needed by a wheelchair user, and taking further steps to persuade them where appropriate. Despite this, Ministers acknowledged that wheelchair users can still be denied access, disrupting journeys to work, education and social activities and undermining confidence in travelling independently. The Government also outlined wider plans to improve bus accessibility. These include requiring drivers and customer-facing staff to complete disability awareness and assistance training every five years, and making local transport authorities publish an accessibility plan for their bus networks at least every three years. It is also developing a Transport Accessibility Charter intended to support a more consistently accessible journey. Mumsnet users took to the parenting forum to raise the issue with pram folding, with one user starting a thread saying: "Do people really manage to fold their prams in busy buses?. In it, they said: "Technically I have a pram which can be folded with one hand and in a couple of seconds (according to the advert), but practically I also have a baby strapped in, a pram bag attached, a thousand loose items in the bottom and a hundred toys attached. "I just was asked to fold my pram because the bus got a bit busy, but after giving this a quick thought I realised that this would be somewhere between a circus number, comedy and horror show, so I just got off the bus. Are there some Supermamas who just say ‘sure’, clack and done, and if yes, where can I learn this skill, please?" Another responded: "Not that I’ve seen unless the child they have is old enough to sit on a seat while they painstakingly take it all apart / try to use the fold function. Generally people get off if there is a wheelchair or squeeze up if it gets busy." Recommended reading: Others offered tips: "Have a backpack bag and nothing loose in the bottom. I've asked someone seated nearby to hold the baby for a minute if necessary. Better to take a small buggy and fold before you get on though if possible." The petition has already passed the 10,000-signature threshold, triggering a Government response. If it reaches 100,000 signatures before it closes on March 15, 2027, it will be considered for debate in Parliament. Do you think the laws to protect accessible spaces should be stronger? Should parents be made to fold prams? Tell us in the comments below...

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: State Pension age change means 197,000 pensioners miss out on Winter Fuel Payment
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An estimated 197,000 pensioners will miss out on this winter's Winter Fuel Payment because of a change to the State Pension age, as payments begin arriving in bank accounts this week. People who turn 66 might assume they qualify for the annual payment, worth between £100 and £300. But the gradual rise in the State Pension age from 66 to 67 means reaching your 66th birthday is no longer enough. According to The Solar Co, around 197,000 people who turned 66 before the end of this year's qualifying week will miss out because they had not yet reached their State Pension age. The qualifying week ran from September 21 to September 27, 2026. Anyone born after June 27, 1960 does not meet the age requirement for this winter's payment. That means someone born on June 27 qualifies, while someone born just one day later does not – even though both will have turned 66 by the end of September. People born between June 28 and September 27, 1960 must wait until they are 66 years and three months old to reach State Pension age. George Penny, Home Energy Expert at The Solar Co, said: "The Winter Fuel Payment is a tax-free annual payment from the government that helps older people cover the cost of heating their homes during the colder months. The amount varies between £100 and £300, depending on your age and living circumstances. "Many people assume that turning 66 means they’ll get the Winter Fuel Payment, and until this year, that was true. But with the state pension age now rising, your 66th birthday is no longer the date that counts. "Someone born on 27 June 1960 qualifies this winter, while someone born the next day doesn’t, even though both turned 66 well before the qualifying week. "If you’re expecting your first payment, check your State Pension age before including it in your winter budget." The Government's eligibility rules confirm that people must have been born on or before June 27, 1960 to qualify for the 2026/27 Winter Fuel Payment, provided they meet the other conditions. Most eligible pensioners will receive their payment automatically in November or December. Those with a personal income above £35,000 will have the money reclaimed by HMRC through the tax system. Recommended reading: For households facing higher heating bills, George has also shared four ways to keep warm and make savings this winter. 1. Check what other support you could get Missing out on the Winter Fuel Payment does not necessarily mean you will be left without help. George said: "Missing out on the Winter Fuel Payment doesn’t mean you can’t get help elsewhere. The Warm Home Discount takes £150 off eligible households’ electricity bills this winter, and most people receive it automatically. "If you think you qualify but haven’t heard anything by the end of January, contact the Warm Home Discount helpline." 2. Heat the rooms you use rather than the whole house Rather than switching off the heating altogether, George recommends concentrating warmth in the rooms where you spend most of your time. He said: "Rather than cutting back on heating, focus it where you spend your time. Close doors to keep heat in, turn down thermostatic radiator valves in unused rooms, and keep your main living space at a comfortable temperature, ideally at least 18°C." 3. Use a heated throw instead of a plug-in heater A heated throw could cost around 8p to run for three hours, compared with approximately £1.58 for a typical plug-in heater over the same period, according to George. He said: "If you’re sitting still in the evening, heating the person is far cheaper than heating the room. Using a typical plug-in heater for three hours costs around £1.58, compared with just 8p for a heated throw. That’s a saving of £1.50 a night, or about £45 over a month of daily use. Costs vary depending on the model and setting, so check the label. Never leave a heated throw on unattended or use one that’s frayed or damaged." 4. Make the most of free warmth from the sun Opening curtains and blinds during daylight hours can help bring some natural warmth into your home, even on colder days. George said: "Even on a cold winter’s day, sunshine coming through a window can help warm a room at no cost. Open the curtains and blinds on south-facing windows when the sun is out, so the light can reach the room. "As soon as the light starts to fade, close them again to help keep that warmth in. Thick or lined curtains work best. Tuck them behind radiators rather than letting them hang over the top, so the heat goes into the room instead of towards the window."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Little-known UK airport rule that could see electronic devices confiscated
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: If you are planning a winter getaway for the next coming weeks or already have a holiday booked for next summer, you might want to make sure you are aware of all of the airport rules you must follow. Most people travelling will at least be carrying a mobile phone with them and some might bring a laptop. Travellers are being warned about a little-known airport rule that can lead to your electronic devices like your phone being taken away. Your devices can be taken away if they do not switch on. (Image: Getty) The UK government has shared information about the hand luggage restrictions at UK airports. It says that travellers must have their devices charged and be able to switch them on when requested. The website reads: “Make sure your electronic devices are charged before you travel. “If your device does not switch on when requested, you will not be allowed to take it onto the aircraft.” If you cannot turn on your electronic device when asked by airport security, they have the right to confiscate it. This rule is not exclusive to British airports with many American and European airports also having the same rule in place. Airlines will allow passengers to take things like their mobile phones, laptops, and even electric shavers in their hand luggage and hold luggage. E-cigarettes are allowed in hand luggage but cannot be taken in hold luggage. The rules can vary between different airlines so you will want to check specific restrictions for your airline. If you have any lithium batteries, most airlines like easyJet and Ryanair will have strict rules on how these must be stored if you are bringing them with you. Many airlines say lithium batteries must be stored in your hand luggage rather than your checked baggage. Recommended reading Passengers could be made to fold prams as Government reviews wheelchair access laws Airline suspends all flights after 17 years as it files for insolvency Four in 10 Brits holding off on buying a house in the hope prices will drop Other items like cameras can be taken in both hold and checked luggage but there might be some restrictions on specialist equipment like professional video cameras. You can also take hair curlers that contain a gas cartridge on a plane as long as the safety cover is fitted on it at all times. Did you know your electronic devices had to be charged up at the airport? Let us know in the comments.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Historic church wall to be replaced after ‘extensive degradation’ beyond repair
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. The wall around a listed church is set to be replaced after it was found to have deteriorated to the point that “repair is not possible”. Permission was granted to demolish the wall surrounding St Mary’s Church in St Neots by hand, keeping as much good brick as possible. A structural survey of the wall found it to be “generally in poor condition throughout, with extensive degradation of brickwork and mortar”. Vegetation was also seen to be growing on the wall which showed signs of “movement” and “evidence of previous inappropriate repairs”. A Section Of The Boundary Wall Around St Mary'S Church, St Neots. Credit: Google Maps A planning document from Huntingdonshire District Council said: “The structural engineer concluded that the walls are heavily degraded to an extent that repair is not possible and recommended the demolition and reconstruction of the affected sections.” An objection was raised by the council’s conservation officer who was concerned the wall’s replacement would “result in the loss of historic fabric” and “evidence of traditional construction methods and materials”. The officer said “insufficient information” was given to “justify this harm” and said the proposed use of modern materials and construction techniques “could adversely affect the character and appearance of the wall”. But after the plans were amended with a detailed method statement, the officer removed their objection and “accepted that the existing walls had reached the end of their lifespan”. A neighbour did not object but raised a number of concerns and said much of the wall’s deterioration was due to “previous repairs undertaken using cement-based mortar”. They said that “unless appropriate materials are utilised, a rebuilt wall could experience similar problems in the future”. They advocated for the use of traditional materials and construction techniques, including lime mortar, in line with “recognised conservation best practice”.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Knifeman was 'hearing voices saying he was going to be attacked', court hears
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A knifeman accused of attempted murder in an attack on a train in Huntingdon last year was "hearing voices" and "believed he was going to be attacked", a court heard. Several people were injured on an LNER train from Doncaster to London King's Cross on November 1, 2025 which was forced to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon. Anthony Williams, 33, denies 14 counts of attempted murder: ten of them in relation to the LNER train, three said to have happened in Peterborough and one at Pontoon Dock DLR station in London. Dr Bernard Chin, a consulting forensic psychiatrist at North London NHS Foundation Trust, was cross-examined by Gillian Jones KC as the defence made their case at Cambridge Crown Court on November 17. Dr Chin assessed Williams shortly after the incident on the LNER train. The court heard that Williams said: "I was paranoid people were going to attack me, they were coming for me, cars were going to run me over. "I was hearing a lot of voices, feeling a lot of fear. "I was extremely paranoid, I knew people were after me, the cars were following me. "I went to the river because no cars could run me over there." Dr Chin told jurors that Williams had said he believed his house was bugged and he had been sleeping outside in the woods, but was still hearing voices. The court heard that the voices were reportedly getting worse by Halloween 2025. Dr Chin told the court that Williams said: "I was on TikTok asking for a sign and it showed a video of someone stabbing someone. "It was a warning to me. I needed to protect myself." The court heard that when Williams was on the LNER train, he said he continued to hear the voices. Dr Chin told jurors that Williams said: "I just kept hearing 'you are going to get attacked, they are going to kill you' through the speakers on the train. "I wasn't really thinking, at the time I just needed to protect myself. "It was me or them." The court heard that Dr Chin diagnosed Williams with schizophrenia, a diagnosis echoed by another professor. He told jurors he defined schizophrenia as a form of psychosis, where one is unable to tell reality and the inner world apart, describing it as a "severe and enduring mental illness". The court heard that while Williams was likely to have been intoxicated with alcohol, this was unlikely to have caused or sustained the psychosis, and the test for insanity was not met. Earlier this month, Williams pleaded guilty to 10 counts of wounding with intent relating to the incident on the LNER train, the wounding with intent of a man at Pontoon Dock DLR station in the early hours of November 1 and to the wounding with intent of a 14-year-old boy in Peterborough on October 31, as well as a number of other offences. The trial continues.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Major British retail chain put up for sale after closing down 150 stores
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A major high street retailer has been put up for sale. TGJones, formerly known as WH Smith and trading for more than two centuries under that brand, is being put up for sale by its owner, Modella Capital, which has appointed advisers from Teneo to oversee the process. The retailer operates around 350 shops and employs 3,500 people. The sale process comes amid broader turbulence in the retail sector, with Poundland also facing financial uncertainty. A post shared by TGJones (@tgjonesuk) TGJones was acquired by Modella last year when London-listed WH Smith decided to offload the business after 233 years of trading on the UK high street and focus on its travel retail operations instead. Since the purchase, the chain has closed around 150 stores as part of a restructuring plan, following rebranding and declining sales. Now, the high street chain has been put up for sale, Sky News reports. In a joint statement, TGJones and Modella Capital said: "High-street retailer TGJones has received unsolicited offers for the business; management and owner Modella Capital have jointly agreed to instruct Teneo Corporate Finance to review these offers and undertake a market-testing exercise." Alex Willson, chief executive of TGJones, said: "As ever, our focus is on providing a great experience for customers, especially with the critical Christmas period coming up. "We continue to execute our turnaround plan, which is improving our performance month by month. "We're grateful to our fantastic colleagues for their commitment; and to our suppliers, our owner and other stakeholders for their continued support." Joe Price, managing director of Modella Capital, said the business was struggling at the time of acquisition and required tough decisions to secure its future. Mr Price said: "When TGJones was acquired in 2025, it was a loss-making business with an uncertain future. "Turning it around meant taking some hard decisions, including closing stores through a court-approved Restructuring Plan. "We are extremely grateful to our colleagues from across the business for their continued support. "The turnaround is starting to deliver, and we are seeing improved trading results." summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Martin Lewis warns shoppers why gift cards are the worst Christmas gifts of all
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Martin Lewis has issued a Christmas warning to shoppers thinking of buying gift cards, saying vouchers often become worthless if a retailer goes bust or the recipient fails to spend them before they expire. The Money Saving Expert said people should think carefully - gift cards are often seen as an easy option for Christmas because they allow friends and family to choose something from a shop they like. But Mr Lewis said shoppers should not assume vouchers are as safe as giving cash. He acknowledged that some people feel more comfortable giving a gift card than handing over money, saying: “Many find giving a gift card more socially acceptable than cash. “I get it. Cash gifts just are not very British. “Yes unfortunately, vouchers have risks.” One of the biggest dangers is that a retailer could go bust. If that happens, gift cards may no longer be accepted, meaning the recipient could lose the value of the present. Mr Lewis said: “If the store goes bust, gift vouchers usually become worthless.” He also warned that shoppers should check the expiry date before buying a voucher, as some have deadlines that may not be made clear enough. “Many have expiry dates, which often are not made clear enough,” he said. His advice was to consider how financially secure the retailer is and whether the recipient is likely to spend the voucher quickly. “So, think carefully about the likely financial strength of the retailer, and how quickly they'll be used,” he said. Mr Lewis suggested that shoppers who are unsure should choose cash instead. “If in doubt, cash, or money in the bank, is the ultimate gift voucher. It is totally flexible and usable anywhere.” This follows advice on his website Money Saving Expert, which says: "It's always better to give cash rather than a gift card – it's less risky and ensures the recipient will be able to buy some sort of present even if their favourite store goes under." The post continues: "Always remember gift cards and vouchers are likely to have expiry dates - check yours and make a note so you don't forget to use them in time." A review of 18 major retailers found that nine will restart the expiry countdown if customers make a balance enquiry, meaning shoppers could get more time without having to spend anything. Confused.com personal finance expert Tara Evans said: "Before you start your Christmas shopping, check whether you already have gift-card money you could put towards it. It is easy for a present to end up in a drawer or an old email and be forgotten about." The rules vary between shops, with some offering a fresh expiry period after a balance check, while others extend cards following a purchase. Boots and H&M, for example, restart the expiry period following a transaction or purchase. Other retailers offer longer-lasting vouchers. Apple and TK Maxx/Homesense gift cards have no expiry date, while Amazon cards are valid for 10 years from issue. Morrisons and ASOS give customers 24 months from purchase to use their gift cards, with no extension available.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Rare Royal Mint 20p coin sells for more than 400 times face value on eBay
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Royal Mint 20p piece desired by coin collectors has sold for more than 400 times its face value during The circulated Puffin 20p coin, which features King Charles III on the reverse side of the coin, sold for £82.08 on eBay, after sparking a mini bidding war with 18 bids. The Royal Mint records a circulation mintage of 525,000 for the 2023 puffin 20p. Its design features a puffin facing left, with a distinctive bill and detailed plumage, as part of a collection depicting British plants and animals. A 2008 20p piece is among the most sought after coins in the UK because of a minting error. It is known as a mule coin because an accidental mix-up at the Royal Mint left it with no date on either side. Featuring Queen Elizabeth II on the front, the coin shows part of the Royal Shield of Arms on the reverse. A production blunder occurred in November 2008 during a redesign of circulating British coinage, when an older heads die was paired with the new shield reverse. The Royal Mint confirmed that fewer than 250,000 coins out of 136 million 20p pieces struck in 2008 and 2009 were affected by the mistake. A spokesperson for the Mint previously said: "In November 2008 a number of 20p coins were incorrectly minted, resulting in the coins being undated. "This problem affected less than 250,000 coins of the 136 million 20p pieces minted in 2008-09." The 50 pence piece has become the most valued and collected coin in the UK, with many collectable designs appearing on its heptagonal canvas. Its 27.5mm diameter makes it the largest of any British coin, and allows space for decorative pictures. It has often been used to celebrate big events over the past 50 years of British history. The rarest coins tend to be of the greatest value, with the mintage (number of coins with each design made) being the fundamental attraction for collectors. Along with the design, other aspects of the coin which increase value are the condition of the coin and whether it has an error in its design. The way in which it is sold can also determine the coin’s value - while some coin collectors will bid vast amounts of money on eBay or at auction, others opt for more robust valuations by selling via a coin dealer. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Petrol price rise pushes UK inflation to highest level in 12 months
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: UK inflation has climbed to its highest level in a year after petrol and diesel prices rose again, adding to pressure on household budgets. The Consumer Prices Index (CPI) measure of inflation reached 3.6% in October, up from 3.5% in September, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS). The latest figure was in line with economists' forecasts and marks the fourth month in a row that inflation has increased. It also leaves inflation well above the Bank of England's 2% target. Higher fuel costs and changes to tobacco duty helped push the rate upwards, with motorists facing another rise at the pumps. ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said: “Inflation rose slightly in October, with fuel prices once again a major contributor to the increase. “Annual costs of both raw materials and goods leaving factories continue to climb, driven by higher crude oil and petrol prices, respectively.” The average price of petrol increased by 5.2p per litre between September and October, the latest figures showed. The rise came as tensions in the Middle East continued to put pressure on oil prices, pushing up the cost of filling up for drivers. Jenny Holt, Customer Savings & Investment Director at Standard Life, said the latest increase would be “unwelcome news” for households already dealing with the high cost of living. She warned that prolonged inflation could have a lasting impact on household finances, adding: “With winter energy bills and fuel costs adding to the pressure, a return to persistently high inflation risks making it even harder for households to plan for their financial futures.” While savers may benefit from higher interest rates, she warned they may not be enough to keep pace with inflation, meaning the real value of their money could still be eroded. Ms Holt added that rising living costs could make it harder for people to prioritise retirement saving. However, she said pension investments had “typically outpaced inflation over the long term”, while stopping contributions could mean missing out on employer payments, tax relief and potential investment growth. Recommended reading: Charlie Evans, Money Expert at Compare the Market, said the latest figures could mean interest rates remain higher for longer. He said: “With inflation moving further away from the Bank of England's 2% target, today’s figure could also mean that interest rates remain elevated for longer, leaving mortgage holders and those with loans or credit card balances facing continued financial pressure.” He warned that higher fuel and energy costs could feed through to the price of everyday goods and services, while homeowners coming to the end of fixed-rate mortgage deals could have to budget for higher repayments. Louise Halliwell, Group Savings Director at Kent Reliance, said its latest SaveUp research showed more than a third of UK adults were saving more than usual, despite pressure on household budgets. She said: “The picture isn't the same for everyone, however. Gen X households are often balancing mortgage repayments with the cost of supporting both children and ageing parents, and 44% say a lack of disposable income is preventing them from saving more.” Ms Halliwell said people did not need to put away large sums to build a financial cushion, and encouraged savers to regularly review savings and cash ISA rates to make sure they were getting a competitive return. She added that households should plan for the months beyond Christmas, saying: “Setting a realistic budget for December while keeping something back for January can help households start 2027 on a stronger financial footing.”

The council "does not intend to progress" plans to build housing developments on three Huntingdonshire car parks after 90% of residents opposed the scheme. Plans by developer Capital & Centric and Huntingdonshire District Council (HDC) to build homes on three large car parks in St Neots, Huntingdon and St Ives sparked fury among residents in August. The plans for the St Neots Tebbutts Road car park include two five-storey buildings, up to 83 homes and units for independent businesses. The newly released Gateway 1 report reveals that out of resident responses, 91.2% opposed the plans in St Ives, 89.8% opposed the plans in St Neots and 87% opposed the plans in Huntingdon. After the completion of the Gateway 1 stage, which included public engagement, technical surveys, and concept designs, the council "does not intend to progress to Gateway 2 with Capital and Centric on the current schemes", the report reveals. Residents turned out in force to share their views about the plans to develop Tebbutts Road (Image: Emily Stevens) In a summary report of the Gateway 1 report by members of HDC's senior team, it states: "The scale and consistency of public opposition is focused on the fundamental choice of sites rather than design detail; unresolved strategic parking and accessibility issues remain; and the economic case does not outweigh the identified concern regarding parking function and public feedback." The main concern raised was the impact of redeveloping central surface car parks on the vitality and accessibility of town centres. The council’s decision follows pre-application advice from the planning authority, which stressed the need for a comprehensive parking strategy before any redevelopment could be considered. Officers concluded that the evidence did not provide a strong enough case to justify further investment in the next stage of the project. An independent review of the Capital & Centric commission will continue, and the technical work completed to date will remain available for future use. The full report will be discussed at an extraordinary meeting of HDC at 7pm on Tuesday, November 24.

A former village saw mill will be demolished to make way for affordable homes despite fears from residents over increased traffic. South Cambridgeshire District Council’s planning committee approved the proposal for 34 affordable homes at the former timber mill on Histon Road in Cottenham. Though the site lies on the green belt, planning officers recommended the scheme for approval as it was “proportionate to Cottenham village”. Luke Webb, planning director at the applicant Living Space Housing, said it would be a “positive use of a current brownfield site” and they aimed to start building as “early as possible in 2027”. Cottenham Parish Council objected to the plans as they feared they would overwhelm local infrastructure, noting that 34 homes had already been approved nearby. Jo Brook said the parish council recognises the need for affordable housing but this “does not automatically make every site suitable for development.”. She said families would face a half hour walk to primary school or nursery which would encourage them to drive. She said: “For families, that’s a considerable journey and many will inevitably choose to drive. “This is particularly concerning when the school is already exploring a scheme to close Lambs Lane at drop-off and collection times because of existing parking and congestion problems.” Ms Brook added that it is “well documented” that the surrounding properties on Histon Road “flood regularly”. Cllr Heather Williams, of The Mordens, said she “can completely understand” their concerns about the cumulative impact, but it has to be weighed against housing need. The Conservative councillor said: “We can see from the officer’s report that there is need and, to be quite frank, there is going to be an increasing need for a long time. “I think there is a danger with all these applications that you don’t end up actually putting all the social housing together and I would say that this is probably its limit for that.” Cllr Dr Martin Cahn, of Histon and Impington, said that Cottenham is “a very unusual village” as it is “an extremely long village”. The Lib Dem councillor said: “Where is the centre? It’s strung along a long distance – any development in Cottenham is going to be too far from some of the facilities. “I don’t see that as a reason to refuse it and it will be a valuable addition to our social housing, which is a high priority in our district.” Cllr Anna Bradnam, chair of the committee, said there was a “substantial justification” for housing in the area and added that the proposal now has a “very comprehensive surface water drainage scheme”. The Lib Dem councillor said: “It’s possible that this will actually make it less likely that those properties on Histon Road flood – let us hope so.” The plans were approved unanimously by the planning committee.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP State pensioners over 80 to get extra cash boost on top of £374 annual rise
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Many older state pensioners - aged over 80 - are in line for an extra cash boost to their weekly payments from April, on top of the annual increase confirmed under the triple lock. The additional payment is available to certain pensioners who reached State Pension age before April 2016 and are receiving the old basic State Pension. Unlike those who qualify for the newer State Pension system, older pensioners can receive an additional payment when they reach the age of 80, provided they meet the qualifying conditions. The change comes as millions of pensioners prepare for the next annual State Pension increase, which will take effect from April 2027. The basic State Pension is expected to rise by 3.9% under the triple lock, taking the weekly rate from £184.90 to £192.10. This represents an increase of £7.20 a week, or approximately £374 a year, for someone receiving the full basic State Pension. The triple lock guarantees that the State Pension rises each April by whichever is highest of inflation, average earnings growth or 2.5%. The Government has confirmed it will remain in place for the 2027/28 financial year. In a statement to parliament, DWP secretary Pat McFadden said: "I have concluded my statutory annual review of State Pension and benefit rates under the Social Security Administration Act 1992. The new rates will apply in the tax year 2027-28 and will mainly come into effect from 12 April 2027. "I am pleased to announce that the basic and full rate of the new State Pensions will be increased by 3.9%, in line with the increase in average weekly earnings in the year to May-July 2026. "This delivers on our Triple Lock commitment throughout this Parliament to increase these rates in line with the highest of growth in prices, growth in earnings or 2.5%. From April, the full annual rate of the new State Pension will increase by around £490. The full annual rate of the basic State Pension will increase by around £375." He later added: "Other State Pension and benefit rates covered by my statutory review will be increased by 3.5%, in line with the increase in the consumer prices index in the year to September 2026. This includes most working-age benefits and other benefits for people below State Pension age; benefits to help with additional needs arising from disability; Statutory Payments including Statutory Sick Pay and Statutory Maternity Pay; and Additional State Pension. The Pension Credit Savings Credit maximum amount will also increase by 3.5%." Recommended reading: The additional payment for people aged 80 and over is known as the over-80 pensio, or Serps. It is designed to provide extra support to older pensioners who receive a lower rate of State Pension under the previous system. The old basic State Pension was closed to new claims in April 2016, when the new State Pension system was introduced. People who reached State Pension age before that date generally receive the old basic State Pension, alongside any additional State Pension they built up through their National Insurance contributions. Those reaching State Pension age after April 2016 instead qualify under the new system, which has a higher maximum weekly rate and operates under different rules.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Strictly Come Dancing lift rules explained - when are they illegal and the penalties?
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Lifts can create some of the most memorable moments on Strictly Come Dancing, however, they are not allowed in every routine. The rules around lifts are often a source of confusion for viewers, contestants, and even the judges themselves. Here is a guide to what makes a lift illegal on Strictly, which dances allow them, and how the judges handle rule-breakers. A lift is defined as any movement where a dancer has both feet off the floor with assistance or support from their partner. Strictly judge Craig Revel Horwood highlighted the rule in 2024 after Pete Wicks and professional partner Jowita Przystał included two lifts in their Rumba. He said one foot should have remained on the floor and described both moves as "totally illegal", adding that couples could lose marks for doing so. However, the definition relies on whether the airborne movement was supported by the partner, not simply if both feet left the floor. There is some room for interpretation. In 2022, Ellie Simmonds was helped down from a table by Nikita Kuzmin during their Paso Doble. Head judge Shirley Ballas deducted a point for the 'assisted lift', while Revel Horwood said the issue was that it lasted too long. He suggested that a brief, supported descent would have been acceptable. Lifts are banned in the 10 core ballroom and Latin dances featured on Strictly Come Dancing: In these routines, a lift is considered an illegal move. Lifts are permitted in some of the show’s other styles, including: Lifts are banned in the 10 core ballroom and Latin dances on Strictly Come Dancing. (Image: BBC/Guy Levy) They are also allowed in contemporary and jazz routines. American Smooth routines can include lifts, although the exact number permitted may vary based on the show’s current rules. Performing an illegal lift does not result in automatic disqualification. Instead, judges have the option to deduct points. In 2022, Ballas clearly stated she was deducting one point from Ellie Simmonds for an assisted lift. Revel Horwood also mentioned marking Dani Dyer and Nikita Kuzmin down during their week 8 routine (Paso Doble) on Strictly 2026 due to the use of illegal lifts. A post shared by BBC iPlayer (@bbciplayer) However, enforcement is not always consistent. During Wicks’ 2024 Rumba, Ballas said she would "let them slide", while Revel Horwood insisted they should be marked down and even suggested disqualification. He later admitted this was unlikely, saying the show had "never really disqualified anyone," but stood by the idea that illegal lifts should affect the score. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: UK motorists urged not to ignore this common night-time driving problem
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Drivers who see blurred headlights or halos around lights are being urged to get their eyesight checked. Adam Aslam, director at Nevies Opticians, said changes in vision can be particularly noticeable when motorists are driving after dark. He said streaks, glare and blurred lights can have different causes and advised people whose sight is affected to ask an optometrist for advice. One possible cause is astigmatism, a common condition that can make headlights, streetlights and road signs appear blurred or distorted, particularly at night. The NHS says astigmatism can cause blurred vision, headaches and eye strain, and recommends visiting an optician if someone has symptoms. It explains that astigmatism means the eye is shaped more like a rugby ball than a football, causing light to focus in more than one place in the eye. It says the condition does not always need treatment, but glasses or contact lenses are among the options. The NHS also advises going to an optician if you have not had an eye test for two years, and says regular tests are important. Mr Aslam said: “Many people assume everyone sees headlights the same way they do, so they may not realise there could be an issue with their vision. “If lights appear unusually bright, blurry or surrounded by halos, it’s worth booking an eye examination to have your vision checked.” Even motorists with healthy vision can find driving after dark more challenging during the winter months, according to the optician. He also shared five ways motorists can prepare for journeys in low light, including cleaning the inside as well as the outside of their windscreen. Dust, residue and condensation on the glass can scatter light and make glare from oncoming headlights worse, he said. His advice is to clean both sides regularly and clear condensation before setting off. Mr Aslam also recommends avoiding a bright phone screen just before a journey and giving your eyes a moment to adjust to the dark. He advises drivers not to use their phones while driving. Changes in driving habits can be worth noticing, too. According to Mr Aslam, of Nevies Opticians, avoiding unfamiliar routes or driving after dark, slowing down more than usual and relying heavily on road markings can be signs that vision has changed. Anyone who has adapted their behaviour in these ways should consider an eye test, he said. Repeated star-shaped lights, streaks or halos should not simply be assumed to be normal, particularly if they affect how clearly someone can see. Motorists should also check that they have the right lights on, as daytime running lights often do not illuminate the rear of a car, according to Mr Aslam. He recommends switching headlights on in poor visibility and using dipped beam when other road users are nearby. The Highway Code advises drivers dazzled by oncoming headlights to slow down and, if necessary, stop. Mr Aslam added: “People routinely service their cars, check their tyres and replace worn wipers, yet many overlook their eyesight. “Your vision plays a huge role in how safely you drive, particularly during the darker months. “If you’ve noticed changes in your sight, booking an eye test is a sensible step.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: WhatsApp users warned this group chat mistake could lead to criminal charges
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A simple mistake in a WhatsApp group chat could leave people facing criminal charges under new laws, a legal expert has warned. Ruth Peters from Olliers Solicitors said an image automatically saved from a group chat can lead to serious charges, even if the recipient did not ask for it. New offences covering possession and publication of specified pornographic images came into force in England and Wales on November 6 under the Crime and Policing Act 2026. They do not apply to every explicit image, and receiving an unsolicited image does not automatically mean someone has committed an offence. But those found in breach of the new laws could find themselves facing criminal charges and time in jail. The new rules cover pornography that explicitly and realistically depicts strangulation or suffocation, certain incest-themed penetrative sexual activity, or sexual activity involving someone who is, or is pretending to be, under 16. The people depicted must appear to a reasonable person to be real, according to government guidance. Whether someone possesses an image is a question of fact for a court, but the guidance says it could include material stored on a device, in a personal account or in cloud storage. The maximum sentence for possession is two years for material depicting strangulation or suffocation or certain relatives, and three years for material depicting someone who is, or is pretending to be, under 16. Publication carries a maximum sentence of five years for all three offences. Ms Peters said Olliers Solicitors had encountered around 10 current or ongoing cases in which people faced serious consequences after images from group chats were found on their phones. She recalled a case involving an image of bestiality found during a phone examination in an unrelated investigation that resulted in no further action. The Disclosure and Barring Service dealt with the image offence with a caution, but was subsequently considering whether to place the person on a barred list, potentially affecting their employment, she said. Ms Peters said: “The important thing is to understand that possession can be a continuing act. “It is not necessarily about whether you actively went looking for something or whether you downloaded it yourself. “People need to be aware of what is on their devices and understand that images shared in group chats can have serious consequences.” WhatsApp users found breaking the new laws could find themselves facing criminal charges and time in jail. (Image: Yui Mok/PA Wire) The Ministry of Justice says possession can be a continuing act and advises people to permanently delete or otherwise get rid of images covered by the offences. WhatsApp users may have a defence if they were sent an image without asking for it and did not keep it for an unreasonable length of time. There may also be a defence if they had not seen the image before and did not know or have cause to suspect that it was covered by the offences. Ms Peters said: “People arrested for offences where the police need to examine their phones will often have their devices checked by officers. “An image automatically saved from a group chat can lead to very serious charges. “While receiving an image you have not asked for is not necessarily an offence, if that image stays on your device for a period of time, you could potentially face prosecution. “Even if you didn't specifically opt to save that image, it may still remain on your device.” Were you aware of the new pornographic image laws introduced earlier this month? "My thoughts are with the women whose courage brought him to justice. "I appeared on TV, radio and live charity shows with him, and whilst we played it up for the cameras and in the media, I considered it a professional relationship, rather than a personal one. Brand began his career as a TV presenter and comedian and became a Hollywood star, appearing in films such as Forgetting Sarah Marshall, Hop and the Despicable Me franchise.
