summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Drivers warned easy £10 fix could help avoid £2,500 fine and 3 points on licence
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Drivers are being warned about a £2,500 fine which they could receive if they don't make an easy £10 fix. While you won't use your windscreen wipers on every outing, they certainly come in handy on wet days and when you need to improve your vision by clearing the windscreen. If you have damaged or broken windscreen wipers, it's important they're replaced because, as John Hood, the general manager at Auction4Cars.com explains, they can result in a £2,500 fine and three points on your licence. The vehicle company surveyed 2,000 UK drivers and found that almost a fifth of them (19%) have admitted to driving with broken or damaged windscreen wipers. Did you know how to spot when your wiper blades need replacing? (Image: Getty) Auction4Cars.com said that many drivers get behind the wheel despite their vehicles having common defects. Mr Hood said: "Autumn is one of the worst times of year for visibility on the road. "Rainy weather and spray from other vehicles puts more demand on your wipers, so it's important that they work properly. "If your wipers don't clear your windscreen well, you're putting yourself and other road users at risk. "Getting caught with worn-out wipers could land you a £2,500 fine and three points on your licence." If you're not sure if your windscreen wipers need replacing, Mr Hood has shared some advice to help you notice when they aren't up to scratch. He said: "If your wipers leave smears, make a squeaking noise or miss patches on your windscreen, it's usually a sign the blades are worn out. "Look for fraying or cracks in the rubber – these can stop the blades from clearing water effectively." Mr Hood said that, while you'll need to take into account how often the vehicle is used and what the weather has been like, "as a general rule, drivers should replace them every six months to a year". He said they're usually around £10 to replace and "compared to the cost of an MOT retest or a fine, it's a small price to pay that can make a huge difference to visibility, especially in the autumn months." The RAC added: "When you lift the wiper off the glass and you see that the rubber looks cracked, split, or is beginning to peel away from the frame, this means that the blades won't make proper contact with the windscreen and need replacing. "Finally, if you are driving during heavy rain and you have reduced visibility even if the wipers are moving, then it is important not to ignore it. "This is because worn wipers can seriously compromise safety. "Regular car maintenance involves checking the blades and cleaning them can extend their life, but once they show visible wear, replacement is the safest option." The RAC also shared a step-by-step guide for anyone who needs to replace their windscreen wipers. Lift the wiper arm away from the windscreen so that it locks and is upright, then find the release clip and either press or slide it to take the old wiper blade away. The RAC warns: "Carefully remove it, making sure the bare metal arm doesn't snap back onto the glass as this could cause several issues." Recommended reading: Then you'll need to "align the new blade with the hook or connector and push it into place until you hear a click." Once this is done, you need to "gently" return the wiper arm to the windscreen and then do the same again with the other blade if you're replacing both. When you have finished adding new blades, test them by using washer fluid so you can see if the wiper blades move over the windscreen correctly. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Help us fight youth homelessness this Christmas with Centrepoint
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: This Christmas, too many young people will find themselves facing homelessness and the uncertainty that comes with it. When a young person is in crisis, practical support can make all the difference. Having access to everyday items that we often take for granted, such as food and toiletries, can provide comfort, dignity and a sense of stability at an incredibly difficult time. To help combat this growing issue, Newsquest has joined forces with youth homelessness charity Centrepoint calling on communities across the country to support young people facing homelessness this winter. A gift of £20 could provide vital food and toiletries for a young person facing homelessness this Christmas through an emergency hardship voucher. (Image: Steve Franck) That support can be a lifeline, helping a young person access the essentials they need while they take their first steps towards a secure future. Newsquest readers can donate here and help provide vital support to a young person this Christmas. You can also sign up to be a campaigner here. As a campaigner, you'll be the first to hear about opportunities to take action, from signing petitions and contacting decision-makers to sharing campaign messages with your community and helping raise awareness of the issues affecting young people facing homelessness. Centrepoint’s CEO Seyi Obakin explains why now is such a crucial time to share your support for the charity below: Newsquest CEO, Henry Faure Walker, and Centrepoint CEO, Seyi Obakin. (Image: Jeff Moore) This Christmas, national attention is rightly focused on ending rough sleeping. On his first day as Prime Minister, Andy Burnham stood outside Number 10 and made it his "moral mission" that nobody should be left without shelter by Christmas. At Centrepoint, we share that ambition. For 57 years, we've worked alongside young people facing homelessness, providing safe accommodation and specialist support to help them rebuild their lives. It is hugely encouraging to see the government backing this mission with significant investment. Winter can be especially dangerous for those without a safe place to stay, and every person helped off the streets is another person protected from harm. But homelessness doesn't end when Christmas does. Getting someone off the street is a vital first step, but lasting change means giving them the stability and opportunities they need to move forward. Because a home is more than a roof over your head. It's the foundation from which people can study, work, maintain relationships and build a future. Many readers will recognise how difficult life can feel for young people today. Perhaps you have a son, daughter, niece, nephew or grandchild taking their first steps into adulthood. Even with the support of family, finding an affordable place to live, securing a job and becoming independent can feel daunting. Now imagine trying to do all of that with nowhere safe to call home. When many people think about homelessness, they picture rough sleeping. But for most young people, homelessness is hidden. It's sleeping on a friend's sofa because there's nowhere else to go. It's riding buses through the night to stay warm. It's spending hours in a fast-food restaurant because it feels safer than being outside. These young people are often still going to college, turning up for work and trying to carry on as normal, all while worrying about where they'll sleep that night. No young person should have to live that way. And yet too many do. They have been let down by the very systems that should protect them and denied the security most of us take for granted. Homeless young people need more than emergency help. They need long-term support to rebuild their confidence, continue their education, find employment and develop the skills that will help them thrive. This matters to all of us, but it matters most to young people like Vicky. In the letter below, she shares what it was like to experience homelessness as a young person and the difference that support made when she needed it most. Her story is deeply personal, but it is far from unique. Behind every homelessness statistic is a young person with hopes, ambitions and potential. This Christmas, let's not only help them find safety today, but ensure they have the opportunity to build a brighter future tomorrow. One person who Centrepoint has helped is Vicky. After sofa-surfing with family members, sleeping rough, and seeking shelter in a McDonald’s, Vicky is now living in Centrepoint’s Independent Living Programme, providing her safe, affordable housing. (Image: Rebekah Kennington) Vicky has written to Prime Minister Andy Burnham to emphasise how important the Centrepoint’s work is. These are her words: Dear Prime Minister, As a young adult with lived experience of homelessness, I really appreciate your commitment to end rough sleeping. Things haven’t always been easy for me. When my mum became seriously ill, my life changed almost overnight. My brother and I were still young, but suddenly we were trying to keep our home going without the support we needed. Eventually, it became impossible and I lost my home. Shouldn’t there have been systems in place to support my family when we were plunged into crisis? At first I couch-surfed with a family member, but they could only help me for so long. I didn’t want to be a burden, so I ended up sleeping rough. I was staying awake all night, and turning up to work exhausted the next day. The only place I could stay safe and warm was in McDonalds because it was lit and there were lots of people there. One night an older person sat down opposite me and asked if I was okay. That interaction really stuck with me. Homelessness so often gets ignored, but I know you agree, Prime Minister, we all have a responsibility to notice and act on it. That person told me about Centrepoint, and I eventually called their Helpline and was able to access their services. The first thing the support worker I met did was give me a Pot Noodle as I hadn’t eaten for a few days – it felt so good. That emergency support was a lifeline. But what helped me move forward was what came next. Centrepoint helped me navigate the complicated housing system, and always guided me through difficult moments. When I got a call to say I had somewhere to live I was shaking. I kept thinking they’d made a mistake. Then I cried, because I finally had a bed I could sleep on. A safe place I could go to. Today, I live in Centrepoint’s Independent Living Programme, where rents are capped at a third of income. Having affordable and stable housing means I can work, save money and plan for my future with confidence. So many more of these homes are needed around the country, so all young people can have the same foundation. Prime Minister, I hope you achieve your goal of ending rough sleeping this Christmas. But I also urge you to remember that homelessness doesn’t end when the festive season does. Young people need urgent support when they're in crisis, but they also need long-term solutions that let them look ahead with hope. Vicky Centrepoint is on a mission to end youth homelessness by 2037. But to get there, they need a growing movement of people willing to stand up for homeless young people and help change the systems holding them back. As well as donating to the Christmas campaign here, where a gift of £20 could provide vital food and toiletries for a young person facing homelessness, you can also sign up to be a campaigner here. As a campaigner, you'll be the first to hear about opportunities to take action, from signing petitions and contacting decision-makers to sharing campaign messages with your community and helping raise awareness of the issues affecting young people facing homelessness. Together, we can build the public and political support needed to ensure every young person has a safe place to call home and the foundation to build their future. When a young person is in crisis, practical support can make all the difference. Having access to everyday items that we often take for granted, such as food and toiletries, can provide comfort, dignity and a sense of stability at an incredibly difficult time. That support can be a lifeline, helping a young person access the essentials they need while they take their first steps towards a secure future.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Newsquest and Centrepoint launch Christmas campaign to support homeless young people
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Newsquest, the UK's largest local media group, and Centrepoint, the UK's leading youth homelessness charity, have launched a major Christmas campaign calling on communities across the country to support young people facing homelessness this winter. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP cuts warning as major benefits shake-up could leave claimants with less cash
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Some young people could see their benefits cut under a major DWP shake-up, with those who refuse offers of work, training or employment support potentially losing financial help. Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden has confirmed that some young people will receive less financial support in future under recommendations expected in a major review of youth unemployment. Former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn is due to publish his independent report on Tuesday, November 17, setting out proposals to tackle the growing number of 16 to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (Neets), which topped one million this year. One of the biggest proposals is reported to be to move some young people currently receiving health-related benefits onto a new 'youth allowance', paid at the standard rate of Universal Credit. Mr Milburn has acknowledged that some young people would receive less financial support under his plans. Those who refuse a proposed legal guarantee of work, training or employment support could also risk losing their benefits. Mr Milburn is also expected to recommend gradually cutting the employer National Insurance contributions paid on workers aged 21 to 24 over five years, initially focusing on retail and hospitality. According to the BBC, the plans would double the threshold at which businesses start paying employer National Insurance on earnings from this age group, from £5,000 to £10,000. However, the changes would only be introduced "when economic conditions allow". Mr Milburn is expected to argue that a blanket cut would not be the best use of the several billion pounds of public money it could cost, particularly if young people cannot find jobs after gaining new skills. Mr McFadden has backed the proposed legal guarantee, arguing that employment support needs a stronger legal foundation and would give young people "more certainty about what they're entitled to". Speaking to Sky News' Sunday Morning programme, he said the Government needed to make changes not "in spite of being Labour people", but "because we're Labour people". "It's a different proposition from last year, and I hope that Parliament views it in that light," he said. The Government will be hoping to avoid another Labour rebellion after ministers were forced to water down proposed welfare cuts last year. Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said the legal entitlement "might sound a nice thing to do" but "doesn't make sense". However, she described the move away from "handing out cash for relatively mild conditions" and towards employment support as "the right direction of travel". Reform UK's Danny Kruger said he was "encouraged" by "the suggestion that we need to be much stricter about benefits for young people who should be supported into work or should be working". Recommended reading: The review is also expected to call for the proportion of children considered school-ready at the start of reception to rise from 75% to 90%. Mr Milburn is expected to warn that too many five-year-olds struggle with everyday tasks such as using cutlery or going to the toilet. He has previously warned that tackling youth unemployment could take a decade and billions of pounds, arguing that "crude cuts" would simply result in young people appearing elsewhere in Government spending figures.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Environmental disaster fears after 14,000 litres of oil dumped in ditch off A14
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Calls for urgent action to avert an environmental disaster have been made after an estimated 14,000 litres of waste engine oil was dumped into a Huntingdonshire ditch. Robert Neilson has raised concerns after being alerted to the illegal 'fly-tipping' by a family member who farms the area off the A14 between the Leighton Bromswold and Catworth junctions. Mr Neilson, who lives in Ramsey, said his relative found the oil while working on the farm earlier this week. “He told me he contacted the Environment Agency straight away because he was so concerned about the amount of oil and the environmental disaster it could cause,” said Mr Neilson. Read more Families given five weeks' notice of Huntingdonshire disabled day centre closure Just under half of children in Huntingdon miss out on NHS dentist visits Decision looms on 600-home plan for St Neots amid flood of objections Hunts man accused of distributing indecent images of children named New plan to replace ‘potentially unsafe cladding’ agreed He said Environment Agency officers had visited the site, but no action had yet been taken to clear the mess. “I have been told the Environment Agency estimates that it's between six or seven tanker loads of the used engine oil that's been dumped – around 14,000 litres. This is not an accident. You don't accidentally dump that much oil into a ditch,” said Mr Neilson. He is worried that without action, the oil will make its way into the River Ouse at Huntingdon. Mr Neilson said the ditch currently contains little water, so the oil is not moving much, although some has reached a nearby brook. But heavy rain could send water from the A14 into the ditch, giving the oil enough water to reach the River Ouse. “This is an environmental disaster waiting to happen. That amount of oil is going to have a massive impact on the wildlife; it will kill fish and affect birds and other animals,” said Mr Neilson. He said the Environment Agency needed to act quickly before rain, adding that a digger could scoop most of the oil from the ditch. "Obviously someone has come along into the layby with their tanker full of oil and simply opened the tap. It was probably done after dark so no one would probably take much notice, and think it was someone parked up for a nap," said Mr Neilson, who added: "This is absolutely disgusting. It is vandalism, and the worst kind of fly-tipping and action is needed pronto." An Environment Agency spokesperson said: "We've installed barriers to help protect Ellington Brook from the appalling dumping of oil on the A14 and are advising National Highways on clean-up measures to limit the environmental impacts." The spokesperson added that National Highways is leading the clean-up and, where appropriate, can take enforcement action where its drainage network has been misused. The police are responsible for investigating any suspected criminal activity and can support Environment Agency investigations through measures such as CCTV and ANPR enquiries.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Russell Brand shares message after he was reportedly moved to Cambridgeshire prison
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Laura Gallacher has shared a message from her husband Russell Brand, who has served the first week of his 10-and-a-half-year prison sentence for rape and sexual assault. The disgraced comedian was jailed this week after being found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others during his career. He was reportedly moved from HMP Wandsworth in London to HMP Littlehey, near Huntingdon, last week, according to The Sun on Sunday. The prison offers a large variety of extra-curricular activities for its inmates, including yoga, choir and indoor bowls. Earlier this year Brand and Gallacher began releasing a weekly YouTube podcast called Sunday Service, which they carried on recording throughout his trial. On Sunday, Gallacher released another episode which began with her reading a passage from Brand’s bible. The 39-year-old, who is the daughter of Ryder Cup-winning golfer Bernard Gallacher, said during the episode: “Russell has asked me to read something to you.” Reading the message from a notebook, she went on: “Beloved brothers and sisters in Christ, God bless you for your support. “As you know, I am not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening. “The good news is that Christ is with us when we choose him, and I do. “I am incarcerated in HMP Littlehey, little as in small, and hey as in hey, I’m in the biggest sex offenders’ prison in Europe. “The good news is that I have already seen that the staff here are strong, they are kind, and they are dedicated. “And as for my fellow prisoners, I now know that I am in no position to judge anyone. “I don’t know which other men here are not guilty, and the ones that are, they are people that Christ died to save, like you and me, let us all love, pray for, and forgive one another as God forgave us.” Gallacher choked up as she said: “Please support my treasured wife and family. I feel your prayers, your brother in Christ. Russell.” She began the episode by saying she is here to “continue the good work that was being established here in this Sunday service community, something very, very close to mine and Russell’s heart”. “It may look different, but the ambitions are very much the same, and we trust God, and we trust his plan, and we trust everything he’s doing right now,” she added. “Even though it’s painful, and obviously, will take some getting used to for me to even sit here and not have my companion and my person with me, but I want to continue, and I’m grateful for the support.” Gallacher said she is speaking to her husband, adding: “He’s okay, and he’s praying.” Brand was sentenced to a 10-and-a-half-year prison term on Monday afternoon. He is expected to serve two-thirds of his prison sentence before being released on licence. He will be on the sex offenders’ register for life.

An artist's impression of the new retirement development (Image: Churchill Living) The development aims to help older residents maintain independence while offering the benefits of a supportive community, including a lodge manager, a 24-hour careline system, a communal lounge, and a guest suite. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Kath Sansom recently visited Ready Steady Roll, which has two sites - one near Kimbolton, and another in Peterborough - here's what she thought In an age when so much socialising revolves around screens, there's something really refreshing about gathering around a table, picking up some board games and spending a few hours laughing with friends. Ready Steady Roll is the sort of place you could easily drive past without ever knowing it exists. Yet this award-winning board game café was exactly what we were looking for when we stumbled on it during a Google search while looking for a halfway meeting place that offered more than the usual coffee shop or pub catch-up. As life gets busier, maintaining friendships when living in different towns many miles apart can become surprisingly difficult – so finding somewhere worth travelling to is a challenge. Thankfully, Ready Steady Roll offered the perfect solution, with an afternoon packed with laughter, nostalgia and friendly competition. The venue boasts an extensive games library with options ranging from light-hearted family favourites to deeper strategy games. Our afternoon began in unfamiliar territory with Shoot for the Stars, a “general knowledge” game with questions like how many beans in a can of Heinz. We then opted for a healthy dose of nostalgia, transporting back to childhood with the classics Frustration and Operation, before picking up Doodle Rush, a quick-fire drawing game. Whether you're a seasoned gamer or someone whose experience begins and ends with Ludo and Monopoly, there's something to tempt everyone of all ages with every genre imaginable neatly packed on well organised shelves – most of which we'd never heard of before. Board games are only half the story. The café serves a great selection of food and drinks, and we happily worked our way through impressive coffee, chips, sausage rolls and cakes during our four-hour visit. The table service meant we could stay immersed in the games while the food and drinks arrived at our table, helping create an unhurried atmosphere. Perhaps what stood out most was the welcome. The venue feels warm, cosy and genuinely inviting, somewhere that encourages you to settle in and stay awhile. It was a joy to escape to. There is also a strong community feel. Alongside regular daytime gaming, the venue hosts board-game evenings where people can come along, meet fellow enthusiasts and join games with others. For anyone looking to expand their social circle or simply find opponents for a favourite game, it's a lovely idea. What makes Ready Steady Roll special is that it offers something increasingly rare: a chance to slow down. No notifications, no scrolling, no rush. Just good company, good food, plenty of laughter and hundreds of games waiting to be explored. For three friends from across the region, Ready Steady Roll turned an ordinary catch-up into a memorable day out, leaving us already planning our next visit. Need to Know Where: Studio 5, Ivy Lodge, Rushden Road, Sharnbrook, MK44 1ND. Cost: £4 for adults and £3 for children for a two-hour session. Weekday term-time sessions are £2. Opening times: check the Ready Steady Roll website and social media channels for current opening hours.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Microsoft has fully restored services following a major global IT outage. The disruption affected police forces, the NHS, businesses, courts, and schools. The US-based company confirmed this morning (November 14) that services were fully restored for all remaining affected customers. In a statement on its Microsoft 365 status page, the company said: "We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions. We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services. This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions. Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration. We will provide a full post-incident report once our review is complete. — Microsoft (@Microsoft) November 13, 2026 "Further updates can be found at MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center." The outage, which began around 6pm GMT on Thursday, November 12, disrupted email, messaging, and other Microsoft 365 services. The UK Government and others worldwide were forced to activate contingency plans. Microsoft said on Friday the disruption was due to a "technical issue not related to cyber or AI agents." Baroness Lloyd of Effra, the UK Government’s cyber minister, said the problem mainly affected back-office functions. Baroness Lloyd said there had been "limited reports of impact on frontline service delivery" and the incident had been "inconvenient and disruptive". She confirmed she had spoken with Microsoft UK chief executive Darren Hardman about the outage. Monitoring website Downdetector first showed a spike in users reporting problems with Microsoft Teams in the UK at about 6.15pm on Thursday. It recorded a surge in complaints, with more than 130,000 users in the US reporting problems with Outlook at its peak on Thursday evening. Millions of its customers were unable to send and receive emails through Outlook, while Microsoft’s Copilot AI assistant, Teams and other Microsoft 365 services were also affected for many. Other AI chat platforms, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude, were disrupted. Police forces in England and Wales said on Friday that they could not receive crime reports online. NHS England said staff had switched to "long-standing measures" to manage the outage, including the use of paper records. Rail passengers were unable to access e-tickets for their journeys as they couldn't open the emails in their Outlook inboxes. National Rail warned travellers to use alternative methods to access their tickets. A spokesman said: "We’re aware of the ongoing Microsoft global outage, which may be affecting customers’ ability to access their train tickets via their email inbox. "If you’re unable to locate or access your tickets through your email due to this issue, you may still be able to access your tickets by visiting the website or app where you purchased your tickets from and logging into your account. ‼️We’re aware of the ongoing Microsoft global outage, which may be affecting customers’ ability to access their train tickets via their email inbox. 🔗Latest Information and advice can be found here: https://t.co/pYa714hR8k — National Rail (@nationalrailenq) November 13, 2026 "We recommend doing this before you travel to ensure you have your tickets readily available for your journey. "This may not be possible if you checked out as a guest – please contact your ticket retailer directly if you are unable to access your tickets. "If you are still unable to access your ticket, please contact a member of onboard staff or station staff for advice." Other rail operators, including Southeastern, Chiltern Railways and London North Eastern Railway (LNER), reported similar problems with emailed tickets. AirExplore, based in Slovakia, was founded in 2008 and began ACMI (wet leasing) operations in 2010. It provided aircraft and crew to UK carriers, including Jet2 and TUI, through ACMI  arrangements, helping support services across the UK and Europe. AirExplore aircraft have been seen at major UK airports, including Manchester, Bristol, Newcastle International, and London Stansted. The airline was acquired by Avia Solutions Group in June 2023. AirExplore officially ceased operations on Tuesday (November 10) and submitted a request to surrender its Air Operator Certificate (AOC). In a statement posted on its website, the airline said: "The Slovakian ACMI and charter airline AirExplore has ceased operations on 10 November 2026 and has submitted a request to surrender its Air Operator Certificate (AOC). "We thank all our employees, customers, partners, and team for their support over the years." No reason has been given for the closure. Meanwhile, UK-based Global Airlines has been ordered into compulsory liquidation. The UK startup, which planned to use a fleet of Airbus A380 planes, was formally ordered to wind up by the Insolvency and Companies Court on Wednesday (November 4), according to The Gazette. The winding-up petition was originally filed in May, with several hearings taking place in the following months, including the most recent in October. With the order now in place, an officer of the court, known as the official receiver, has taken control of winding up the company. A post shared by Global Airlines ® (@globalairlines) Government guidelines state that once a winding-up order is issued, the company’s bank accounts are typically frozen and its assets sold off to repay creditors. Companies have the right to apply for cancellation of a winding-up order within five working days if they believe the action is unwarranted. Global Airlines is still listed as "active" on Companies House, though its most recent accounts are overdue. Global Airlines has been contacted for comment. Darryl Preston, police and crime commissioner, said: "Funding projects like the Trusted Adult Scheme (TAS) delivers on many levels offering the group new and different experiences in supported environments. Young people can access mentoring, activities and safe spaces through the scheme. (Image: Trusted Adult Scheme) "Often young people need someone to talk to, to confide in and this trust is something which only grows when they feel safe, seen and heard within an inclusive environment." The programme, led by criminology lecturer Dr Paul Nelson, includes young people who are not in education, employment, or training (NEET), who may be exhibiting risky behaviours. Since its inception, the commissioner has committed more than £200,000 of Home Office grant funding to the scheme, securing its future until March 2028. Dr Nelson said: "By receiving further funding for two years we can provide art sessions, music studios to record in, gaming and street art sessions alongside outdoor activities like laser tag. The Trusted Adult Scheme supports young people across Cambridge and Peterborough (Image: Trusted Adult Scheme) "The 13 to 18-year-olds come to us needing support, guidance and encouragement – seeing them leave as matured individuals just can't be measured." Each week, the scheme offers activities such as street art, sports, gaming, creative arts and crafts, and one-to-one mentoring. Young people have shared positive feedback about their experiences. New funding will help the youth programme continue until 2028 (Image: Trusted Adult Scheme) One participant said: "TAS is the first place I’ve felt listened to. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs libraries not removing David Walliams books, council confirms
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire libraries will not be actively removing David Walliams’ books from their shelves, the council has confirmed. Cambridgeshire County Council said its libraries will not be taking action to withdraw the author’s titles after an ITV News and The Guardian investigation saw him accused of sexual misconduct this week. Mr Walliams, 55, known for titles such as The Boy in the Dress and Gangsta Granny, wrote more than 40 books, which generated a revenue of £100 million by 2019. He has been accused of inappropriate sexual behaviour with girls allegedly as young as 15. He has also been accused of inappropriate conduct and sexual harassment at his former publisher HarperCollins, and while working on Britain’s Got Talent. Mr Walliams has denied all allegations of misconduct. Cambridgeshire County Council confirmed that Cambridgeshire Libraries "will not be actively removing" his books. A council spokesperson said: “Cambridgeshire Libraries is part of Libraries Connected, the body which represents all Public Library Services in England. "Libraries Connected has issued the below statement, which is consistent with our own Stock Policy, and specifically addresses the writings of David Walliams." Libraries Connected, which represents public library services across England, said that while all books should be available unless illegal, stock is routinely refreshed based on demand. Libraries Connected said: "In this case, we understand that demand for Walliams’s books has fallen significantly in recent years. "We would therefore expect the number of copies in circulation to decline naturally as they are replaced by newer and more popular titles, particularly as he is now without a publisher." Decisions about whether to keep Mr Walliams' books in Cambridgeshire schools will be made by governing bodies or trustee boards, the council confirmed. The council added that should the Department for Education issue any guidance, this would be shared with schools.

Ben Obese-Jecty, MP for Huntingdon, posted to Facebook that he had met with the St Ives Town Team to discuss how best to “regenerate the heart” of the town. The Conservative MP said pedestrianising Market Hill and Bridge Street could give an “opportunity for businesses to thrive in St Ives”. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Royal Mint Beatrix Potter 50p coin sells for more than 400 times face value on eBay
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Royal Mint Peter Rabbit 50p coin has sold on eBay for more than £200. The Royal Mint's Beatrix Potter collection began in 2016, marking 150 years since the author's birth. The first Peter Rabbit design showed a close-up of the character facing forward, complete with whiskers. Other 2016 designs featured Squirrel Nutkin, Mrs Tiggy-Winkle and Jemima Puddle-Duck. Four more designs arrived in 2017, featuring Tom Kitten, Benjamin Bunny, Jeremy Fisher and another Peter Rabbit. The 2018 Peter Rabbit and Flopsy Bunny designs each had a circulating mintage of 1.4 million. The Peter Rabbit editions from 2019 and 2020 were not put into general circulation. The seller described the coin as a 2016 Royal Mint Peter Rabbit 50p in silver proof, with a fineness of 0.925. The listing eventually sold for a total of £219.20, including a £9.03 buyer-protection fee. The Royal Mint lists the 2023 Atlantic Salmon 50p as the rarest circulating 50p, with a mintage of 200,000. Next on its list is the 2009 Kew Gardens 50p, with 210,000, followed by the 2011 Olympic football design, with 1,125,500. The date matters: the Royal Mint's table also records two million Atlantic Salmon 50p coins dated 2025. Other low-mintage circulating designs include the 2011 Olympic wrestling, judo and triathlon coins, alongside the 2018 Peter Rabbit and Flopsy Bunny 50ps. Mintage is the number of coins made, and a lower figure can make a design harder for collectors to find. A coin's condition, design, material and demand from collectors can also affect what someone is willing to pay. A genuine error can be of interest to collectors, but a seller's description alone is not independent verification. The Royal Mint advises buyers of second-hand coins to check for original packaging and, for proof editions, a certificate of authenticity. A specialist valuation can help an owner establish a coin's history and likely value.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: PM gives flat owners new powers to challenge 'unfair' service charges
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Millions of leaseholders are set to gain new powers to challenge unfair service charges. The government says more than three million leaseholders in England will benefit from the reforms, with the first changes planned for April 1, 2027. The measures are due to be introduced in stages through to November 2028, subject to parliamentary approval. From April 2027, leaseholders will be able to request information about their service charges, including details from previous years. Landlords will need a good reason to refuse to provide the information, according to the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. Service charges are fees paid by leaseholders or tenants to cover the maintenance, repair and management of shared areas of a building. The ministry says the changes will give leaseholders a clearer picture of how their building is managed, maintained, repaired and insured. The first stage also includes stronger protection against having to pay a landlord's legal costs when challenging a charge. Landlords will need court or tribunal approval to pass on legal costs, while leaseholders will gain a right to recover their own legal expenses, the government says. Further measures are planned for November 1, 2027, when leaseholders will receive clearer information about charges, including details of building insurance and administration fees. There will also be stronger protections against excessive or unreasonable fees for arranging and managing insurance. Private landlords will have to use standardised service charge demand forms and provide financial accounts and annual reports from November 2027. Councils and housing associations will have until November 1, 2028 to introduce those forms, accounts and reports for their leaseholders. Kion Ahadi, chief executive of the Leasehold Advisory Service, said: "Service charges are the most common issue leaseholders contact us about. "We welcome these changes as an important step forward in helping people understand what they are paying for and challenge costs they believe are unfair. "Leaseholders need clear information about how their money is being spent and a fair opportunity to raise concerns. "Better access to that information and stronger protection from landlords’ legal bills will give them more confidence to hold their landlord to account."

The Government has published its annual review of benefit payments, setting out how much claimants will receive from April 2027. Working-age and disability benefits will rise by 3.5%, with the new rates mainly coming into effect from April 12, 2027. Inflation-linked benefits and tax credits will rise by 3.5% from April 2027, in line with the annual increase in the Consumer Prices Index (CPI) rate of inflation for September 2026. Universal Credit standard allowances will receive an additional uplift as specified in the Universal Credit Act 2025. The basic and new State Pensions will be uprated by 3.9% from April 2027, in line with the annual increase in the Average Weekly Earnings (AWE) index for May–July 2026. Universal Credit is currently paid to more than 8.4 million people across the UK. Due to the increase in line with CPI, and the additional uprating factor, in 2027/28 Universal Credit standard allowances will increase: Universal Credit is a means-tested benefit designed to help with living costs for people on a low income, out of work or unable to work. The number of people claiming it has increased as the DWP continues its managed migration programme, which is moving people from older benefits onto the newer system. Around 2.2 million Universal Credit claimants are in employment, while a significant number of others are not expected to work because of health conditions or caring responsibilities. Recommended reading: Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden confirmed the increases in a statement to Parliament following the Budget. He said: “The new rates will apply in the tax year 2027-28 and will mainly come into effect from April 12 2027. “The other state pension and benefit rates covered by my statutory review will be increased by 3.5%, in line with the increase in the consumer prices index in the year to September 2026. “This includes most working-age benefits and other benefits for people below state pension age; benefits to help with additional needs arising from disability; statutory payments including statutory sick pay and statutory maternity pay; and additional state pension. The pension credit savings credit maximum amount will also increase by 3.5%.”

Bogdan Gasparov, 40, used cash-trapping devices to steal more than £16,000 from at least 180 ATMs between May and October 2026. Police found him hiding in a loft crawl space during a raid on his Hardie Road home in Dagenham. Detective Sergeant Mike Simpson from ERSOU's Proactive Economic Crime Team (PECT) said: "This was not opportunistic offending. "Gasparov carried out a calculated campaign of theft, targeting cash machines across the country and repeatedly returning to steal money that belonged to unsuspecting customers. "What makes this case even more brazen is that Gasparov had previously been convicted for similar offences and deported from the UK, only to return illegally and resume the same criminal behaviour. "He clearly believed he could stay one step ahead of investigators. He couldn't. "Thanks to the determination of our officers and the strength of the evidence gathered, he has now been brought to justice once again." He also struck near Nottingham, Oxford, Somerset, Bristol, Derby, Gloucester, Lincoln and the West Midlands, as well as in parts of Scotland and Wales. The scheme involved Gasparov posing as a legitimate customer, fitting homemade cash-trapping devices to ATMs, and leaving the area. When genuine customers attempted to withdraw money, the cash would become trapped in the device. Gasparov would then return later to retrieve the device and the stolen funds. CCTV from several locations repeatedly placed Gasparov at the scenes. A search of his vehicle uncovered clothing worn during the offences, homemade cash-trapping devices and tools to make them. The full new State Pension will increase to £250.70 a week, up from £241.30, while the full basic State Pension will rise to £192.10 a week from £184.90. The increases amount to an extra £9.40 and £7.20 a week respectively, giving eligible pensioners hundreds of pounds more over the course of a year. The new figures have been set out in a House of Commons Library briefing published on Wednesday, November 11, covering the benefit and pension rates announced for the 2027/28 financial year. Both the basic and new State Pension will rise by 3.9% from April 2027, in line with the annual increase in average weekly earnings between May and July 2026. The increase is part of the Government's commitment to the State Pension triple lock, which means payments rise each year by the highest of inflation, average earnings growth or 2.5%. The full weekly rates will be: Over a full year, the increase works out at around £488.80 for someone receiving the full new State Pension and £374.40 for someone receiving the full basic State Pension. The new State Pension applies to people who reached State Pension age on or after April 6, 2016. The basic State Pension is the core payment under the old State Pension system, for people who reached State Pension age before that date. The figures are the full weekly rates. The amount an individual receives will depend on their National Insurance record and whether they qualify for the full entitlement. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The DWP has revealed they plan to freeze the maximum amount Brits can claim in benefits from next year. The Department for Work and Pensions updated their website on Wednesday, November 11, to outline proposed benefits rates for the 2027-28 tax year. Benefits caps are used by the government to limit the total amount of money claimants can receive and it applies to most people over 16 and below State Pensions age. -Widowed Parent’s Allowance (or Widowed Mother’s Allowance or Widow’s Pension if you started getting it before 9 April 2001) The current annual maximum for couples (with or without children) or single claimants with a child of qualifying age is £22,020 or £25,323 for those in Greater London. The annual maximum for single adults households this tax year, which ends in April, is £14,753 or £16,967 in Greater London. This is proposed to be frozen for the 2027-28 tax year, meaning Brits won't be able to claim more than this amount between April 2027 and 2028. The monthly equivalent is also planned to be frozen at £1,835 and £2,110.25 (Greater London) for couples, with or without children, or single claimants with a child of qualifying age. Single households without children face the same freeze, with the maximum remaining at £1,229.42 and £1,413.92 in Greater London. Weekly equivalents are planned to remain at £423.46 and £486.98 (Greater London) for couples, with or without children, or single claimants with a qualifying-age. The weekly maximum for single households is planned to remain at £283.71 or £326.29 (Greater London). This is despite the Office for National Statistics' most recent inflation rate being recorded at 3.6% in September and many economists forecasting that this is expected to rise next year. The government explains that the cap may not start for nine months if someone is claiming Universal Credit but this depends on their earnings. Recommended reading: Brits are not affected by the benefits cap if they or their partner get Universal Credit because of a disability that 'stops them from working' or get it because they care for someone with a disability. They're also exempt if they get Universal Credit and they or their partner earn £881 or more a month combined, after tax and National Insurance contributions.

With the order now in place, an officer of the court—known as the official receiver—has taken control of winding up the company. Government guidelines state that once a winding-up order is issued, the company’s bank accounts are typically frozen and its assets sold off to repay creditors. Companies have the right to apply for cancellation of a winding-up order within five working days if they believe the action is unwarranted. The company, which was founded in 2019, acquired its only aircraft in May 2023, and claimed to be the first new A380 owner in eight years. Its maiden flight, operated under a damp lease from Hi Fly Malta, flew from Glasgow to New York-JFK on May 15, 2025. After completing just four transatlantic flights, the aircraft was placed into long-term storage in Tarbes, France, on July 16, 2025, with no known return-to-service date. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Support for pubs only ‘lip service’ after budget says landlady
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridge pub landlady has accused the government of only paying “lip service” to supporting hospitality following the latest budget. Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey delivered the first budget of Andy Burnham’s government last month, with a number of changes for pubs. This includes raising the threshold for Small Business Rates Relief in England from £12k to £18k – meaning businesses with a rateable value below this will pay no business rates. But pub operators will also face higher wage bills with the national living wage for workers aged 21 and over increasing from £12.71 an hour to £13.21. Both changes will come into effect from April 2027 and alcohol duty will also increase in line with inflation from February 1. Hayley Pellegrini, who runs five pubs in the city with her husband Steve including The Portland Arms and The Alex, said she does not feel small businesses are getting the support they need. The 56-year-old said: “We work ridiculous hours and what we pay ourselves we worked out is probably below minimum wage. “But it’s a case of we just have to suck it up and get on with it. “I don’t feel like we are getting the support we need – they aren’t doing anything, they want to be seen as being pub goers and that but they aren’t doing anything. “It’s not just pubs, it’s small businesses in general – we have friends who have small businesses and they are struggling as well.” She said small businesses are discouraged from expanding as they will lose relief and face higher wage bills from increased national insurance contributions and the rise in wages. Ms Pellegrini said it was harder for them as a living-wage employer, but that they’re “fortunate” to be based in Cambridge with a steady stream of business from students and tourists. She said: “Why am I going to employ someone with no experience, when I could be paying someone with ten years of experience the same? I think we are losing the next generation of hospitality managers, in 10 or 15 years we might find we haven’t brought up the next generation of managers.” She said the government was being “narrowminded” by not considering a reduction in VAT – with more than 400,000 signing the VAT’s the Problem petition to cut it from 20 per cent to 10 per cent, in line with other countries in Europe like France, Spain and Italy. Ms Pellegrini said: “We were hoping that Andy Burnham was actually going to be the one who will do something, but now we think – ‘ah, here we go again’. “What worries me is our retirement – we’re so busy trying to keep the business afloat we aren’t actually able to put anything away for our retirement and we’re going to be a burden on the government. “I work long, unsociable, hours often seven days a week to keep this industry going – who am I doing this for? “The slice of the pie being taken off us is just getting bigger and bigger and bigger. “It seems to be targeted at small businesses while companies like Amazon pay a tiny proportion of tax. “Something needs to be redistributed – the rich are getting richer and the rest of us are working our butts off to try and make a living.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Rare fish 'considered locally extinct' found in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A rare fish thought to be extinct locally has been discovered in Cambridgeshire. The sturgeon, weighing 15lb, was found on the banks of the Twenty Foot Drain last week, the Environment Agency said. According to the Zoological Society of London, the UK is home to two native species of the fish. The Atlantic and European sturgeon can both reach up to five metres long and can live for more than 60 years. They are among the most critically endangered group of animals on the International Union for Conservation of Nature's Red List. The Environment Agency said it hadn't been made aware of any catch reports in the drains or surrounding rivers. "We have absolutely no idea what the story with this one is," a spokesperson said. They added: "Native sturgeon are considered locally extinct in our patch, although historically there have been reports from the River Great Ouse. "Reports exist of a 130lb sturgeon being caught in Huntingdon way back in 1754. "There have been introductions of the species in France in recent years with some of these fish migrating across the channel and being caught in UK waters." It is illegal to keep sturgeon in fisheries in England due to the risk of hybridisation with the few remaining native European sturgeon in the UK's waterways. Have you got a story you want to share? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Families given five weeks' notice of Huntingdonshire disabled day centre closure
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Families of adults with learning disabilities have raised concerns over plans to move a Huntingdonshire day service from St Ives to Huntingdon with just five weeks' notice. Cambridgeshire County Council has told users of the CATS centre in Bull Lane, St Ives, their families, carers and advocates that the service is due to move to Huntingdon Community Centre on December 7. In a November 2 letter, Cambridgeshire head of provider services Mandy Langley told the Singh family that activities and support would move to the Huntingdon centre, around six miles away. The family says the letter was the first it knew about the plans and questions why relatives were not consulted before the announcement. Surj Singh said his brother has Down syndrome, is non-verbal and relies heavily on familiar people and surroundings. He said the family feared moving the service could seriously affect his brother and others who rely on familiar routines. The family has questioned whether the new centre is suitable, citing noise, summer heat, staffing, supervision, privacy, facilities and personal care. The Singh family complained to the council on November 5 and asked it to pause the move until families had been consulted and individual needs and transition plans addressed. Read more Just under half of children in Huntingdon miss out on NHS dentist visits Decision looms on 600-home plan for St Neots amid flood of objections Hunts man accused of distributing indecent images of children named Thief who stole orangutan statue from garden centre pictured New plan to replace ‘potentially unsafe cladding’ agreed Mr Singh said his brother’s needs raised serious questions about whether the new setting and arrangements would suit him and others with different support needs. The family wants to know when the decision was made, what assessment and consultation took place, and how staffing, personal care and individual suitability will be assured. Mr Singh said his brother had been away from the service because of ill health, and the family had spent weeks planning his return with social services and the provider without hearing about the move. The family has also questioned the move’s timing, just weeks before Christmas. The council said the move was planned because fewer people were using CATS St Ives. It said Huntingdon Community Centre already provides day services and has room for St Ives users, allowing it to "make better use of our buildings and resources". The council said familiar staff would continue supporting users and similar activities would be available in Huntingdon. But Mr Singh said the family feared the Huntingdon centre was much larger and noisier than the St Ives site. The council said users would still have access to the St Ives community while being offered opportunities in Huntingdon. The council said users would be offered extra visits to the Huntingdon centre in November to prepare for the move. It said there would be no break in service and that the St Ives centre would operate until the move. The council said it would discuss any changes to care arrangements or transport with those affected. The letter said: "We are committed to supporting everyone through this change and making it as smooth as possible." The family says the council has acknowledged its complaint but has yet to answer its concerns. A Cambridgeshire County Council spokesperson said: "From Monday, December 7, the council will be bringing together the CATS day service in St Ives with services provided at Huntingdon Community Centre for adults with learning disabilities. "Huntingdon Community Centre already provides a wide range of activities and opportunities, including the Blossom and Bloom Café and TAG Bikes. "Bringing the services together will give people attending CATS access to a broader choice of activities, opportunities to build confidence and independence, and the chance to meet and develop relationships with new people. "Our priority is to ensure a smooth transition for everyone affected, and we will continue to work with individuals and their families throughout the process, including reviewing any transport arrangements required. "The move will also bring services together on one site, providing greater operational resilience and making the best use of council resources. “We can confirm this complaint is being investigated and we have contacted the family to explain the complaints process."

The campaign covers Bedfordshire, Luton, Milton Keynes, Cambridgeshire, Peterborough and Hertfordshire. Dr Fiona Head, medical director at NHS Central East Integrated Care Board, said: "There are simple things we can all do to help ourselves and those around us stay well this winter. "One of the most important is getting vaccinated if you’re eligible, to help protect yourself and those around you. "Flu and COVID-19 can cause serious illness, particularly for those who are more vulnerable, and vaccination can help reduce your risk of becoming seriously unwell. "It's also important to be prepared. Make sure you have the medicines you need at home and order repeat prescriptions in good time. "If you do become unwell, knowing where to go can help you get the right advice and support, whether that’s from your local pharmacy or NHS 111." The campaign urges people to protect themselves, prepare for winter and stay well. 'Protect' focuses on getting eligible flu and COVID-19 vaccinations, practising good hygiene, and taking care around others when unwell to help prevent the spread of illness. 'Prepare' is about keeping everyday medicines at home, ordering repeat prescriptions early, and using the NHS App to order repeat prescriptions. 'Stay well' encourages people to look after both their physical and mental health, and to use the right services when they need support, such as Pharmacy First for many common conditions or NHS 111 when they need urgent medical help but are unsure what to do. Dr Head said: "Winter is a challenging time for health services, and we’re working closely with our NHS providers and partners across the region to prepare for the months ahead. "We want people to stay safe and well, but we also want everyone to know that the NHS is here when they need it." summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP disability benefit increase from 2027 for people who need care or mobility help
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The DWP revealed that a million Brits could receive more Disability Living Allowance money from April next year. The Department for Work and Pensions updated their website on November 11 with proposals to increase the weekly payments. The current rates only cover the tax year between April 6 2026 and April 5 2027 so from April 6 next year new rates will apply. These increases are labelled as 'provisional' but the Government website's update history shows the previous provisional figures reflected the final figures to the penny. Disability Living Allowance, which helps cover the costs of extra personal care or mobility, has two components - care and mobility. Both of these are split from highest to lowest rates of payment depending on how severe the need for support is. People are eligible for the care component if they need help with things like washing, eating, cooking, communicating needs, dressing or using the toilet. They may also need supervision to 'avoid putting yourself or others in danger' or to have dialysis. The highest rate is paid to those who need 'help or supervision throughout both day and night, or if a medical professional has said they're nearing the end of their life'. This payment is proposed to rise from the £114.60 per week being paid during the current tax year to £118.60 per week for the 2027-28 tax year. The middle rate is described as being suitable for those who need 'frequent help or constant supervision during the day, supervision at night or someone to help you while on dialysis'. The lowest rate is for those who 'need help for some of the day or with preparing cooked meals' and this rate is proposed to increase from £30.30 per week to £31.35. The mobility component is for people who either cannot walk, can only walk 'short distances without severe discomfort' or who could become 'very ill if they try to walk'. People may also get this if they have no feet or legs, are 100% blind or you were between ages 3-64 on April 11 2011 and have been certified as 'severely sight impaired'. Recommended reading: Other criteria include those at least 80% deaf, those who need someone with them when outdoors or those who are 'severely mentally impaired' with behavioural problems. The lower rate of payment is for those who need 'guidance or supervision outdoors' and this would rise from £30.30 per week to £31.35 in the 2027-28 tax year. The higher rate is for those who have 'any other, more severe, walking difficulty' than covered in the lower rate and this would increase from £80 to £82.80 under the proposed new rates. Payments are usually sent directly to claimants bank accounts every four weeks and if their circumstances change they are told to contact the Disability Service Centre.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: MoneySavingExpert warns Virgin customers to check for 'sneaky' paid add-on
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Virgin Experience Days shoppers are being urged to check whether they were signed up to a paid membership without realising. MoneySavingExpert said its team found the £9.99-a-year Memory Makers+ subscription was being added to orders through a pre-ticked box at checkout. The consumer website said it spotted the issue when it visited the company's website on October 30 and reported it to the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA). MoneySavingExpert said Virgin Experience Days changed its website after the issue was raised, so the membership box was no longer selected by default. The membership offers discounts on purchases, free greeting cards and other benefits, and renews automatically each year. CMA guidance says businesses must obtain a customer's express consent before charging for optional extras. It says a pre-ticked box does not provide that consent when a customer must take action to avoid an extra charge. The regulator also says customers who did not expressly agree to an additional charge are legally entitled to claim a refund. MoneySavingExpert recommends searching email inboxes, including junk and spam folders, for an account activation message to check whether the membership was added. It advises customers who want to cancel or request a refund to contact memorymakers@virginexperiencedays.co.uk. A Virgin Experience Days spokesperson said: "Memory Makers+ remains a relatively new addition to our business, and we continually review and refine the programme based on performance data, customer feedback and regulatory developments." The company said most customers saved more than the cost of membership on their first purchase and that it received positive feedback about the scheme. The spokesperson added: "In the small number of cases where a customer wishes to cancel, we operate a seven day a week support operation where queries are handled within 24 hours."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Air ambulance teams safely trial hospital treatment for prolonged cardiac arrests
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: East Anglian Air Ambulance has successfully trialled a hospital treatment for patients in prolonged cardiac arrest at emergency scenes. EAAA teams used the treatment on patients in prolonged cardiac arrest outside hospital as part of the ERICA-ARREST feasibility study. The study tested whether helicopter emergency medical service clinicians could safely use resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) to improve blood flow to the heart and brain during resuscitation. Resuscitative Endovascular Balloon Occlusion of the Aorta (REBOA) is a minimally invasive procedure that involves inserting and inflating a balloon within the aorta to temporarily control blood flow. (Image: East Anglian Air Ambulance) Dr James Price, consultant emergency physician at Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust and HEMS consultant and consultant lead for research and development at EAAA, said: "Patients who remain in cardiac arrest despite prolonged resuscitation efforts currently have very limited treatment options and face extremely poor outcomes. "Our study has shown that REBOA can be delivered safely by pre-hospital critical care teams and can improve blood pressure during cardiac arrest, helping to direct blood flow to the organs that matter most. "While this study was not designed to determine whether REBOA improves survival, these findings provide a strong foundation for further research and represent an important step forward in exploring new treatment options for this group of patients." Hospitals typically use REBOA to control severe internal bleeding. Doctors insert a small balloon through a groin artery and inflate it inside the aorta, the body’s main artery. Inflating the balloon temporarily blocks blood flow to the lower body and redirects it to the heart and brain. The study tested whether the technique could help patients whose hearts would not restart after prolonged, high-quality resuscitation. Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest remains a major cause of death, and survival rates for patients experiencing prolonged cardiac arrest have not improved in 50 years. The study included 39 patients, aged 58.7 on average, who suffered non-traumatic cardiac arrests outside hospital and did not respond to advanced resuscitation. Doctors attempted REBOA a median of 51 minutes after cardiac arrest, at a very advanced stage of resuscitation. Researchers found HEMS clinicians could perform the procedure safely, with no related complications reported. After inflation, diastolic blood pressure rose by an average of 59 per cent, directing more pressure towards the heart and brain. Of the 33 patients in whom aortic blockage was confirmed, 24.2 per cent achieved a sustained return of spontaneous circulation, and 6.1 per cent survived to hospital discharge. However, researchers emphasised that the study was not intended to determine whether REBOA improves survival, as it did not include a control group. It instead tested whether the procedure was safe outside hospital and improved circulation as expected. Dr Price said the study followed years of work building the clinical skills, safeguards and research systems needed for such a complex treatment before hospital. The research was carried out by EAAA’s research, audit, innovation, and development (RAID) group. He said: "East Anglian Air Ambulance is first and foremost a regional charity looking after critically ill and injured patients across Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire, Norfolk and Suffolk, but alongside that clinical work we have built a research programme led by clinicians who look after these patients every day and want to find better ways of treating them, and ultimately save more lives." He added that the programme had improved EAAA’s overall care, beyond the ERICA-ARREST study. EAAA regularly responds to cardiac arrests across its region, which account for up to 30 per cent of the charity’s medical call-outs. Its teams deliver advanced critical care normally available only in hospital. Researchers say the findings justify further study of whether the treatment improves survival.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hinchingbrooke Hospital plans revised as fresh environmental assessment begins
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A hospital redevelopment is moving forward with a fresh environmental impact assessment underway. Plans to rebuild Hinchingbrooke Hospital have reached a new stage after North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust submitted a revised Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Scoping Report to Huntingdonshire District Council (HDC). The report sets out key changes and asks the council for a new EIA Scoping Opinion to inform the Environmental Statement for the planned application. The trust previously secured an EIA Scoping Opinion from HDC in October 2025, based on proposals developed in August 2025. An artist's impression of what the new staff accommodation will look like and what the courtyard area will look like once installed by Zed Pods Ltd. (Image: North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust) Since then, the scheme has undergone further design changes, prompting the need for a revised EIA. The updated plans include a range of modifications to the original development. These include the removal of the lower ground floor from the new hospital building, the addition of an energy centre north of the main building, and the relocation of the ambulance deck to the south-east of the site. Land at Views Common could be used temporarily as a contractor’s compound during construction, which may last up to eight years, subject to a lease agreement with the owner. The northern car park will remain at ground level, with possible solar canopies added. Plans for a multi-storey car park have been scrapped. A separate application is being prepared for car parking on the adjacent Constabulary Land, which has been removed from the main hospital application. The trust plans to submit an outline application covering new hospital buildings, an energy centre, service and administration facilities, parking, cycle storage, landscaping, drainage and improved access from Views Common Road. It will also cover the phased demolition of existing hospital buildings and the removal of some trees protected by Tree Preservation Orders. Approved enabling works include relocating staff accommodation, demolishing former staff blocks and creating a temporary car park. The trust is seeking separate permission for the Constabulary Land car park to maintain parking capacity during construction. A separate application also covers a new main intake substation to provide the hospital with an independent high-voltage electricity supply. The latest EIA Scoping Report confirms that most environmental topics identified in the 2025 assessment remain relevant. However, archaeology has now been scoped in due to the discovery of ridge and furrow earthworks and the high potential for further archaeological remains at Views Common. It also explains how the project will assess air quality, biodiversity, noise and vibration, transport and access, trees, daylight and sunlight, and wind. The trust is working with HDC, statutory consultees and other stakeholders to keep the planning process on track with the project and policy requirements. The site boundary has been redrawn to reflect the latest design, removing areas covered by separate applications and adding land at Views Common. The report says the development is not vulnerable to major accidents or disasters, so those risks will not be assessed further. That conclusion is based on the site’s location, existing safeguards and lack of nearby hazards such as major pipelines. The report also includes an assessment of how climate change could affect the development and how it can withstand those risks. It considers sudden and long-term climate hazards, the vulnerability of key site elements and existing measures to adapt. The assessment will be developed further as the design progresses. The EIA Scoping Report will support the updated hospital planning application and shape its Environmental Statement. HDC is expected to issue a revised Scoping Opinion after consulting statutory bodies and reviewing the report. Hinchingbrooke is one of seven English hospitals being rebuilt through the national New Hospital Programme because of RAAC, with the new facility expected to open by the end of 2032.

The DWP adds: "The measure will initially focus on benefits where incorrect payments are currently highest, these are: "Other benefits could be added with the approval of Parliament in the future through affirmative regulations." State Pension is explicitly excluded from this power and cannot be added by regulations. According to information issued by the DWP, it will have the "power to require banks and other financial institutions to provide information to help verify a claimant’s entitlement to benefits and identify incorrect payments. "Banks and other financial institutions will be required to look at the data they hold on accounts in receipt of a specified DWP benefit payment and match these accounts to specific eligibility indicators determined by DWP (and defined within an Eligibility Verification Notice) and highlight where the criteria have been met." Banks can only share limited information in response to an Eligibility Verification Notice, for example: They could receive a penalty for oversharing information, such as transaction information. The DWP also adds: "Any information shared through the Eligibility Verification Measure will not be shared on the presumption or suspicion that anyone is guilty of any offence." It gives the example of, for Universal Credit, an individual cannot hold more than £16,000 in savings and remain eligible for Universal Credit, "unless this capital is a result of a specified exception." It will also be a gradual process: "DWP will be gradually rolling out the use of the Eligibility Verification Measure in a test and learn environment to allow for sufficient time for business to establish best processes." When fully rolled out the Department estimates that DWP will identify between 50,000 and 100,000 overpayments as a result of the measure each year.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire businesses urged to create new opportunities for young people
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Businesses across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough are being urged to offer apprenticeships and work experience through a new campaign. Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce will launch its Opportunity Pledge at the CambsB2B South event on Thursday, November 12. Employers attending the event will be invited to make a commitment on a Pledge Wall, with T Level industry placements and internships among the opportunities they can offer. The campaign is open to businesses of all sizes and aims to encourage those that have not offered such opportunities before to take their first steps. Charlotte Horobin, chief executive officer of Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce, said: "Businesses across our region are already experiencing the consequences of skills shortages, and the evidence tells us that developing the next generation of talent must be a priority if we are to sustain economic growth. "We want employers to consider what they can offer, whether that's taking on an apprentice, providing a T Level industry placement or giving someone their first meaningful experience of the workplace." Opportunity - Attendees greet each other during a conference session (Image: Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce) The initiative comes as the 2026 to 2029 Cambridgeshire and Peterborough LSIP highlights challenges facing the region's future workforce. The report identifies that 86 per cent of future workforce demand will be driven by the need to replace existing workers. Those making a pledge will be recognised as Future Skills Champions, with their commitments displayed on the Opportunity Pledge Wall and mirrored online through the chamber's website. Participating employers will receive a digital badge and may have opportunities to feature in future campaign activity and case studies. The campaign will continue beyond CambsB2B South, with businesses able to submit pledges through the chamber's website. Ms Horobin added: "For businesses that have never done this before, we want to demonstrate that there is support available to help them take that first step. "You don't have to be a large employer to make a meaningful contribution. "As the organisation representing the employer voice through the Local Skills Improvement Plan, I would encourage every business attending CambsB2B South to visit the Pledge Wall and consider the role they can play in developing our future workforce." The event takes place at TWI Ltd, Granta Park, Great Abington, Cambridge, and is free to attend, but advance registration is required through the chamber's CambsB2B South page.
