John Evans, known to many as "Basha," now lives at Bayleaf Care Home in Huntingdon and has shared his story in the days surrounding Remembrance Sunday. Mr Evans spent a period of his life living locally in Papworth and served in the Special Forces and the Parachute Regiment during his long military career. A spokesperson for Bayleaf Care Home said: "In the days leading up to Remembrance Sunday, John had been a little quieter than usual. "But following the memorial service in Huntingdon, we saw a different side of him. "Proudly dressed, with his medals taking pride of place, it was clear just how much the occasion meant to him. John Evans is better known to many as Basha (Image: Bayleaf Care Home) "For those of us getting to know John, discovering more about his past has been a privilege." In the week following Remembrance Sunday, Mr Evans began to open up about his past, sharing stories of a life that took him far beyond the streets of Papworth. He also spoke with those around him about his love of model aircraft and woodwork, and the importance of friendship. John remains in contact with some of the men he served alongside, and Bayleaf Care Home plans to host around 10 of them at an upcoming veteran lunch. John lived in Papworth for a large portion of his life (Image: Bayleaf Care Home) The spokesperson said: "At Bayleaf, we believe that every person has a story worth telling. "The experiences, achievements, friendships and memories that make someone who they are should never be lost or overlooked. "This Remembrance Sunday reminded us that behind every medal is a person, behind every uniform is a lifetime of memories, and behind every story is someone worth taking the time to know."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Former Cambs police officer turned up to work 'smelling strongly of alcohol'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A police officer who turned up to work smelling of alcohol would have been sacked for gross misconduct, a hearing found. Former PC Ciaron Hickey, who served with Cambridgeshire Constabulary, attended a first aid refresher course at force headquarters on September 10, 2025. He arrived late, explaining that this was due to him mistakenly attending a local police station. A member of the Public and Personal Safety Training Team (PPST) detected the smell of alcohol on Mr Hickey’s breath after having a brief conversation with him outside the classroom. The PPST trainer confirmed he smelt of alcohol and reported it to the sergeant present. Mr Hickey was removed from the classroom and later admitted drinking alcohol the night before. A preliminary breath test showed 18 micrograms of alcohol per 100ml of breath. A second test an hour later showed 9 micrograms, and he was taken home. At the time of the incident, he was already under a written warning for a similar offence, having reported for duty on September 11, 2024, with excess alcohol in his system. A police misconduct hearing held at Lysander House in Bedfordshire on October 21 concluded that Mr Hickey’s actions amounted to gross misconduct. The panel found that he breached standards on fitness for duty, orders and instructions, and discreditable conduct by attending training "smelling strongly of alcohol". Mr Hickey resigned from the force on October 19, 2026, did not attend the hearing and was not represented. His federation representative confirmed he did not wish to engage with the proceedings. The panel accepted his early admission and co-operation with the investigation as mitigating factors, but said they did not outweigh the seriousness of his actions. The report stated: "The panel considered that the proven conduct was so serious as to justify dismissal and even more so, when considered together with the live written warning for similar conduct." The panel also considered the "personal difficulties" he was experiencing, but said they did not outweigh the seriousness of his conduct. As Mr Hickey was no longer a serving officer at the time of the hearing, the panel could not impose a formal disciplinary sanction. Instead, it recorded that he would have been dismissed without notice had he still been employed. ACC Vaughan Lukey chaired the misconduct panel, alongside independent members Davide Corbino and Bryan McAlley. David Tyme served as the legally qualified person.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New illegal Fire Stick warning issued as police investigating financial records
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A fresh illegal Fire Stick warning has been issued after police are cracking down on users by tracing payments through sellers’ bank accounts. The alert comes amid growing concerns over the widespread use of modified TV Fire Sticks and so-called “dodgy boxes”. These devices enable users to access premium content from providers such as Sky, TNT Sports, Disney+, and Netflix for free. However, those using the devices have been warned that police are now using financial records to find those culpable. Former detective Rav Wilding issued the warning during an appearance on BBC Morning Live. He explained that police are investigating financial records linked to the sale of modified Fire Sticks, which allow users to access premium TV content for free. Mr Wilding said: "They’re going for the distributors. "They’re going for the sellers. "They are having a lot of success. "But actually, once they’ve got the seller, they’re going through their accounts. "They’re seeing who has been paying the money for these illegal things, and if they’ve been paying them for these sticks then people should possibly expect a conversation or two if the police want to know why they’ve been paying them money for this." The illegal devices typically cost between £30 and £100 and provide unauthorised access to subscription-only TV services, including live football. Although owning a standard Fire Stick is legal, Mr Wilding said using one to stream pirated content is a crime. He said: "It’s a crime. "It’s not allowed. "Owning the stick itself is not a crime, but using it for this purpose is. "They (subscription service providers) are losing money to this, so they have been reaching out and are taking action against those people using them illegally as well. "So I wouldn’t say it’s something you should do. "It is actually a crime and it can have a nasty fine, a huge fine and also a custodial sentence for users and sellers of these things." A post shared by Amazon Fire TV (@amazonfiretv) In the UK, downloading or streaming pirated content can be a crime, but prosecutions of individual viewers remain extremely rare. Despite this, several people have been jailed this year as the clampdown on illegal streaming devices in the UK continues. Recommended reading: Those caught using or selling a 'dodgy' fire stick/box and streaming premium content without paying are in breach of Section 11 of the Fraud Act 2006. It says a person will be in breach if they obtain services "without any payment having been made for or in respect of them or without payment having been made in full". A person found guilty of this kind of offence could face a hefty fine, or even a prison sentence in extreme cases. What is your favourite TV show to watch? Let us know in the comments.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Poundland issues major update as UK stores at risk of closure
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Poundland has issued an update today (November 12), following the end of a 10-day period that allowed it to continue to try and secure a potential rescue deal. In recent months, the future of Poundland has been uncertain, with last-ditch efforts hoping to save the struggling retailer. The chain filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the end of October, which expired at midnight last night. Asked if the company was going into administration on Thursday, managing director Barry Williams told reporters: “We’re going to go and have a board meeting now to have those conversations.” Now, Poundland has issued an update, informing customers of its future plans. Poundland customers have been assured that its stores are open as normal for at least the next 10 working days. The Board of Poundland Limited said: “Over the past two weeks, Poundland has been operating under the statutory protection of a Notice of Intention (NOI) to appoint Administrators. “Amid an ongoing sale process, and with funding agreed to enable the business to continue trading during this period, the Board of Poundland has today resolved to make an application for a second NOI with a view to identifying the best available prospects for shareholders, creditors and our people. “This extends the current protections over the business for a further 10 working days. “Our stores remain open as usual during this period, and we thank our colleagues, suppliers and customers for their incredible and continued support.” Poundland has roughly 600 shops and 11,000 employees across the UK. Ahead of the announcement, Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice said: “Hopefully the directors will be able to extend the notice of administration period from tonight to allow time for a deal to be done with a new buyer for Poundland. “This will protect many thousands of jobs and keep an important value retailer on the High Street, for hard-pressed consumers worried about rising bills.” After a meeting with MPs on the Commons Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, Mr Williams thanked the chain’s staff, whose jobs are at risk. He told Sky News he was “representing 11,000 colleagues” as well as thousands in the broader supply chain and “maybe even the retail industry” at the meeting. Asked whether he could guarantee the security of jobs and keep the business going in the run-up to Christmas, he said there were “no guarantees at this point”. It is understood that Poundland’s owners, Gordon Brothers, have enabled the release of around £10 million of funding for things such as paying staff, taxes and suppliers of stock. The extension to Wednesday’s deadline could mean the prospect of a deal that would satisfy the company’s creditors remains on the table. Advisers have been in talks with parties interested in buying the brand or parts of the business such as swathes of shops. Recommended reading: It has held talks with potential bidders including Tesco over proposals to buy up to 150 stores, and other chains such as Iceland and Lidl. Investment firm Xyra Holdings emerged as a potential buyer for the whole business, while Irish firm Martin Property Group is believed to remain interested. Gordon Brothers previously rejected a takeover offer from Martin Property Group but management named the firm as the preferred bidder last month. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: HMRC Child Benefit rates to rise in April 2027 - new payment amounts explained
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: HMRC has revealed that millions of families could receive more money in Child Benefit from next April, with new weekly payment rates now appearing on the Government's website. Parents currently receive £27.05 a week for their eldest or only child, with an additional £17.90 paid for each other child. However, these payments are set to increase again for the 2027/28 tax year, according to an update to the Government's Child Benefit information page on November 10. The provisional figures show that the weekly rate for an eldest or only child will rise to £28, while payments for each additional child are expected to increase to £18.55. This would give families an extra £49.40 a year for their eldest or only child, and an additional £33.80 annually for every other child they claim for. The figures are currently marked as 'provisional', meaning they are not yet confirmed as final rates. However, the Government website's update history shows that previous provisional Child Benefit rates have subsequently matched the final amounts announced. The weekly rate of Guardian's Allowance is also expected to increase, rising from £22.95 in 2026/27 to £23.75 in 2027/28. Guardian's Allowance is an additional payment for people bringing up a child whose parents have died. In some circumstances, it can also be claimed where one parent has died and the surviving parent cannot look after the child. Child Benefit is available to parents or guardians responsible for a child under 16, or under 20 if they remain in approved education or training. Only one person can claim Child Benefit for each child, but there is now no limit on the number of children families can receive payments for. This follows the abolition of the two-child limit in April this year. Previously, the restriction meant parents could generally only claim Child Benefit for a maximum of two children. However, some families may face a tax charge if their earnings exceed the High Income Child Benefit Charge threshold. The charge applies if either parent has an individual income of more than £60,000 in tax years from 2024/25 onwards. For tax years up to and including 2023/24, the threshold was £50,000. Child Benefit is usually paid directly into a claimant's bank account every four weeks. Claiming also provides valuable National Insurance credits, which can help protect a parent's entitlement to the State Pension.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: More than one million yellow box fines issued - what are the rules and how to appeal
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: More than a million yellow box junction penalties have been issued by councils in England and Wales since 2023, research suggests. Used car retailer cinch said 37 councils reported issuing 1,047,472 penalty charge notices between 2023 and 2026, with nearly £58 million in penalty payments also reported. The company sent Freedom of Information requests to 217 authorities across the UK, but the penalty figures reported are not a total for every council or for the whole country. The underlying council responses were not supplied with the release and could not be independently checked. Its figures include 347,614 notices in 2025 and a further 231,458 in 2026 up to July. In Hackney, the number rose from 314 in 2024 to 8,567 in 2025, while Buckinghamshire recorded an increase from 3,618 to 16,120. Liverpool recorded 7,622 notices in 2025, compared with 3,376 the year before, according to the research. At Dennis Road Roundabout in Surrey, the number rose from 1,557 in 2024 to 9,101 in 2025. Cinch said councils had received more than 100,000 challenges since 2023 and accepted over 18,000. Those included 6,954 accepted challenges in Redbridge out of 27,615 received, and 3,582 out of 8,328 in Cardiff. Ben Welham, a motoring expert at cinch, said: "Yellow box junctions help to keep traffic moving, but they can be difficult to navigate, particularly in busy towns and cities where traffic is constantly stopping and starting." Yellow box junctions have criss-cross markings designed to keep traffic from blocking the road. Under rule 174 of the Highway Code, drivers must not enter until their exit road or lane is clear. There is an exception for drivers turning right who are held up only by oncoming traffic or other vehicles waiting to turn right. At a signalled roundabout, drivers must not enter a box unless they can cross it completely without stopping. The Northern Ireland Highway Code sets out the same box-junction rules. Penalty amounts and payment periods depend on the issuing authority, so motorists should check the details on their notice. For example, Newcastle City Council says its yellow box penalty is £70, reduced to £35 if paid within 21 days. In England and Wales, a motorist who believes a council PCN is wrong can make a formal challenge, known as a representation, to the authority that issued it. Cinch says drivers generally have 28 days to challenge a notice and should provide supporting evidence, such as photographs or available camera footage. Check the notice for the applicable deadline and instructions, including how to view any footage. If the authority rejects the formal challenge, GOV.UK says there are 28 days after receiving the rejection notice to appeal to an independent tribunal. The appeal is made to London Tribunals for a PCN issued in London, or the Traffic Penalty Tribunal for one issued elsewhere in England or Wales. Scotland and Northern Ireland have different appeal arrangements, so drivers there should follow the instructions from the issuing body. If an appeal is successful, the PCN is cancelled and the motorist does not have to pay.

Plans are set to be approved to replace “potentially unsafe cladding” on blocks of flats in Cambridgeshire. The Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority’s growth committee recommended the new Local Remediation Acceleration Plan, or LRAP, be approved. The plan details the authority’s strategy for replacing cladding which does not meet fire safety standards on residential buildings of five stories or more. The building owner has ultimate responsibility for carrying out the work but a new bill currently being considered by Parliament could introduce fines of up to £500k for those who fail to fix the issues without delay. Cllr Sarah Conboy, chair of the committee, said: “This comes from a very difficult place, many of us will remember the heart-wrenching experience that happened at Grenfell. “The horrendous loss of life, but also the impact it had on a whole community as well as everybody involved in responding to that incident.” It was earlier revealed that there are ten high-rise flat buildings of seven stories or more in Cambridgeshire – all in Cambridge – which still need cladding replaced. “This was along with 62 medium-rise flats, of five or six stories, across the county according to the latest report presented to the committee. “It added that a few buildings have come in and out of scope 'during detailed assessment'. The combined authority has previously said they are “confident” in meeting the government’s targets that cladding on high-rises be replaced by the end of 2029 and end of 2031 for medium-rises – deadlines introduced in 2025. The updated plan, replacing the LRAP approved in 2025, addresses “key risks” including “landlord reluctance, contractor capacity and developer disputes”. The report presented to the committee added that “contractor capacity and quality of workmanship is a particular risk given this is a nationwide task”. Sean Hedger, the remediation manager, said that replacing cladding is a “lengthy process” which can take up to two years. He said he was concerned about the term “unsafe buildings” as it could worry residents, reassuring them that they are still safe to live in. He said: “Just because a building requires remediation of the external wall system it does not mean that the building is unsafe to live in. Responsible persons would often put in interim measures such as an upgraded fire alarm system to enable simultaneous evacuation instead of a stay put policy.” He said that in areas of the country where residents have had to move from their flats, this is “generally” due to “a mixture of fire safety and structural issues as well”. Cllr Ros Hathorn said this was “such important work” and they are the growth committee so their remit includes housing and development. She said: “Actually this is one of the most important things we need to do because Grenfell caused massive damage, but also damaged people’s confidence in living in flats. “And actually we need to rebuild that reassurance and until we do that it is going to be very challenging to respond to the housing crisis so this is such an important piece of work.” The committee recommended the plan be approved when it goes to the CPCA board for a final decision later this month.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Funding threat could render world-leading Cambridgeshire telescope defunct
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A world-leading radio telescope could be shut down if its funding is withdrawn. The Cambridge Telescope, at the Mullard Radio Astronomy Observatory in South Cambridgeshire, is one of seven e-MERLIN radio telescopes that work as a single powerful instrument. Its future is uncertain after the Science and Technology Facilities Council and UK Research and Innovation proposed ending all operational funding for e-MERLIN after March 2028. Cllr Bridget Smith, leader of South Cambridgeshire District Council, has written to the Secretary of State urging a review of the decision and warning of its potential impact on UK science. Read more Cyclist seriously injured in van hit and run as police appeal for witnesses Four roads near Ely set to close for marking and surfacing works Tributes pour in remembering beloved Littleport pub landlord Young boy taken to hospital after crash involving bike and car In a November 10 letter, she said ending funding without a replacement plan posed an "existential threat" to e-MERLIN and could leave the Cambridge Telescope "defunct." Cllr Smith said: "This is a world-leading scientific facility, right here on our doorstep, and we are facing the very real prospect of losing it. "Once we lose facilities like this, we can't simply bring them back. "Decades of expertise and scientific achievement could be lost for good. "It's extraordinary that the Government is talking about making Cambridge the engine of Britain's economic growth while allowing the funding to disappear from the very scientific infrastructure that makes this area so special. "The Government needs to put its money where its mouth is. "If Ministers are serious about backing Cambridge and British science, they need to step in and save this telescope." The telescope, owned and operated by the University of Manchester, works alongside six others across England. The network’s 200km spread gives it a 200km baseline and resolution comparable to the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes. It has helped produce more than 1,000 peer-reviewed papers and supports thousands of researchers worldwide. The funding row comes as the Government promotes Greater Cambridge and the Oxford-Cambridge Growth Corridor as engines of economic growth. In her letter, Cllr Smith argued that e-MERLIN supports the wider research and innovation economy by attracting investment and creating highly skilled jobs in science and engineering. She warned that losing the facility could undermine the future success of the growth corridor. South Cambridgeshire MP Pippa Heylings also voiced concerns. Ms Heylings said: "Cambridge is known across the world for its ground-breaking science, and this telescope is part of what makes that possible. "You cannot build a world-leading science economy by dismantling the world-leading science facilities we already have. "Yet that is exactly what these cuts risk doing. "This isn't just about one telescope. "It's about the future of British science, the skilled jobs and expertise we depend on, and whether the Government is genuinely committed to the growth it keeps promising. "We need a proper long-term funding solution, not a decision that could throw away decades of scientific achievement." Cllr Smith has called on the Government to work with UKRI and STFC to find a sustainable long-term funding solution before the existing arrangements expire in March 2028. She also wants any final decision delayed until its scientific, economic and strategic effects are fully assessed. The letter was also sent to Liberal Democrat MPs Pippa Heylings, Ian Sollom and Charlotte Cane, and to the party’s science, innovation and technology spokesperson Victoria Collins. The observatory has also been the subject of concerns over East West Rail, with the University of Cambridge warning that electromagnetic interference and vibration could jeopardise research.

In addition, the double-mini roundabout at the B1043 Huntingdon Road, Priory Hill Road and Mill Lane intersection would be changed to a staggered T-junction, as the developers claim it had previously been identified as "a safety concern". summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Just under half of children in Huntingdon miss out on NHS dentist visits
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Just under half of young children in Huntingdon are missing out on NHS dental care, which is below the national average. Practice Radar figures show 53 per cent of children in Huntingdon saw an NHS dentist in the year to March 2026. That compares with 58 per cent across England when measured on the same basis. The gap is even wider among younger children, with just 41.3 per cent of those aged between one and five in Huntingdon seeing an NHS dentist during the year. The figures come amid ongoing national concerns about access to NHS dentistry, especially for younger children. Practice Radar analysed NHS Business Services Authority data to estimate child dental attendance in all 543 English constituencies. The analysis found large regional differences, with the proportion of children seen by an NHS dentist ranging from 32.2 per cent in the City of London and Westminster to 74.5 per cent in Sheffield Hallam. In 62 constituencies, fewer than half of children saw an NHS dentist during the year. The study also examined tooth decay among five-year-olds, but those figures are reported by council area rather than constituency. In Huntingdonshire, 11.4 per cent of five-year-olds had experienced tooth decay in the 2023/24 survey, compared with 22.4 per cent nationally. Huntingdon is therefore not among the 60 constituencies with below-average NHS dental attendance and significantly higher childhood tooth decay. Practice Radar warned that the two figures cover different geographic areas. The 53 per cent attendance rate covers children living in Huntingdon, while the 11.4 per cent decay rate covers the wider Huntingdonshire council area. The research also examined NHS dental contracts in the area. The analysis included seven NHS general dental contracts in Huntingdon, with a median payment of £34.51 per unit of dental activity (UDA). A UDA is the NHS measure for dental work, with different treatments given different values. Across England, the median constituency had an NHS dentist visit rate of 58.6 per cent for children and 47.5 per cent for one- to five-year-olds. Fewer than 40 per cent of one- to five-year-olds saw an NHS dentist in 111 constituencies. There are signs of improvement across England, with 508 out of 543 constituencies recording a higher proportion of children seen by an NHS dentist compared to two years earlier. However, the researchers emphasised that the figures only cover NHS dental care. Children treated entirely privately are excluded, so the figures do not show how many receive dental care overall. Children are counted by where they live, not where their dentist is based, so some Huntingdon residents may receive care outside the constituency. The analysis used NHS Dental Statistics for England 2025/26, tooth-decay data from the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities and population estimates from the Office for National Statistics. A recent Cambridgeshire MP survey found nearly half of respondents were not registered with an NHS dentist, while about half had paid privately after struggling to access NHS treatment. Local NHS dentists have told an MP that contracts are financially and operationally "unviable", with practices losing money on NHS work and subsidising it through private income.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: David Walliams content removed from iPlayer after sexual misconduct allegations
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The BBC is removing content featuring David Walliams from iPlayer. It follows an investigation into sexual misconduct allegations against the comedian and writer. Multiple women have accused David Walliams of sexually inappropriate behaviour and grooming, including when they were teenagers, according to an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News. Walliams denies all allegations against him. A BBC spokesperson said: "These are serious allegations. "As such, the BBC is looking carefully at all material featuring and written by David Walliams on our platforms. "We are in the process of removing some programmes, including Little Britain, whilst this review is underway." Other affected shows include The Wheel and Would I Lie To You. ITV announced this afternoon that it is set to air a new documentary tonight about the allegations. David Walliams: Power and Silence will air tonight at 10.50pm on ITV1. The hour-long special is available to stream now on YouTube or ITVX. It comes following a three-year joint investigation by ITV News and The Guardian. The investigation alleges Walliams preyed on teenage girls and young women for sexual purposes. David Walliams was today (November 10) named as the celebrity who tried to block publication of his identity amid allegations of “inappropriate sexual activities” with girls and young women. Multiple women accuse Walliams of “grooming” them as teenagers, while another described her alleged encounter with Walliams as “sexual assault”. Walliams is also accused of inappropriate conduct and sexual harassment at his former publisher HarperCollins, and while working on Britain’s Got Talent. Responding to the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams denied all allegations against him. He said: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with... I realise I did not always take people’s feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. “And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did... “I am not a sexual predator... I have not broken the law... I am devastated that some of the women I met ten to twenty years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.” Walliams, 55, brought legal action against Independent Television News (ITN) and Guardian News and Media (GNM), publisher of The Guardian, ahead of the two organisations reporting allegations against him, including of sexual misconduct and potential criminal activity. Lawyers for the media organisations previously told the High Court in London the allegations involved Walliams’ alleged “abuse of power and status” to contact young women and try to engage in “inappropriate and exploitative sexual activities”. Walliams denied the claims and unsuccessfully sought an injunction to prevent these publications because of the risk he would take his own life, after two previous suicide attempts. The author was granted anonymity during the proceedings, which was lifted after his injunction bid was dismissed and GNM and ITN published their investigations on Tuesday. During a two-day trial in October, the court was told by the media organisations’ lawyers that the allegations were gathered after “a wide-ranging and rigorous investigation” and that there was a “strong” public interest in publishing them. Gavin Millar KC said that reporters from the media organisations had spoken to more than 100 people, including more than 30 sources with first-hand accounts as well as Walliams’ friends and colleagues. Walliams’ lawyers said that he had initially attempted suicide after receiving letters from ITN and GNM asking for his reply to the allegations, because of “long-term trauma and the fear of trial by media”. Sara Mansoori KC, representing Walliams, told the court that any publication relating to him about these allegations “would have a potentially fatal impact”. The barrister said: “The only reason they would not be fatal is because the claimant would be locked up and prevented from his desire to end his life.” Judge Mr Justice Nicklin refused the bid for an injunction, ruling it would be an “exceptionally serious interference” with freedom of expression. In the 52-page judgment, he also said that granting the injunction would not treat the man’s psychiatric condition or eliminate his elevated risk. He continued that hospitals and health staff caring for Walliams, who was detained under the Mental Health Act in October, meant that the state had “assumed responsibility” for his immediate safety and “can provide significant protection”, which “materially reduces the likelihood of suicide”. The former Britain’s Got Talent judge, known for appearing in comedy shows including Come Fly With Me and Little Britain alongside Matt Lucas, has sold more than 60 million copies of his children’s books globally. They include The Boy In The Dress, Fing, and Gangsta Granny, the latter of which was turned into a one-hour BBC special in 2013, followed by a sequel starring Sheridan Smith in 2022. Walliams’ book publisher HarperCollins dropped him in December 2025, after an investigation into allegations he had “harassed” young women, which Walliams strongly denied. Earlier this month, theme park Alton Towers permanently closed its World Of David Walliams attraction, which featured rides inspired by the books. Walliams left Britain’s Got Talent in 2022 after he apologised for making “disrespectful comments” about auditioning contestants during filming breaks in January 2020 at the London Palladium. In 2023, Britain’s Got Talent producer Fremantle apologised and reached an “amicable resolution” with Walliams after the remarks he made while on the show were leaked.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Workers over 21 given £910 cash boost confirms Andy Burnham
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Millions of workers are in line for a pay rise next April, with Andy Burnham's Government confirming a 3.9% increase to the National Living Wage. The increase means people aged 21 and over who work full-time on the minimum rate will see their gross annual earnings rise by £910 from April 1, 2027, according to HM Treasury. The National Living Wage will increase from £12.71 to £13.21 an hour, with around 2.3 million workers across the UK expected to benefit from the changes. Younger workers will also receive a boost, with the National Minimum Wage for those aged 18 to 20 rising by the same percentage. Their hourly rate will increase from £10.85 to £11.27, also from April 1. The 3.9% increase is higher than the latest Consumer Prices Index (CPI) inflation figure, which stood at 3.5% in the 12 months to September 2026. Confirming the changes, HM Treasury said: "To support low-paid workers across the UK, the government is raising the National Living Wage and National Minimum Wages, which is expected to benefit around 2.3 million workers. "On 1 April 2027, the National Living Wage will increase by 3.9% to £13.21 per hour, equivalent to an increase of £910 in the gross annual earnings of a full-time worker on the National Living Wage. The National Minimum Wage for 18- to 20-year-olds will also increase by 3.9% to £11.27 per hour. "By accepting the Low Pay Commission's recommendations in full this year, the government is ensuring workers are rewarded fairly for their work, while protecting jobs, backing businesses, and strengthening the conditions for economic growth." The £910 annual increase applies to someone aged 21 or over working full-time on the National Living Wage. It is a rise in gross earnings, meaning the figure is before Income Tax and National Insurance deductions. The new hourly rate of £13.21 will apply from April 1, 2027. Workers aged 18 to 20 will see their minimum hourly pay increase by 42p, from £10.85 to £11.27. The latest increase also marks a change in the pace of pay rises for younger workers. Since Labour returned to power in 2024, the National Minimum Wage for 18 to 20-year-olds has increased by 26%. The 2027 rise brings their increase into line with the percentage increase for workers aged 21 and over, rather than giving younger workers a larger proportional uplift. The 3.9% increase is above the latest CPI inflation rate of 3.5%, recorded by the Office for National Statistics in the year to September 2026. Recommended reading: The Low Pay Commission (LPC), which advises the Government on minimum wage rates, had previously said the National Living Wage would need to rise by around 3.7% in 2027 to reach £13.18 an hour, keeping pace with its expectations for average pay growth. However, in March, it changed the LPC's remit to give it more scope to consider labour market conditions when setting the minimum wage for 18 to 20-year-olds. The new rates will take effect on April 1, 2027.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Woman with MS delivers 16,000-signature petition calling for fairer PIP assessments
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A woman living with multiple sclerosis (MS) in Huntingdon has delivered a petition signed by over 16,000 people to the UK Government. The petition calls on the government to make Personal Independence Payment (PIP) fairer for people with MS. It was delivered on November 3 by 56-year-old Sharon Docherty, who has secondary progressive MS. She was joined by Janis Winehouse, Amy Winehouse’s mother and also living with MS, and Neil Duncan Jordan MP. Sharon said: "During my assessment, it appeared the assessor had not read any of the medical evidence I'd submitted. "It also felt like the questions they asked did not allow me to explain the full nuances of living with a condition like MS." MP Neil Duncan-Jordan PIP hand in (Image: Sharon Docherty) The petition was organised by the MS Society to coincide with the government’s review into PIP, the Timms Review, which will be published later this month. Sharon worked closely with the charity to develop the campaign. More than 150,000 people in the UK live with MS, including an estimated 1,900 in Cambridgeshire. The neurological condition affects the brain and spinal cord and can cause a wide range of physical and cognitive symptoms that often fluctuate or remain invisible to others. PIP is designed to help disabled people cover the extra costs of living independently, but the assessment process has been widely criticised as "rigid" and not reflective of variable conditions like MS. Sharon said: "At times, the system can feel as though it is designed to discourage people from applying rather than support those who need help." She said receiving PIP has allowed her to engage in activities recommended by her therapist, but she's due to be reassessed in five years' time despite having a progressive condition. The MS Society is calling for a more flexible, person-centred approach to PIP, including lifetime awards for people with long-term, progressive conditions and an end to unnecessary reassessments.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Martin Lewis issues 'awful' energy bill warning as price cap set to jump by £276
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Martin Lewis has warned households struggling with energy bills that costs are likely to get worse before they get better, as millions of people face the 'awful' prospect of a sharp rise in January. On his X account, the Money Saving Expert founder said: "The latest predictions for the January Price Cap - AWFUL, up 28.8%! This is our internal MSE document where we average three forecasts and how its changed over the past few weeks as wholesale rates have continued to rocket." It comes as energy analysts predict the Ofgem price cap could jump by 16 per cent at the start of 2027, adding hundreds of pounds to the annual bill of a typical household. Experts at Cornwall Insight forecast that the cap will rise by £276, taking it from £1,723 to £1,999 a year for a typical dual-fuel household from January 2027. The prospect of another increase will be particularly worrying for families heading into one of the coldest and most expensive periods of the year, when heating demand typically rises and daylight hours are shorter. There are also fears the increase could be even bigger if the conflict involving the US, Iran and Israel continues to disrupt energy markets and push up wholesale gas prices. The latest predictions for the January Price Cap - AWFUL, up 28.8%! This is our internal MSE document where we average three forecasts and how its changed over the past few weeks as wholesale rates have continued to rocket. PS Jan prediction is getting much more locked in as we're 85% through the 19 August to 17 November 2026 assessment period. April & July predictions are much more crystal ballgazing. — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) November 3, 2026 There has been some positive news for households, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham announcing a series of measures intended to ease pressure on energy bills. These include removing VAT from domestic energy bills, which is expected to save the average household around £45 to £50, and a £100 winter energy payment for around 20 million households living in Council Tax bands A to D. The Government has also confirmed plans to scrap gas standing charges, which are fixed daily fees households pay regardless of how much gas they use. Best to keep the heating on low all day? Does foil behind radiators work? Is now the time to fix? Got questions on energy bills, energy efficiency, solar panels & more, that's next week's @ITVMlshow. I'll be joined by specialist heat engineers so pls post questions by reply. — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) November 6, 2026 However, Martin Lewis warned that consumers could have to wait until late 2027 or even January 2028 before the change takes effect. Chancellor John Healey said the Government would ask Ofgem to deliver the removal of the charges in 2027, or as soon as possible afterwards. Speaking about the timetable, Mr Lewis said: "The gas standing charge, on the price cap anyway, is to be scrapped in 2027. What does 2027 mean? Well, as it's part of the price cap, it definitely won't be before the 1st of October." The typical gas standing charge is currently around £108 a year for households paying by direct debit or prepayment meter. Under the planned changes, this fixed cost will be moved into the unit rate – the amount customers pay for each kilowatt-hour of gas they use. That means the reform will not automatically cut everyone's bill. Instead, households that use less gas should benefit, while those who use more could pay more. Mr Lewis said: "This isn't about saving money in totality. This is about a structural change and I've always argued that – for fairness – so that those low users who struggle at the moment to cut their bills because so much of it is about the standing charge, and I get so many messages about this, that won't happen anymore." He estimated that the change could add roughly 0.8p to 0.9p per kilowatt-hour to the gas unit rate, although he stressed this was only a rough calculation and the final figure would depend on energy prices at the time. He added: "What does it mean? Lower users will pay less, higher users will pay more. And actually, because there are quite a lot a low number of very high users and it's done on the mean average, it actually works out 60 per cent of people will pay less, 40 per cent of people will pay more." The Government estimates that around 60 per cent of account-holding households could save an average of £45 a year as a result of the change. In a statement, the Government said: "Tens of millions of households will no longer pay standing charges on their gas bills as the Government gives families more control over what they pay and some more breathing space. "A standing charge is a fixed daily fee added on top of a household gas bill, regardless of how much gas has been used. A household could use no gas at all but still must pay the standing charge. "The Chancellor will announce an end to this unfair and outdated practice. He will ask Ofgem to deliver removal of these charges – which are £108 a year for the typical household on average – in 2027 or as soon as possible after. "Instead, these fixed costs will be paid on the unit rate, which could save 60% of account-holding households around an average of £45 off their annual bill." The Ofgem price cap currently stands at £1,723 a year for a typical dual-fuel household paying by direct debit. This is a 3.6 per cent increase on the previous three-month period. The price cap sets the maximum rates suppliers can charge customers on standard variable tariffs for each unit of gas and electricity, as well as the daily standing charges. It is not a limit on the total amount a household can pay, meaning bills will be higher for those who use more energy. Cornwall Insight expects the cap to rise by 16 per cent in January 2027, reaching £1,999 a year – an increase of £276. The consultancy said: "The price cap is expected to rise by 16% compared to October, reaching £1,999 a year for a typical dual-fuel household in January 2027, an increase of £276 and the largest rise since January 2023." It said the increase was largely being driven by escalating conflict in the Middle East, which continues to disrupt gas supplies in the UK and around the world. The consultancy added that EU gas storage stocks had fallen to their lowest September levels in 15 years, adding to pressure on the market. It also warned that some of the price increases had already been reflected in the calculation for January's cap. Cornwall Insight said: "Ofgem sets the wholesale part of the cap using prices from a fixed period known as the observation window. With that window for the January cap now nearly halfway through, the price rises seen in September are already locked in, making a January increase all but certain."

Ofsted recommended that leaders improve the consistency of curriculum delivery to ensure all pupils, especially those needing adaptations or capable of greater challenge, could build securely on previous learning. The report also called for stronger leadership to ensure improvement work is properly assessed and changes are consistently embedded. Debra Beachus-Wells, chair of governors, said: "Brington isn't just a school; it's a whole community, one that is inclusive and welcoming to all pupils and parents. "Since Mrs Baish took on the headship in May 2025, she has achieved such positive improvements across the school. "The progress made is clear for everyone to see and is reflected in the recent Ofsted report. "The Governing Board is fully committed to continuing to work closely with Mrs Baish, the staff, pupils and parents to build on this success. "Together, we want to keep moving the school forward, making further improvements and ensuring Brington continues to be the fantastic school and community that we all know it can be. "We are proud of what has been achieved so far and excited about what we can accomplish together in the future." The report said overall absence was 3.9 per cent in 2025/26, compared with 5.1 per cent nationally. Persistent absence was 8.4 per cent, compared with 14.4 per cent nationally. Mrs Baish said: "This is a celebration of our whole school community – our wonderful children, dedicated staff, supportive governors and families. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: How Virgin Media 02 customers can keep free emails as service ends
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Virgin Media is closing its free email service, leaving account holders to decide whether to transfer or move elsewhere. Users who want to keep their existing address can switch to Junara, an email provider owned by Atmail. The change affects addresses ending in virginmedia.com, virgin.net, ntlworld.com and blueyonder.co.uk. Virgin Media says it is contacting affected account holders in phases and they will have at least 45 days from the first communication to decide what to do. They can sign up with Junara, download their emails and data before moving to another provider, or close their account. Junara says users whose accounts are suspended after their deadline have another 120 days to sign up and reactivate them. After that period, the account and its data will be permanently deleted and cannot be recovered, the provider says. Virgin Media stopped offering email accounts to new customers in May 2022. Current Virgin Media broadband, landline or TV customers who move to Junara will be offered their first 12 months free, subject to a 99p transfer fee. Customers who have told Virgin Media they need additional support will be offered their first 18 months free. Former Virgin Media customers who no longer have those services will need to sign up to a standard Junara plan to keep their email service. Those who do not want to transfer can download their data and move to another provider, including a free service. Virgin Media says its messages about the change will not include clickable sign-up links, and customers should be cautious of unexpected requests for personal details, passwords or payment information. A Virgin Media spokesperson said: "As we focus and prioritise our investments and resource on ensuring our customers have the best connectivity experience, we've taken the decision to close the remaining Virgin Media email accounts. "We are transferring our email service to Junara, a specialist cloud-based email provider owned by Atmail, giving users a clear route to keep their existing Virgin Media email address if they choose to. "We're writing directly to all impacted customers to clearly explain the changes and will provide a 45-day window to either sign up with Junara, move to an alternative email provider, or close their account. "To support users through this transition, all current Virgin Media customers wishing to move to Junara will receive their first year of service free of charge, with additional support available for those who need it."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP starts bank checks on benefit claimants – what officials can now see
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has confirmed it has issued its first notice requiring banks to check accounts linked to benefit payments, marking the start of a major new crackdown on fraud and incorrect claims. The new powers mean banks and other financial institutions must check certain accounts against information supplied by the DWP to help establish whether people are still entitled to the benefits they receive. The measure could affect people claiming Universal Credit, Pension Credit and New Style Employment and Support Allowance (ESA), with the Government estimating it will save taxpayers £1.2billion over five years. Work and Pensions Minister Lilian Greenwood confirmed the first eligibility verification notice had been issued in a written statement to Parliament on October 26, explaining: "I am informing the House that the Department for Work and Pensions has issued the first eligibility verification notice under powers introduced by the Public Authorities (Fraud, Error and Recovery) Act 2025, which amends the Social Security Administration Act 1992." The checks are designed to identify potential problems with benefit entitlement, particularly where someone may have more savings than the rules allow or has spent too long abroad. However, the DWP has stressed that the new powers do not give officials unrestricted access to people's bank accounts. Banks cannot hand over full statements or details of everyday spending, and a flag does not automatically mean someone has committed fraud or will lose their benefits - the full details are clarified here . The Eligibility Verification Measure (EVM) applies to three benefits: Under the system, the DWP sends banks and other financial institutions information known as 'eligibility indicators'. These are based on benefit rules relating to a claimant's capital, such as savings, and the amount of time they have spent abroad. Financial institutions then check the information they hold on accounts receiving specified DWP benefit payments. If an account meets one of the indicators, the bank must share limited information with the department. The checks can also cover linked accounts and joint accounts. The account does not necessarily have to belong to the person claiming the benefit – it could belong to someone else if it is linked to the account receiving the payment. The new powers do not give the DWP direct access to people's online banking or allow officials to monitor accounts in real time. Banks and financial institutions can share limited information if an eligibility indicator is met. This can include: However, banks cannot share full bank statements, details of individual transactions, how someone spends their money or the specific locations where transactions took place. They are also banned from sharing sensitive personal information about a person's background, such as political opinions or religious beliefs. Financial institutions could face fines if they disclose information they are not permitted to share. Today we discussed a new Bill to crack down on fraud. It's fair enough to go after those ripping off public money, but one section of the Bill has become a vehicle for bank spying powers, mandated by the DWP targetting benefit claimants. These new eligibility verification powers allow suspicionless surveillance - not a good precedent - and needs to be challenged, however much taxpayers money we're told mass financial monitoring will recoup. — Claire Fox (@Fox_Claire) May 15, 2025 A bank flag does not automatically mean someone has committed benefit fraud or will lose their payments. The information is intended to act as a prompt for the DWP to carry out further checks, rather than proof that someone has done something wrong. In her statement to Parliament, Ms Greenwood said: "The information received will act only as a prompt for further checks." She added: "Information received through EVM will not, in isolation, imply that a person is guilty of any wrongdoing or that their benefit entitlement will change." If information supplied by a bank suggests someone might be receiving an incorrect benefit payment, the DWP will review their claim. It could find that they are no longer eligible or that the amount they receive is wrong. The department may then contact the claimant to ask questions or request further information to establish whether they are still entitled to the benefit. The minister said: "DWP will have regard to all information relevant to a benefit decision, including information that was not obtained through EVM. Decisions will continue to be made by trained departmental staff through established processes." This means any decision about benefit entitlement or payments will be made by DWP staff, rather than automatically following information received from a bank. The department says it will contact people through their Universal Credit online journal if they have one. Those without an online account may be contacted by phone, letter or text message. Claimants are advised to respond as soon as possible to avoid their payments being delayed or stopped. Anyone who disagrees with a decision can ask the DWP to look at it again through a process known as a mandatory reconsideration. The new guidance also reminds claimants that they must keep the DWP informed if their circumstances change. This is particularly important for people whose benefit entitlement is affected by savings, income or time spent abroad. Changes that should be reported include: The DWP warns that failing to report a change promptly could mean someone receives too much benefit and has to repay the money. People who provide incorrect or incomplete information, or fail to report a change, could also face prosecution or a fine. If a claimant is unsure whether a change affects their payments, they should check the eligibility rules for the benefit they receive or contact the relevant DWP office. In her October 26 statement, Ms Greenwood told MPs that the department had issued its first eligibility verification notice under powers introduced by the Public Authorities (Fraud, Error and Recovery) Act 2025. She said: "This marks an important step in the Department’s use of data to assist with identifying and preventing fraud and error, correcting inaccurate benefit payments sooner and helping prevent avoidable debt." Recommended reading: The minister said the measure was expected to save taxpayers £1.2billion over the next five years. She added that it would help ensure people received the support they were entitled to while protecting public money and addressing suspected fraud. The department will initially introduce the system through a controlled test-and-learn phase, allowing it to assess how it works before expanding its use. We're closing a loophole in Universal Credit Serious offenders detained for hospital treatment will no longer receive benefits while their living costs are being met by the NHS Watch Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden discuss the changes on @GMB https://t.co/ibm9VjDQ1w — Department for Work and Pensions (@DWPgovuk) October 20, 2026 Ms Greenwood said this would allow the DWP to assess "systems, data quality, operational impacts and customer outcomes" before the measure was scaled up. The Government says safeguards have been built into the legislation and a statutory code of practice, which sets out how the powers can be used and how personal information must be protected. Ms Greenwood told Parliament: "The measure contains a number of clear and vital safeguards."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: The rare wildlife species that can be found in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire’s fens, wetlands and waterways are home to some very unusual species of wildlife. If you're an avid birdwatcher, an aspiring lepidopterist or simply an animal lover, you'll want to keep a look out for these amazing creatures. So without further ado, here are some of the rare wildlife species that can be found in Cambridgeshire. Otters have made a remarkable comeback in Cambridgeshire after once being driven close to extinction by pollution and habitat loss. They are now regularly spotted along the River Great Ouse, the River Cam and waterways such as Fen Drayton Lakes. Footage from Cambridge City Council shows an otter caught on camera at Logan's Meadow Local Nature Reserve. The UK's biggest and rarest newt is widespread across lowland England, particularly in wetlands. It has spotted flanks, a striking, orange belly, warty skin and is almost black in colour. The great crested newt is common in wetland environments (Image: Peter Hagger) The UK's tallest bird, standing at an impressive four feet, is instantly recognisable but disappeared from Britain for centuries. When a trio of migrating birds were blown off course in 1979, ending up in Norfolk, reintroduction projects began and there are now around 160 in Britain. If you're lucky, you can spot them in the Cambridgeshire Fens. Cambridgeshire’s wetland habitats are important for the bittern, a secretive heron whose distinctive booming call can be heard during spring and summer. Once extinct in the UK as a breeding species, its numbers have recovered through habitat restoration projects. According to the RSPB, the species is now thriving at the Ouse Fen nature reserve. A bittern in open flight (Image: Nigel Sprowell) According to the Essex Wildlife Trust, the East of England is the only place in Britain where water vole populations are increasing. However, they are under serious threat from habitat loss by the American mink. It can be distinguished from the brown rat by its furry tail and rounded nose.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A controlling partner who subjected his victim to a decade of abuse and even strangled her has been jailed for more than two years. Anthony Bernard, 49, of Croyland Road, Walton, Peterborough, pleaded guilty to engaging in controlling or coercive behaviour in an intimate or family relationship and intentional strangulation. His abuse came to light after an incident on August 11, when he emptied his partner’s wardrobe, took her belongings, and threatened to burn them in a car. Police uncovered more than a decade of coercive and controlling behaviour during their investigation. Bernard had installed cameras around the home to monitor the victim, restricted her contact with friends, and tried to prevent her from having hobbies. He regularly questioned her about her whereabouts, went through her phone while she slept, and checked her smartwatch to track how far she had travelled. If she was out longer than expected, he would accuse her of cheating. When the victim challenged his behaviour, Bernard became aggressive and verbally abusive, often punching walls in anger, leaving her frightened. In June last year, he pinned the victim against a wall and strangled her during an argument. Anthony Bernard admitted engaging in controlling or coercive behaviour (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Bernard was jailed for two years and three months and given a restraining order at Cambridge Crown Court on Wednesday, November 4. Detective Constable Isabelle Wilding said: "Bernard subjected his victim to years of controlling behaviour, monitoring her movements, restricting her contact with friends and invading her privacy. "His behaviour left her frightened and was designed to strip away her independence and control different aspects of her life. "I hope this sentence gives her some reassurance and sends a clear message that coercive and controlling behaviour is domestic abuse and we will take reports seriously." To report concerns or for more advice and support on domestic abuse, including coercive control, visit Cambridgeshire Police's dedicated web pages.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Reform councillor complains to Parliament over MP’s response to 199-home plan
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A Reform UK councillor has complained to Parliament about MP Sam Carling over a 199-home development between Ramsey and Bury. Cllr Karan Maheshwari, who represents Ramsey on Huntingdonshire District Council, has submitted a complaint to the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards. It concerns North West Cambridgeshire MP Mr Carling’s response to Cllr Maheshwari’s request for him to intervene in planning application 25/01382/OUT, for 199 homes between Ramsey and Bury. A copy seen by this publication is dated November 2 and marked “DRAFT – NOT SUBMITTED”, but Cllr Maheshwari later confirmed he submitted it on November 3 and received confirmation on November 4. The dispute began after Huntingdonshire District Council’s development management committee said it was minded to reject the scheme. Cllr Maheshwari says he asked Mr Carling to urge the Secretary of State not to “call in” the application. A planning application being called in means the Government takes responsibility for deciding it instead of leaving the final decision with the local authority. Mr Carling replied in social media posts included with the complaint: “Karan, this is misinformation. MPs have no power over planning.” Mr Carling also said intervention with the Secretary of State could trigger a judicial review and give the council another route to overturn its refusal. Cllr Maheshwari disputes the suggestion that his request amounted to misinformation. He argues that, although an MP cannot decide a planning application, an MP can make representations about a planning case. The row continued the next day when Cllr Maheshwari posted a further criticism of Mr Carling and urged him to stand up for residents. The councillor accepts in his complaint that the post contained “direct political criticism”, including a call for Mr Carling to stand down if he would not represent residents’ concerns. Mr Carling replied that there was “absolutely no need for full-on personal nastiness” and said voters wanted politicians to work together. He added: “I am not going to engage. Particularly when most of what you're doing is AI-generated anyway.” The AI reference forms another part of Cllr Maheshwari’s complaint. The Reform councillor argues that using AI to research or draft material should not by itself discredit someone’s arguments. He stresses that he is not accusing Mr Carling of unlawful discrimination and accepts that the comments do not prove a wider policy of refusing to engage with AI users. Instead, Cllr Maheshwari asks whether residents’ or elected representatives’ concerns could be dismissed because they used AI to prepare their arguments. The complaint asks the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards to consider whether the exchanges breached Rule 11 of the House of Commons Code of Conduct. Rule 11 covers conduct serious enough to damage the reputation and integrity of the House of Commons or MPs generally. Cllr Maheshwari accepts that the rule sets a high bar and that an ordinary political disagreement would not normally be enough. The complaint acknowledges that the Commissioner may decide the matter is not serious enough to investigate. If that happens, Cllr Maheshwari has asked the Commissioner to consider whether the concerns should instead be raised with Mr Carling under a separate parliamentary procedure, without a formal investigation. He says the complaint is not intended to stop robust political debate or force Mr Carling to support a particular planning position. Instead, it asks for scrutiny of how elected representatives handle public concerns. The document includes screenshots of the exchanges and copies of Cllr Maheshwari’s posts as evidence. A Facebook post at the centre of the dispute has since been removed, but Cllr Maheshwari says he does not know who deleted it or why and makes no allegation about its removal. Mr Carling has been approached for comment. The application was submitted by David Wilson Homes South Midlands.

I am devastated that some of the women I met ten to twenty years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.” Walliams, 55, brought legal action against Independent Television News (ITN) and Guardian News and Media (GNM), publisher of The Guardian, ahead of the two organisations reporting allegations against him, including of sexual misconduct and potential criminal activity. Lawyers for the media organisations previously told the High Court in London the allegations involved Walliams’ alleged “abuse of power and status” to contact young women and try to engage in “inappropriate and exploitative sexual activities”. Walliams denied the claims and unsuccessfully sought an injunction to prevent these publications because of the risk he would take his own life, after two previous suicide attempts. The author was granted anonymity during the proceedings, which was lifted after his injunction bid was dismissed and GNM and ITN published their investigations on Tuesday. During a two-day trial in October, the court was told by the media organisations’ lawyers that the allegations were gathered after “a wide-ranging and rigorous investigation” and that there was a “strong” public interest in publishing them. Gavin Millar KC said that reporters from the media organisations had spoken to more than 100 people, including more than 30 sources with first-hand accounts as well as Walliams’ friends and colleagues. Walliams’ lawyers said that he had initially attempted suicide after receiving letters from ITN and GNM asking for his reply to the allegations, because of “long-term trauma and the fear of trial by media”. Sara Mansoori KC, representing Walliams, told the court that any publication relating to him about these allegations “would have a potentially fatal impact”. The barrister said: “The only reason they would not be fatal is because the claimant would be locked up and prevented from his desire to end his life.” Judge Mr Justice Nicklin refused the bid for an injunction, ruling it would be an “exceptionally serious interference” with freedom of expression. In the 52-page judgment he also said that granting the injunction would not treat the man’s psychiatric condition or eliminate his elevated risk. He continued that hospitals and health staff caring for Walliams, who was detained under the Mental Health Act in October, meant that the state had “assumed responsibility” for his immediate safety and “can provide significant protection”, which “materially reduces the likelihood of suicide”. The former Britain’s Got Talent judge, known for appearing in comedy shows including Come Fly With Me and Little Britain alongside Matt Lucas, has sold more than 60 million copies of his children’s books globally. They include The Boy In The Dress, Fing, and Gangsta Granny, the latter of which was turned into a one-hour BBC special in 2013, followed by a sequel starring Sheridan Smith in 2022. Walliams’ book publisher HarperCollins dropped him in December 2025, after an investigation into allegations he had “harassed” young women, which Walliams strongly denied. Earlier this month, theme park Alton Towers permanently closed its World Of David Walliams attraction, which featured rides inspired by the books. Walliams left Britain’s Got Talent in 2022 after he apologised for making “disrespectful comments” about auditioning contestants during filming breaks in January 2020 at the London Palladium. In 2023, Britain’s Got Talent producer Fremantle apologised and reached an “amicable resolution” with Walliams after the remarks he made while on the show were leaked.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 5 film and television locations you can visit in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Famous film and TV locations are closer than you might think. Cambridgeshire has quietly become a star of the screen, with its historic streets, rural villages, and grand buildings providing the backdrop to some of cinema and television’s most memorable moments. From Netflix’s The Crown to ITV’s Grantchester, the county has featured in a growing list of productions, attracting fans keen to follow in their favourite characters’ footsteps. Here are some of Cambridgeshire’s best-known filming locations. Wansford Station and the Nene Valley Railway near Peterborough has been used for not one, but two James Bond films. (Image: Nene Valley Railway) Ely Cathedral is one of Cambridgeshire’s most spectacular filming locations. The cathedral stood in for Westminster Abbey in Netflix’s The Crown, including during wedding and coronation scenes. More recently, Bradley Cooper filmed one of Maestro’s most memorable scenes inside the cathedral. Cooper played legendary American composer and conductor Leonard Bernstein, and directed and co-wrote the film. For one of the film's major scenes, Cooper recreated Bernstein's celebrated 1973 performance of Gustav Mahler's Resurrection Symphony at Ely Cathedral. The sequence was filmed inside the cathedral with a live orchestra, choir and extras, and much of it unfolds in a single six-minute take. Visitors to Ely can walk through the cathedral used for one of the Oscar-nominated film’s major musical sequences. The Green Man n Grantchester is used by ITV for its detective drama Granchester starring Robson Green. (Image: Google Street View) Few places in Cambridgeshire are as closely linked to a television programme as Grantchester is to Grantchester. The picturesque village provides the setting for ITV’s detective drama of the same name, which uses several real locations. Fans can explore the village’s buildings and landscapes, which regularly appear on screen alongside Robson Green, Tessa Peake-Jones, Kacey Ainsworth and Al Weaver. One particularly recognisable location is the Church of St Andrew and St Mary, which has appeared in Grantchester as the village church and churchyard. Grantchester Meadows is another location visitors can enjoy for free. The meadows beside the River Cam feature in Grantchester and offer fans a taste of the countryside behind the programme. The meadows are also worth visiting in their own right, especially for fans who want to combine screen tourism with a riverside walk. Fans can stop for a drink at The Green Man pub, frequented by Geordie and his colleagues in the show. It lets visitors step inside a genuine screen location instead of viewing it from the road. Wisbech offers a very different look, with the Fenland town’s historic streets appearing in films and television productions. Peckover House in Wisbech has been used for films including Dean Spanley starring Peter O'Toole. (Image: Image: National Trust Images Jemma Finch) The town is known for its Georgian architecture, particularly North Brink, which overlooks the River Nene and has an impressive row of period properties. The National Trust’s Peckover House, a Georgian merchant’s home dating from 1722, also stands on North Brink. Productions filmed in Wisbech include the 1994 television adaptation of Martin Chuzzlewit, David Copperfield from 1999 to 2000 and the 2008 film Dean Spanley. The 2022 independent film Wild Bones was also filmed in Wisbech. Peter O’Toole filmed Dean Spanley in Wisbech in 2007 alongside Sam Neill, Bryan Brown and Jeremy Northam, with Peckover House and Wisbech Castle among the locations used. Visitors can explore much of the town’s Georgian heritage on foot, especially around North Brink, South Brink and the River Nene. James Bond fans have good reason to visit Peterborough: the area provided locations for two 007 films. The Nene Valley Railway featured in 1983’s Octopussy, starring Roger Moore as James Bond. Wansford Station became the fictional Karl Marx Stadt station, while filming also took place around Orton Mere and Ferry Meadows. The Bond franchise returned to Peterborough for 1995’s GoldenEye, Pierce Brosnan’s first 007 film. The Nene Valley Railway hosted action scenes involving the film’s imposing Russian armoured train. The former British Sugar factory at Woodston also featured in GoldenEye. Part of the site became a Russian rail depot, and Peterborough provided the backdrop for the tank chase’s finale. The former industrial site has been redeveloped, but the Nene Valley Railway remains open, so Bond fans can still visit a location featured in two 007 films. Just outside Cambridgeshire’s modern boundary, Burghley House is one of the wider region’s most impressive filming locations. Burghley House, just over the border near Stamford was used for the 2005 series of Pride and Prejudice among other films and TV series. (Image: Burghley House) Read more 5 Christmas markets and fairs to visit in Cambridgeshire this winter 'A sad loss': Hunts residents react to beloved department store closing 1,700 Cambridgeshire households urged to claim unclaimed Healthy Start support Tom Littler appointed to lead Arts Theatre Cambridge ahead of 90th anniversary Nearly 4,000 Huntingdonshire households could continue paying no council tax The Elizabethan mansion is best known for appearing as Rosings Park, Lady Catherine de Bourgh’s imposing home, in the 2005 adaptation of Pride & Prejudice. The house and grounds are open to visitors during the visitor season, giving film fans a chance to see the grand setting for themselves. From Bradley Cooper conducting inside Ely Cathedral to James Bond racing through Peterborough, Cambridgeshire has made a striking mark on the big and small screens. And with many of the locations open to the public, film and television fans do not have to settle for watching them from the sofa.
