summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Rare Royal Mint 50p coin sells for more than 420 times face value on eBay
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A rare 50p coin has fetched more than 400 times its face value after an online auction. The 2009 Kew Gardens piece drew 19 bids on eBay on November 4. A winning bid of £221.36 landed the coin, with an extra £9.55 buyer protection fee included. Released by the Royal Mint in 2009, the Kew Gardens 50p had a circulating mintage of 210,000. It marks the 250th anniversary of the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew. Its reverse shows the Great Pagoda encircled by a climbing vine, while the obverse carries a portrait of Queen Elizabeth II. The Royal Mint ranks the 2009 Kew Gardens coin as the second-rarest 50p to enter circulation by mintage, behind the 2023 Atlantic Salmon. It says demand for the 50p denomination was low in 2009, accounting for the unusually small number struck that year. The 50p piece has a seven-sided shape and provides space for commemorative designs. The Kew Gardens 50p measures 27.30mm across. A coin's mintage, design and condition can all influence its value, according to the Royal Mint. An unusually low mintage may mean a coin sells for more than face value on the secondary market. Condition can also matter, with coins closer to mint condition potentially worth more. The Royal Mint advises collectors to research secondary-market listings and consult a coin expert if in doubt. The price paid for this graded Kew Gardens coin does not guarantee the same return for another example. Royal Mint figures list these 50p coins among the rarest to enter circulation, ranked by mintage: The 2023 Atlantic Salmon coin has the lowest mintage of any 50p issued for circulation, according to the Royal Mint. Collectors can check the Royal Mint's published mintage figures to find out how many examples of a circulating design were issued.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Thousands of Vauxhall owners warned 'stop driving' over safety issue
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Thousands of Vauxhall drivers have been told to stop driving over an airbag safety risk. Stellantis UK, Vauxhall's parent company, issued the stop-drive instruction for certain vehicles fitted with Takata airbags, which were already part of a recall. Vauxhall says the airbag inflator can degrade over time in high heat and humidity and may explode with excessive force in a crash, causing serious injury or death. Law firm Bond Turner estimates the recall affects 320,000 vehicles and is investigating potential claims over motorists' losses. The firm's estimate is not a confirmed count of vehicles currently subject to the stop-drive instruction. Vauxhall says drivers who receive a stop-drive warning should stop using the vehicle as soon as it is safe to do so. Its recall page lists the following models under the stop-drive action: Astra Hatch (2005 to 2015), Astra Van (2006 to 2013), Astra Twin Top (2006 to 2015), Vectra (2005 to 2008) and Signum (2005 to 2008). Not every vehicle in those model ranges is necessarily affected, and owners should check their vehicle identification number (VIN) to see whether their car is included and what action is advised. Vauxhall says the only exception to the stop-drive instruction is a direct journey, without stops, to a pre-booked recall repair appointment, provided the vehicle can be driven there lawfully. Other models are subject to the recall but not the stop-drive instruction, and their owners should still take action as soon as possible. These are the Astra J and Astra GTC (2010 to 2018), Meriva B (2010 to 2017), Mokka and Mokka X (2013 to 2018), Cascada (2013 to 2018) and Zafira C (2012 to 2016). Drivers can use Vauxhall's vehicle recall checker to check their VIN and register for a free repair. The 17-character VIN can be found on a V5C registration certificate or in the vehicle. Owners who cannot register online can call Vauxhall's recall helpline on 0800 917 9285. Vauxhall says registered keepers of affected vehicles will be sent a letter and should make sure their contact details are up to date with the DVLA. Bond Turner is looking into whether motorists may be able to recover expenses linked to the recall, including alternative transport, replacement vehicle hire and loss of earnings. Malcolm Lewis, head of group litigation at Bond Turner, said: "For many people, their car is essential to everyday life, whether that is getting to work, taking children to school or fulfilling family and personal commitments." Mr Lewis said: "Our investigations will look at who may be legally responsible for the losses experienced by affected motorists, including the cost of alternative transport and replacement vehicle hire, loss of earnings and other associated expenses." Vauxhall says it has made mobility solutions available for customers affected by the stop-drive action and asks them to discuss any specific needs with their retailer when booking.

Nationwide said it was increasing rates across most of its variable-rate savings accounts from December 1. Members with a Reward Single Access ISA will see their rate increase from 2.80% to 3.05%, while Reward Saver and Reward ISA rates will rise from 2.75% to 3%. Its M Plus Saver rate will rise from 1.75% to 2% on balances up to £25,000, while the rate on balances above that amount will increase from 1.25% to 1.50%. The savings announcement comes as figures from the Current Account Switch Service (Cass) reveal that 411,384 current account switches were completed between July and September 2026. That was up 55% on the 265,083 recorded during the same quarter last year, and the highest quarterly total since the final three months of 2023. September was the busiest month, with 152,299 switches completed. The latest figures take the total number of completed switches in 2026 to 1,019,912. Nationwide was among the biggest beneficiaries in the second quarter, recording a net gain of 23,636 customers switching to it. It was followed by Barclays, with a net gain of 21,169, NatWest with 20,287 and Monzo with 17,544. Do you understand ISAs? They’re changing: cash, shares, LISAs and more, what you need to know and do now! Plus State Pension tax help, mortgage rate rises & more. All in the new Martin Lewis podcast... https://t.co/O7b14FLwb2 https://t.co/RCrSyznDx9 And elsewhere... — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) November 5, 2026 Other providers saw more customers leave than join. Halifax recorded a net loss of 20,728 switches, while TSB lost 17,008 and Santander lost 14,124. The figures are based on information voluntarily provided by banks and building societies and cover switches made through Cass, rather than every account move. Fred Powell, head of current accounts at Nationwide, highlighted the society's “fairer share” payments to members, its promise to keep branches open until at least the start of 2030 and services including dementia clinics. Abigail Foster, a personal finance expert at Compare the Market, said: “With over one million switches completed so far in 2026, it’s encouraging to see so many people exploring their options. “With continued pressure on household budgets, ensuring that your money is working as hard as possible is essential. “Switching accounts could potentially provide better interest rates, lower fees, and enhanced benefits.” John Dentry, product manager at Pay.UK, which owns and operates Cass, said: “The huge range of providers underscores the competitiveness of the market.” The Current Account Switch Service is designed to make moving banks or building societies easier. Customers can also move their current account outside the scheme if they prefer. Small businesses with a turnover of up to £6.5million, small charities with an annual income below £6.5million and small trusts with net assets below £6.5million can also use the service. Smaller banks are also trying to tempt customers to switch by offering perks and rewards on their current accounts. Zopa, for example, has revamped its Biscuit current account to let customers choose the benefits that best suit their spending habits. The free account pays 1% AER variable interest on all balances and offers fee-free card spending abroad, while customers can select one additional benefit: 2.75% AER variable interest on their balance, 3% cashback on up to £150 of eating-out spending each month, or 3% cashback on up to £150 of Direct Debit payments each month. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP confirms State Pension age change - people with these birthdays face longer wait
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: People approaching State Pension age are being warned they could have to wait several months longer before receiving their first payment as the Government continues its phased increase from 66 to 67. The change is being introduced gradually over two years, with the State Pension age rising by one month at a time for people reaching 66 during the transition. The next stage begins on November 6 and affects people born between November 6 and December 5, 1960. Rather than receiving their State Pension when they turn 66, this group will have to wait until they are 66 years and eight months old before becoming eligible. For someone born on November 6, 1960, that means they will reach State Pension age on July 6, 2027. The delay increases by another month for each subsequent group of birthdays. Those born between December 6, 1960 and January 5, 1961 will have to wait until they are 66 years and nine months old, while the next group will reach State Pension age at 66 years and 10 months. The phased increase will eventually mean people born from March 6, 1961 onwards have to wait until their 67th birthday to claim their State Pension. The State Pension age is currently 66 for men and women, but is rising to 67 between 2026 and 2028. The increase began on April 6, 2026, and affects people born between April 6, 1960 and April 5, 1961. The exact age at which someone can claim depends on their date of birth, with the delay increasing by one month for each successive group. The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) timetable is: The latest increase comes amid calls for the State Pension age to be reduced to 65 for everyone. A public petition calling for the change has attracted thousands of signatures, with campaigners arguing that people in their mid-to-late 60s can face poor health, caring responsibilities and limited options to remain in work. Tim Grimsditch, Managing Director of Unbiased, said: “A public petition calling for the State Pension age to be reduced to 65 for everyone has gathered more than 80,000 signatures and is approaching the 100,000 needed for Parliament to consider debating it. Its argument is that many people aged 65 to 67 face poor health, caring pressures, and limited options to keep working - and the evidence that healthy life expectancy varies considerably by income and occupation gives that weight. “The Government has consistently rejected calls to lower the State Pension age, and the Third State Pension Age Review is currently underway to determine what the age should be in future decades. There’s a difficult balance here: the State Pension is one of the largest items of public spending, and allowing people to claim it earlier would mean paying it to more people for longer. Both sides of this are serious arguments. “Either way, the timing matters for planning. The State Pension age is currently rising from 66 to 67, a change that began in April 2026 and completes in March 2028, affecting people born between March 1961 and August 1977. Legislation already exists to take it to 68 after that. “The practical issue for most people isn’t the State Pension age itself - it’s the gap before it. "Private pensions can generally be accessed from 55, rising to 57 in April 2028, while the State Pension now arrives at 67. Someone who stops working at 63 through ill health or caring responsibilities is funding four years entirely from their own provision. That’s the question the petition is really about, and it’s worth planning for regardless of what happens to it." Recommended reading: The increase from 66 to 67 was brought forward under the Pensions Act 2014. The legislation changed the timetable so that the State Pension age for men and women would rise to 67 between 2026 and 2028, rather than over the longer period previously planned. The DWP said: “The Pensions Act 2014 brought the increase in the State Pension age from 66 to 67 forward by eight years. The State Pension age for men and women will now increase to 67 between 2026 and 2028. “The Government also changed the way in which the increase in State Pension age is phased so that rather than reaching State Pension age on a specific date, people born between 6 April 1960 and 5 March 1961 will reach their State Pension age at 66 years and the specified number of months. “For people born after 5 April 1969 but before 6 April 1977, under the Pensions Act 2007, State Pension age was already 67.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Walkers crisps and Rubicon drink recalled from UK supermarket shelves
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A drink and a snack box feature in this week's round-up of product recalls. The Food Standards Agency (FSA) has published allergy alerts for both products, including details of which batches are affected and what customers should do. The FSA says the 1L cartons may contain sulphites not mentioned on the label, posing a possible health risk to people sensitive to sulphur dioxide or sulphites. Four batches are affected: Anyone with a sensitivity to sulphur dioxide or sulphites who has bought an affected carton should not consume it, the FSA advises. They can return it to the shop where it was bought for a full refund, or contact consumercare@agbarr.co.uk for further information. The FSA says notices explaining the recall will be displayed in retail stores selling the product. PepsiCo is recalling the 655g box of six packs because wheat is not declared on the outer packaging, according to the FSA. The problem concerns an 85g pack of Monster Munch Giants Roast Beef inside the box, which contains wheat and gluten. The affected batch code is 107543, with best-before dates of 21 November 2026 or 16 January 2027. The FSA says the product poses a possible health risk to people with an allergy or intolerance to wheat or gluten, or with coeliac disease. Those customers are advised not to eat the affected product and can contact the PepsiCo Consumer Care Line on 0800274777 or visit contact.pepsico.com/walkers for a full refund. A recall is when customers are asked to return the product, rather than it simply being taken off shelves. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 1,700 Cambridgeshire households urged to claim unclaimed Healthy Start support
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Families in Cambridgeshire are being encouraged to apply for the NHS Healthy Start scheme through a new outreach campaign. Cambridgeshire County Council, in partnership with district and city councils, is targeting around 1,700 low-income households identified via its Low-Income Family Tracker (LIFT) platform. The campaign will run throughout November and aims to raise awareness of unclaimed financial support for healthy food and milk. Councillor Alison Whelan, chair of the Communities, Social Mobility and Inclusion Committee, said: "We know that many families across Cambridgeshire continue to face significant cost-of-living pressures, and Healthy Start can provide valuable support at a time when every pound counts. "Through this targeted campaign, we're helping families access money that they are entitled to, putting additional income into household budgets while supporting healthy eating and giving children the best possible start in life." Healthy Start is a national scheme offering pregnant women and families with young children weekly payments of £4.65 per child under the age of four, rising to £9.30 for infants under one. The funds are loaded onto a payment card and can be used in most supermarkets to buy items such as cow’s milk, fresh fruit, and vegetables. The campaign is part of the council’s wider anti-poverty programme, which includes income maximisation services, targeted outreach, and crisis payments. Just 62 per cent of eligible Cambridgeshire families currently claim Healthy Start, meaning more than £431,000 could be going unclaimed each year. Households that have been identified will be contacted by letter, email, phone call, or text message. Those who do not receive a notification are still encouraged to check their eligibility through the NHS Healthy Start website. Residents are reminded that if they are ever in doubt about the authenticity of a letter, email, text message or phone call, they can contact their district or city council directly for verification. Information on scam awareness is available on the Cambridgeshire County Council website.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Romesh Ranganathan tackles online outrage and family life in sharp Cambs comedy show
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridge welcomed Romesh Ranganathan as part of his sell-out 'Romesh Will Change Your Life' tour, with the evening proving to be anything but a conventional comedy show. A live DJ, a sell-out audience and a comedian with absolutely no intention of playing it safe, the TV star delivered an evening of sharp wit, awkward truths and wonderfully self-deprecating humour. Before the, a live DJ set was accompanied by various clips from Romesh's television appearances, including Rob & Romesh and his recent winning moment on Celebrity Traitors. It was an unconventional opening, but one that immediately established the atmosphere of the evening. From family life and relationships to racism, immigration and wider social issues, no subject was entirely off limits. Romesh moved effortlessly between everyday observations and contentious topics, delivering his trademark dry humour with a healthy dose of self-deprecation. Romesh Ranganathan on the Cambridge Corn Exchange stage (Image: Angela Smith) He also addressed the recent controversy surrounding his BBC TV advert "What has the BBC ever done for me", which attracted online criticism and abuse directed at both him and his wife. Rather than shy away from the subject, he used it as another opportunity to expose the absurdities of online outrage and the world of keyboard warriors. However, some of the evening's biggest laughs came when Romesh turned his attention closer to home. Joking about being fed up with seeing himself on television, he launched into imagined stand-up performances by his wife and son. His ability to impersonate his own family, while simultaneously making himself the butt of the joke, proved a particular highlight, generating some of the most raucous laughter of the night. He weaved jokes about his childhood trauma and his womanising dad into a therapy-themed narrative, which made it feel as though he was baring his soul on stage under the guise of comedy. It is this willingness to ridicule himself, alongside his sharp observations and unapologetic approach to difficult subjects, that makes Romesh such an engaging performer. 'Will Change Your Life' may be a bold promise, but if the measure is an evening of laughter, uncomfortable truths and refreshingly honest humour, Cambridge certainly got its money's worth.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Here is some of Huntingdonshire's most unusual bridges and where to find them
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: From a medieval bridge with its own chapel to a 55-arch causeway, Huntingdonshire is packed with unusual crossings. The district’s rivers, floodplains and Fenland waterways have shaped travel for centuries, leaving medieval crossings and Fen drainage bridges behind. Here are some of Huntingdonshire’s most striking bridges and where to find them. St Ives Bridge One of the county’s most extraordinary bridges spans the River Great Ouse at St Ives. The town’s first bridge was built of wood in 1107, before work began on a stone replacement in the early 15th century. The stone crossing was completed in 1425, and a chapel was added the following year. It is one of only three bridges in England with a chapel. The bridge also still bears the scars of the English Civil War. Parliamentary troops destroyed part of it to hinder Royalist forces, so a temporary drawbridge was installed. When the damaged section was rebuilt in 1716, it was given rounded arches instead of matching the pointed medieval ones, leaving a visible difference today. The chapel has also served as a toll house, inn and private home. The bridge is also a scheduled monument. Huntingdon Old Bridge Another remarkable medieval bridge links Huntingdon and Godmanchester across the River Great Ouse. Grade I-listed Huntingdon Bridge dates from around 1330 and has six pointed stone arches. Historic England says a band of trefoil decoration above two arches probably marks the bridge’s oldest surviving section. Its third arch was replaced by a drawbridge during the English Civil War. The bridge also has a slight kink. Historical accounts say builders started on both riverbanks, but the two sections failed to meet in a straight line. Historic England calls it a "fine and famous example of a medieval bridge". The Nuns' Bridge, Huntingdon The lesser-known Nuns’ Bridge stands on Brampton Road in Huntingdon. Grade II-listed Nuns’ Bridge dates from the 15th or 16th century, was repaired in the 17th and largely rebuilt in the 18th. The stone-and-brick bridge has five arches and brick parapet walls. Unlike many historic bridges, it has avoided modern traffic because the main road now bypasses it. It is both a Grade II-listed building and a scheduled monument. The New Bridges, St Ives Despite their name, St Ives’s New Bridges are more than 200 years old. The extraordinary brick causeway runs about 220 yards across the Great Ouse flood plain and opened in 1822 after being built by the Bury to Stratton Turnpike Trust. Its astonishing number of arches makes the causeway stand out. It has 55 arches, keeping the route across the flood meadows open when the surrounding land flooded. About 1.2 million bricks were reportedly used to build it. One brick carries its own piece of history. One brick bears the date 1822 and the signature of John Turner, who oversaw the work and apparently signed the wet clay before it was fired. The New Bridges are Grade II* listed. Bridge over the River Great Ouse, Godmanchester Godmanchester has another historic crossing a short distance from the famous medieval Huntingdon Bridge. The bridge over the River Great Ouse at The Avenue is separately Grade II listed. It makes a useful stop on a riverside walk, where visitors can see several generations of crossings around Huntingdon and Godmanchester. Forty Foot Bridge, Ramsey Forty Foot For a bridge in a very different landscape, head into the Fens around Ramsey Forty Foot. Forty Foot Bridge carries the road over the Forty Foot River, part of the Middle Level Navigations. The unusual name refers to the waterway, not the bridge’s length. The Forty Foot Drain, also known as Vermuyden’s Drain, is part of the historic network built to drain the Fens. The name traditionally refers to the width of the original drainage channel between the bank tops. The surrounding settlement also took its name from the waterway and bridge, making them defining features of the Huntingdonshire Fen landscape.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Nearly 4,000 Huntingdonshire households could continue paying no council tax
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Thousands of households could continue receiving full council tax support if a key scheme is renewed. Nearly 4,000 of the most financially vulnerable homes in Huntingdonshire currently receive up to 100 per cent support through the district council’s council tax scheme, which is now under review for 2027/28. The scheme cleared its first approval stage after the Overview and Scrutiny (Environment, Communities and Partnerships) Panel met on November 5. Councillor Nathan Hunt, executive councillor for resident services and corporate performance, said: "HDC's up-to 100% Council Tax Support Scheme is one of the most important things we do to keep people out of crisis and build a fairer Huntingdonshire. "It puts money back in the pockets of those who need it most, takes a fair and compassionate approach, and helps make processing the scheme much more efficient." Some 3,997 households currently receive the maximum support, accounting for 4.69 per cent of all households in the district. That is 56 more households than in August 2025 and 104 more than in August 2024. By August 2026, 5,035 households were receiving council tax support, about 5.92 per cent of households in the district. Read more Here is some of Huntingdonshire's most unusual bridges and where to find them Paralympic champion Lauren Steadman to open inclusive community gym in Hunts Cambridgeshire PC praised after cutting deliberate fires at landfill by 81 per cent Beloved African lion Ghana dies aged 16 after declining health at Cambs zoo Four EV charging bays approved at Hunts shopping centre despite parking concerns The scheme, which is means-tested, is designed to reduce council tax bills for working-age residents on low incomes. Central government sets support for pension-age claimants. For 2024/25, Huntingdonshire District Council raised the maximum support under the scheme from 80 per cent to 100 per cent for many claimants. The council also introduced income bands linked to Universal Credit allowances and scrapped the need for claimants to submit a separate application. The council says the change has helped more residents claim support they might otherwise have missed. Under the banded scheme, the highest category gets a full discount, while lower bands offer 75, 50 or 25 per cent support. Eligibility thresholds are updated each year to reflect changes to Universal Credit. The scheme also encourages people to work by ignoring up to £50 a week of their earnings in assessments. The assessment excludes some benefits, including disability payments, Carer's Allowance, child benefit, child maintenance and parts of Universal Credit. The council says the revised scheme has made administration more efficient. Between April and August 2026, 71.44 per cent of changes in circumstances were processed automatically, up from 69.84 per cent in 2025 and 62.52 per cent in 2024. The number of processed changes also rose by 5,400. The average processing time for changes rose slightly to 3.02 days, from 2.86 days in 2025, but remained below 3.42 days in 2024. New claims took an average of 20.79 days to process—up from 18.8 days the previous year but down from 22.7 days in 2024. The council says scheme changes meant 452 fewer council tax bills were issued despite more updates being processed. The council also reported further falls in non-payment reminders and summonses. The scheme reduces the council’s tax base because it is classed as a discount, not a benefit. All authorities that collect council tax in the district share the cost. Officers recommend keeping the scheme’s core principles for 2027/28, while raising income thresholds in line with Universal Credit. The proposals go to the council’s cabinet on November 17, with full council expected to make the final decision on December 16.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Here's some of the historic buildings are at risk in Huntingdonshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Six historic churches have been named on Historic England’s 2025 Heritage at Risk Register. Located across Huntingdonshire, the churches are among nearly 1,000 places of worship in England on the register. Historic England’s annual register highlights buildings and sites most at risk from neglect, decay and other threats. All six Huntingdonshire entries are churches, including Grade I-listed buildings in Huntingdon, Abbots Ripton and Bythorn and Keyston. Four of the six currently have no agreed plan in place to address their condition. Here is a closer look at each site on the register. PARISH CHURCH OF ST JOHN THE BAPTIST, BYTHORN AND KEYSTON The Grade I-listed church is in “poor” condition and has medium vulnerability. The building is in slow decline, and no solution has yet been agreed to address the issues. Read more Nearly 4,000 Huntingdonshire households could continue paying no council tax Here is some of Huntingdonshire's most unusual bridges and where to find them Paralympic champion Lauren Steadman to open inclusive community gym in Hunts Beloved African lion Ghana dies aged 16 after declining health at Cambs zoo Four EV charging bays approved at Hunts shopping centre despite parking concerns PARISH CHURCH OF ST SWITHIN, OLD WESTON The Grade II*-listed church on Brington Road, is in poor condition and has high vulnerability. It faces an immediate risk of rapid deterioration or loss of fabric, with no agreed solution. CHURCH OF ALL SAINTS, OFFORD CLUNY The Grade II*-listed church on High Street faces the same threat. It is in poor condition, has high vulnerability and carries a priority rating of B, meaning it faces an immediate risk of rapid deterioration. A solution had been agreed but was not in place when the site was assessed. CHURCH OF ST MARY, HUNTINGDON The Grade I-listed Church of St Mary on Huntingdon High Street is one of the district’s most prominent buildings at risk. It is in poor condition, has high vulnerability and carries a priority rating of C, indicating slow decay. No solution had been agreed at the time of the assessment. CHURCH OF ST ANDREW, ABBOTS RIPTON The Grade I-listed church on the High Street is in poor condition and has medium vulnerability. Like St Mary’s, it has a priority rating of C, and no repair solution had been agreed. PARISH CHURCH OF ALL SAINTS, BROUGHTON The final entry is Broughton’s Grade II-listed Parish Church of All Saints on Causeway Road. It is in poor condition, has high vulnerability and faces an immediate risk of rapid deterioration or loss of historic fabric. No solution had been agreed when it was assessed. A place on the Heritage at Risk Register does not mean a building will be lost, but it signals that urgent action is needed. The register helps Historic England direct support and resources to the most vulnerable heritage sites. Sites can leave the register after repairs or once a sustainable plan is in place. The 2025 register includes 1,460 buildings and structures across England, along with 986 places of worship, 1,864 archaeological sites, 105 parks and gardens, three battlefields, four protected wreck sites, and 469 conservation areas. This year, 138 sites were added to the register and 129 removed after conservation work. The register underlines the need for investment, community support and long-term planning to protect the region’s heritage.

The inspection followed intelligence that fireworks were being sold there without a licence. Councillor Zameer Ali, cabinet member for communities and public safety, said: "In the lead up to Bonfire Night, the community in this area has been disturbed by several firework-related incidents, which have been widely reported on. "The Arts is a much-loved and storied theatre close to the hearts of audiences and theatre people alike, and it is also an institution of unique potential. "I am delighted that Victoria Beechey will remain as Executive Director and look forward to working together to steer The Arts into new waters as a presenting and producing theatre of international renown." Nigel Hugill, chair of the Arts Theatre, said: "In Tom Littler, we have found exactly that calibre of visionary leader able to advocate and demonstrate the value of humanities in a tech-driven environment. "His exceptional track record is one of creative innovation, deep communal engagement and performing house vitality." Mr Hugill also paid tribute to the theatre’s current interim leaders. He said: "Rachel Tackley and Victoria Beechey have together provided exceptional interim leadership in stewarding a remarkable two years of transformation and renewal at The Arts. "Rachel will step away next summer with our love and unending gratitude."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: BBC licence fee could change as Government makes major announcement on future plans
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A petition calling for the BBC licence fee not to be extended to subscribers of rival streaming services has received a Government response, amid growing questions over how the broadcaster will be funded in future. The petition, which has attracted 18,418 signatures, warns that households could face extra costs if ministers decide to extend the licence fee to people who subscribe to streaming platforms not owned or operated by the BBC. Campaigner Alec Burns, who created the petition, argues the move would be "wholly unacceptable", particularly during the cost-of-living crisis. The petition, which can still be signed, states: "Amid a cost-of-living crisis, we believe the Government should be finding ways to save the public money, not expanding their means of taxation." It also claims the BBC already has a "tarnished reputation" and warns that extending the charge could further damage public confidence in the broadcaster. The Government has now responded, confirming it is considering a range of options for the BBC's future funding but stressing that no final decisions have been taken. In its response, published on November 2, the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport said ministers were considering feedback from a public consultation on the BBC Charter Review Green Paper. It said: "The Government is keeping an open mind on the future funding of the BBC and no decisions have been taken at this stage." The response added that ongoing policy development was looking at the potential impact of different funding arrangements on households, consumers, investment and the wider creative economy. Ministers said the BBC remained a "vital national institution" which informs, educates and entertains audiences across the UK. The Government also highlighted the broadcaster's contribution to the UK's creative industries, saying it supports jobs and growth across the nations and regions. It pointed to research from the Reuters Institute, which found that 59% of UK respondents trusted BBC News in 2026, making it one of the country's most trusted news brands. However, ministers acknowledged that viewing habits have changed significantly as more people turn to streaming services and other ways of watching television. The Government said: "The changing media market and audience viewing habits mean the Charter Review needs to consider whether the current funding model remains suitable for the future." It also revealed that the total number of TV licences in force has fallen by three million since 2017/18. The Government confirmed it is looking at several options to ensure the BBC has sustainable funding in the years ahead. These include making the broadcaster operate more efficiently, generating more commercial revenue and potentially reforming the licence fee itself. Ministers also acknowledged concerns about the cost of the charge for households already struggling with their finances. The response said: "We understand that ensuring the licence fee is affordable is important." It added that the Government wanted to keep costs as low as possible for households while ensuring the BBC had the resources it needed to continue providing its services. The response did not confirm whether people subscribing to non-BBC streaming platforms could eventually be required to pay the licence fee. Instead, ministers stressed that they were still considering consultation responses and engaging with stakeholders. A White Paper setting out the Government's plans for the BBC's future is expected before the end of 2026. Recommended reading: The Government also highlighted existing support for households struggling to pay the annual licence fee. Since February 2025, more households have been eligible for the Simple Payment Plan, allowing them to spread the cost through weekly, fortnightly or monthly instalments. Other support includes: Ministers said the Charter Review was also considering whether further concessions or alternative payment schedules could better reflect different household circumstances.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Shoppers at Tesco, Sainsbury's, Asda, Lidl and more risking £100 parking fines
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Drivers could face a £100 charge for parking outside a supermarket's opening hours. Some supermarket car parks restrict when vehicles can be left there, even if the car park is empty. Select Car Leasing highlighted the issue. Graham Conway, managing director of Select Car Leasing, urged drivers to read signs before deciding whether to park. He said: “Check the signage as you enter the car park carefully before making a decision about whether to stay or not. “Not all store car parks punish after or before-hours parking, but many do, and it’s an issue that’s causing real confusion among motorists.” Mr Conway said the company had seen cases where people were charged after leaving a vehicle for a matter of minutes. Supermarket car parks can be managed by private operators, which issue Parking Charge Notices when they believe conditions have been broken. Some use automatic number plate recognition cameras, with notices sent by post. Other conditions can include limits on the length of a stay, parking within marked bays and restrictions on who can use disabled or parent and child spaces. A private Parking Charge Notice is different from a penalty charge notice issued by a council. In England and Wales, Citizens Advice says drivers should check whether the parking company belongs to an accredited trade association when considering an appeal. It advises that if a non-member puts a ticket on a vehicle, the driver should not contact the company unless it writes to them first. In Scotland, Citizens Advice says someone who wants to challenge a private ticket should first contact the operator, explain their reasons and ask for it to be withdrawn. It says they could also approach the landowner, such as the supermarket, and provide the operator with evidence including photographs of unclear signs. In Northern Ireland, the Consumer Council says a driver who believes a private notice was issued incorrectly may be able to appeal, using evidence such as photographs of damaged signs. It says registered keepers in Northern Ireland cannot automatically be held liable for private parking charges, unlike in England and Wales, and that the driver is liable. An independent appeal may be possible if an operator rejects a challenge, depending on the company and the relevant appeal service.

Four electric vehicle charging stations have been approved at a Godmanchester shopping centre despite concerns about parking and safety near a school. The proposals will see four rapid EV charging bays and associated equipment installed at the King James Retail Centre in Ermine Street. Huntingdonshire District Council planning officers recommended approval despite strong objections from Godmanchester Town Council. Application 26/01647/FUL revised an earlier scheme, cutting the proposed charging spaces from six to four. Plans to install four electric vehicle charging stations at a Godmanchester shopping centre have been approved despite concerns over parking and safety near a school. (Image: Google Maps / Street View) Six existing parking bays will be replaced by four EV charging spaces. Planning officers said the scheme would improve access to rapid EV charging and encourage greener transport. They concluded that it would provide sufficient parking and vehicle movement and would not cause significant harm to neighbours, highway safety or biodiversity. However, Godmanchester Town Council strongly recommended the plans be refused, arguing that dedicating four spaces to EV charging had not been adequately justified given demand for parking at the site. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Officers seize huge stash of illegal fireworks from Peterborough shop
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A large stash of illegal fireworks has been seized from a shop in Peterborough. Officers found unlicensed fireworks at a Lincoln Road shop on November 6 during a joint operation involving Peterborough City Council’s trading standards team, Cambridgeshire Constabulary and Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service. The inspection followed intelligence that fireworks were being sold there without a licence. Councillor Zameer Ali, cabinet member for communities and public safety, said: "In the lead up to Bonfire Night, the community in this area has been disturbed by several firework-related incidents, which have been widely reported on. "While we don't know if these are linked, I am relieved that this sizeable quantity of fireworks has been removed from this address, as it was clearly presenting a hazard to those who lived nearby. "There are obvious serious safety risks in buying, storing, and selling fireworks in an unlicensed premises. "Fireworks are explosives and those sold by unlicensed sellers may not meet safety standards. "They could be improperly stored, incorrectly labelled, damaged and unsafe to use, increasing the risk of injury, property damage and fire." During the visit, officers found more than 21kg of fireworks with net explosive content (NEC). NEC is the total mass of explosive substances, excluding packaging, outer casings, containers, or inert components. These fireworks were subsequently seized. Sam Tucker, Peterborough neighbourhoods inspector, said: "Our officers joined partners in visiting this premises as part of our ongoing efforts to tackle issues involving inappropriate use of fireworks in the city. "Additional patrols will take place in the area tonight and this weekend, and we would strongly urge anyone with any concerns to report this to us, so we can build an accurate picture of anti-social behaviour in the area and work to combat this." Anyone who believes fireworks are being sold illegally can contact the Citizens Advice Consumer Service on 0808 223 1133. If someone is in immediate danger always call 999.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Wetherspoon set to open up to 25 more pubs as sales jump higher
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Up to 25 more Wetherspoon pubs could open this financial year. JD Wetherspoon estimates it could open a further five to 10 managed pubs and 10 to 15 franchised sites in the year ending August 1, 2027. That would be in addition to the six managed pubs and two franchises it has already opened this financial year. The expansion plans came as the pub group reported an 8.2 per cent rise in like-for-like sales in the 14 weeks to November 1, covering its first quarter and a further week. Chairman Tim Martin said: “The company has had a good start to the financial year. “There are still three quarters to go and profit forecasts are very dependent on the level of sales growth.” The six managed pubs opened so far are at Manchester Airport and Heathrow Airport, and in Crewe in Cheshire, Ferndown in Dorset, Dibden Purlieu in Hampshire and Kempston in Bedfordshire. Wetherspoon said it had sold one pub during the period and now had 797 trading managed pubs, alongside 25 franchises. Bar sales rose by 9.4 per cent over the 14 weeks, while food sales increased by 6.8 per cent. Like-for-like growth slowed to 7.5 per cent in the most recent five weeks, compared with 8.6 per cent in the first nine weeks of the quarter. Martin said the company was “comfortable” with market expectations once adjusted for the 53-week financial year. The company put the consensus profit estimate, compiled from seven analysts, at £76.4 million. In the previous 52-week financial year, pre-tax profit fell 28 per cent to £58.6 million as staff and other costs offset higher sales. The company also argued that labour cost increases affect pubs more heavily than supermarkets, estimating the labour cost of a pub pint at £1.68 compared with about 15p for a supermarket pint. Its calculation used an AI-derived estimate of the price of a supermarket pint and wage costs as a percentage of sales. The group argued that the effect had widened the price gap between pub and supermarket pints and reduced employment. Its next trading update is expected on January 20, 2027.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Thousands could unlock £2,600 savings after major government rule change
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Thousands of young people who lack the mental capacity to manage their finances could find it easier to access money held in their Child Trust Funds under new Government plans. The proposed changes aim to remove a complicated legal hurdle that has left many disabled young adults and their families facing lengthy and costly court processes to release savings that belong to them. Under the reforms, parents and carers will be able to approach Child Trust Fund providers directly to access the money on behalf of young people who lack the mental capacity to make financial decisions. The Government said the changes could help between 63,000 and 126,000 young adults who have so far faced difficulties accessing their accounts. Child Trust Funds are long-term, tax-free savings accounts introduced for children born between September 1, 2002 and January 2, 2011. The accounts were designed to give young people a financial asset when they reached adulthood, with money becoming accessible at the age of 18. Justice minister Jake Richards said: “Young people who lack the mental capacity to make financial decisions should be able to access their savings as easily as possible – especially when this money was put aside by loved ones to help them take their first steps into adulthood. “This is simply an injustice that we’re finally putting right and as campaigners have argued for years, change is long overdue. “This legislation will ensure this group of young adults no longer face difficulty from accessing money that is rightfully theirs.” Economic secretary to the Treasury Lucy Rigby said the reforms would help tens of thousands more young people access their accounts. She said: “The changes that we’re introducing will help tens of thousands more young people to connect with their child trust funds - worth on average £2,600 each.” Recommended reading: The Government said it would work with others to develop the new process, including deciding who will be able to access the money, what evidence will be needed and what safeguards should be put in place to protect young people who lack mental capacity. Speaking in the Commons, Ms Rigby said: “The last Labour government introduced child trust funds with the intention that every child in this country could access a financial asset as they enter adulthood, and almost three million young people have already accessed their funds, currently containing an average of £2,600 each.” She added: “I am going to be bringing forward an amendment to the Financial Services Bill. The second reading of which is next week, which will enable the Ministry of Justice to make regulations to put this in action.” Anna Bird, chief executive of Contact, said families had faced unnecessary difficulties when trying to access the money. Earlier this year, two female participants alleged rape and a third claimed sexual misconduct by their on-screen husbands in a BBC Panorama documentary aired in May. In June, a cast member was arrested on suspicion of rape. All three men have denied the allegations. Chief executive of Channel 4, Priya Dogra, said: "Welfare across all our programmes is a primary concern. "Whilst the review praised the welfare protocols in place and made no findings that Channel 4 breached the Ofcom Code or that the format is inherently unsafe, I have to consider when is the right time for Channel 4 to move on from a format. "The recommendations are eminently sensible and feasible, but considering their wholesale implementation provoked fundamental questions about the editorial proposition of a show that, I believe, has now run its course over 10 years." She also addressed the women who made the allegations. Ms Dogra said: "I am very sorry for the distress those women have clearly felt. "I hope our actions – in swiftly commissioning the review and taking clear, decisive steps – demonstrate our commitment to the wellbeing of all contributors and our desire to relentlessly strengthen industry standards." The sixth season of Married at First Sight UK, filmed earlier this year, will not be aired. A planned spin-off series, featuring contestants from the UK and Australian versions, was also halted during the review. The external review was commissioned by Ms Dogra after the allegations surfaced. It was split into two parts: Channel 4 said the reviews did not attempt to judge the allegations, which remain a matter for the relevant authorities. Clyde & Co reviewed more than 31,000 documents and 20 hours of footage. Their findings concluded that Channel 4 and production company CPL had complied with the Ofcom Broadcasting Code and had not breached any regulations in handling the issues raised. However, the review identified isolated incidents where the welfare framework was not fully followed. One example involved participants breaking the code of conduct regarding "prohibited substances." They received a first and final warning instead of being removed from the show. Ms Heggessey’s review also found that some aspects of the programme could "implicitly put pressure on contributors to be intimate" and that participants could "become dependent on production and lose touch with reality," impacting their ability to make decisions. A post shared by Shona Manderson 🪐✨🌸 (@shoniemandy) The review recommended improvements, including reducing the frequency of questions about couples’ physical relationships and discontinuing Intimacy Week and Partner Swap Week. It also suggested changing the show’s "leave or stay" mechanism. Currently, if one person in a couple chooses to leave but the other wants to stay, both must remain for another week. The review proposed allowing a participant to leave if they wish. Despite these concerns, the review described the welfare protocols as "extensive, extremely thorough and of a high standard." Ms Dogra said implementing the recommendations would require a "materially greater level of intervention, monitoring and supervision that would fundamentally alter the format and editorial proposition of the programme." She concluded that, given the maturity of the show and the required changes, ending the series was the right decision. Channel 4 said the budget for Married At First Sight UK will be redirected toward "bold, innovative new programmes from the UK independent production community." Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle was asked whether closer alignment with the European Union could lead to restrictions on the crisps' labels. Speaking to Times Radio host Stig Abell, she compared the issue to the debate about EU rules on bananas during the Brexit referendum. She said: “Oh, Stig. The question comes ahead of a UK-EU summit in Brussels on November 20, where Prime Minister Andy Burnham is expected to seek agreements on food and farming, emissions trading and youth mobility. The proposed food deal is expected to align the UK with EU plant, animal and food trade standards to remove post-Brexit checks on exports. Dame Angela argued that reducing barriers would make it easier for farmers and food producers to trade with Europe. She said: “We’ve got huge potential growth in our economy if we allow our farmers and food producers to be able to export into Europe again without all the huge uncertainty and the costs and frictions that Brexit brought us.” “This will be a deal that improves that situation and it will enable this economy to grow and for us to have higher levels of prosperity than we’ve had before.” The minister declined to commit to giving farmers more time to adapt to the new trading arrangements, saying that removing barriers quickly would bring “huge economic benefits”. Asked on BBC Radio 4's Today programme about the Government's rejection of farmers' calls for a 24-month transition, she said ministers were listening to their concerns. She said: “The transition is a balance between getting and accessing those benefits as quickly as possible, but dealing with some of the transitional issues that you have to deal with whenever you’re moving from one system to another.” Mr Burnham has said the deals could raise GDP by 0.4%, compared with a previous estimate of 0.3%. Meanwhile, former EU Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier suggested the UK could negotiate to rejoin the bloc without being obliged to adopt the euro, but would have to accept freedom of movement and single market membership. He told Sky News: “If it is the choice of the UK to ask for a new negotiation to rejoin, it’s perfectly possible to begin such a negotiation without any kind of obligation to take part in the euro.” On the single market, Mr Barnier said: “There is no … possible negotiation on any kind of cherry-picking or the single market ‘a la carte’.” Mr Burnham has said the Government will “explore options” for a different long-term relationship with the EU after the summit. He has insisted voters would be “the boss” of any changes, amid questions about EU membership and freedom of movement.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Which? warning over common mistake that is making homes colder and bills higher
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Drying clothes on radiators could leave homes colder and bills higher, Which? has warned. In a TikTok video, the consumer organisation advises households to stop putting wet washing directly on radiators and suggests using an airer instead. It says damp clothes can act as a barrier to heat, potentially leaving a room taking longer to warm up and increasing energy use. Which? also raises the risk of mould when moisture from drying clothes ends up in the air inside a home. Which? suggests putting washing on an airer near a radiator rather than covering it, allowing air to circulate around the room. For people who need another option, it suggests a heated airer for smaller loads or a tumble dryer. However, a heated airer does not make the moisture disappear, so the room still needs ventilation. In separate tests of indoor drying methods, Which? found that the cheapest option depends partly on the amount of washing. It says an unheated airer uses no electricity, while its tested heated airers took around four to five hours to dry a small cotton load. The organisation found a heated airer could save money compared with vented or condenser tumble dryers when a small load fits on it in one go. For larger loads that need several rounds on an airer, Which? says a tumble dryer is likely to be cheaper to run. Heat pump dryers have lower running costs than vented and condenser models, according to its comparison, although they can cost more to buy. Ventilation matters whichever indoor drying method is used: South Kesteven District Council advises drying washing outside if possible. If that is not possible, it recommends a heated, well-ventilated room, such as a bathroom with the door closed, and says not to put clothes on radiators. The council advises opening windows wider or using extractor fans where fitted when drying clothes, and keeping permanent vents clear. Energy Saving Trust says condensation forms when moisture in the air meets a cold surface, such as a window. Its advice notes that damp can have other causes too, including leaks, damaged guttering and faults that allow groundwater into walls. Signs of a problem can include persistent condensation, a musty smell, peeling wallpaper or mould, according to the trust. It says the underlying cause needs to be addressed, and leaks or signs of rising damp should be dealt with quickly.

"The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated." The patient, identified by Reuters as a healthcare worker, is expected to be medically evacuated to the UK, though the timing of the flight remains unclear. Only four cases of Ebola have ever been confirmed in the UK, including three involving health workers who responded to the outbreak in West Africa between 2014 and 2015. Dr Damien Tully, associate professor at the Medical Research Council/Uganda Virus Research Institute and London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine Uganda Research Unit, said: "This case is a stark reminder of the risks faced by those responding to the outbreak of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in the DRC. "However, it does not suggest that the virus has become more transmissible or that the threat to the UK has increased." Dr Tully described the infection as "deeply concerning, but it is not entirely unexpected." He said: "Healthcare workers are on the front line of these outbreaks, often treating severely ill patients under extremely challenging conditions. "Even with rigorous protective measures, accidental exposures can occur." Read More He stressed that the risk to the British public "from this planned medical evacuation is extremely low" because Ebola is "transmitted primarily through direct contact with infected bodily fluids, and people are not generally infectious until they develop symptoms." The UK has two high-level isolation units equipped to handle such cases – at the Royal Free Hospital in London and the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle. Dr Tully said: "These facilities are equipped with specialist isolation systems and staffed by highly trained infectious disease teams."

Concerns have been raised as average ticket prices could double following a major Cambridge venue’s refurbishment. The Corn Exchange is set to be redeveloped as part of the wider £95.7m Civic Quarter scheme to revitalise the city centre. The venue, considered the largest performance venue in the East of England, would see upgrades to the main auditorium, improvements to foyers and bar areas, improved seating, acoustics, sound quality and lighting. The wider plans also include work on refurbishing the Guildhall, Market Square and public spaces in-between. A report to Cambridge City Council ’s performance, assets and strategy overview and scrutiny committee said a revived Corn Exchange would act “as the catalyst for a renewed arts and culture scene in Cambridge drawing on its roots which saw it at the forefront of the changing trends in the UK’s music scene.” Sam Scharf, the council’s director of communities, said: “It’s already failed – I mean, last year it rained a bit and we had to cancel Tim Peake. “We then put a short-term remedy in with a bit of leading on top and that is not going to hold up – it’s not got any longevity.” Council officers said income from the venue will help fund the rest of the Civic Quarter scheme and project it will increase by a large amount after the refurbishment. Performances are estimated to increase from 180 a year to 340 and average ticket prices for council-run events from £24 plus VAT currently to £50 plus VAT in year five of the new venue’s opening. Officers said this only applies for events they self-promote and a larger amount of their income comes from hiring the venue out, when they don’t have control of ticket prices. Cllr Beth Gardiner-Smith said: “The business case also notes that the projection of event income is high compared to the benchmark venues. “I think it’s projecting a 43 per cent increase in attendance in year five and similar increases in performances. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Award-winning Hunts pub features in Sidemen YouTube video watched by millions

One challenge was 'take a selfie with a funny place name' and Sidemen members Ethan and Vik seized the opportunity when they arrived at The Cock. The village pub, which is the national dining pub winner twice, is renowned for its "great location and atmosphere". Oliver Thain, founder and owner of The Cock’s parent company Cambscuisine, said the appearance was "brilliant". Mr Thain said: "We had a bit of a laugh when we heard The Cock had made an appearance in a Sidemen video. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Enormous sadness' as beloved Hunts department store to close
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A beloved Huntingdonshire department store has announced with "enormous sadness" that it is set to close its doors for good. Townrow, a family department store business which opened in 1871, insisted the "difficult" decision to close its St Ives store was not taken lightly. Retailer Eaden Lilley went into administration in February 2009 and their 10,000 square foot St Ives store on Bridge Street was purchased by Townrow. The historic independent chain sells clothing, shoes, and kitchenware and also has stores in Maldon and Frinton-on-Sea in Essex. Managing Director Edward Townrow said: "Like many independent retailers, we have faced increasingly challenging trading conditions, rising operating costs and changes in shopping habits. "Despite exploring a number of alternatives, we have regrettably been unable to establish a financially sustainable future for the store in its current form. "What makes this decision particularly difficult is the extraordinary relationship we have with the people of St Ives. "Our customers have been nothing short of wonderful. "Over the years, we have been privileged to welcome generations of families through our doors. "We have shared in their everyday lives, celebrated special occasions with them and formed friendships that extend far beyond the shop floor. "Their kindness, warmth and loyalty have meant more to us than I can possibly express. "I want every customer to know how genuinely grateful we are for their support." Mr Townrow also paid tribute to the "remarkable" team at the St Ives store. He said: "They are the heart and soul of the store, and I could not be prouder of them. "Their dedication, professionalism and genuine care for our customers have made Townrow a very special place." The store will hold a closing-down sale in the coming weeks. Mr Townrow added: "Although this marks the end of a chapter for our existing St Ives store, we remain committed to our other stores and to the values that have defined Townrow for more than 150 years. "Finally, to our customers, our colleagues and the entire St Ives community: thank you, from the bottom of my heart. "It has been an absolute privilege to be part of your town."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: MPs demand timeline for delayed Cambridgeshire special schools with 270 places
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A trio of MPs are demanding answers from ministers over delays to two long-promised special schools. The Cambridgeshire Liberal Democrats have launched a petition demanding a clear Government timetable for building the schools, left in limbo since the change of administration. Charlotte Cane (Ely and East Cambridgeshire), Pippa Heylings (South Cambridgeshire), and Ian Sollom (St Neots and Mid Cambridgeshire) said the Government has repeatedly failed to provide a timetable for the projects in Gamlingay and March, both of which were agreed before the general election and scheduled to open this September. Ian Sollom (St Neots and Mid Cambridgeshire) pictured, Charlotte Cane (Ely and East Cambridgeshire), and Pippa Heylings (South Cambridgeshire), said the Government has repeatedly failed to provide a timetable for the projects in Gamlingay and March (Image: Ian Sollom) The MPs said: "Families were promised these schools and then left in the lurch as the planned opening dates for both schools passed without so much as a shovel in the ground. "And now ministers still refuse to say when they will actually be built. "That simply isn’t good enough." The future of the schools was cast into doubt when the Government revised its building plans. Cambridgeshire County Council had already secured a funding settlement and lobbied for the full amount needed, but despite this, there is still no clear timeline for opening the new special schools. Charlotte Cane (Ely and East Cambridgeshire) pictured, Pippa Heylings (South Cambridgeshire), and Ian Sollom (St Neots and Mid Cambridgeshire) said the Government has repeatedly failed to provide a timetable for the projects in Gamlingay and March. (Image: Charlotte Cane) The MPs warned that the delays are hitting children and families directly. They said: "Every child with special educational needs deserves the right support, in the right place, at the right time. "Parents are fighting tooth and nail just to find a place, while the County Council is forced to pour far more money into private placements. "Children and their families lose out and taxpayers foot the bill, nobody wins." Read more 'Enormous sadness' as beloved Hunts department store to close Inclusive pageant participants celebrated at Huntingdon event Hunts man due in court accused of employee theft and fraud offences named Key report on Hunts car park plans has been received, council confirms Award-winning Hunts pub features in Sidemen YouTube video watched by millions They vowed to keep pressing ministers for action. The MPs said: "We will keep pressing ministers until these 270 places are delivered. "This Government is harming children with their dither and delay. Cambridgeshire County Council is paying for places at private special schools, which cost an average of 2.5 times more than state provision. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Calls to cut state pension age to 65 and free up jobs for younger workers grow
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A petition calling for the state pension age to be cut to 65 for everyone has passed 112,000 signatures, with the campaign now set to be considered for a debate in Parliament. The petition, created by Michelle Gill, argues that lowering the retirement age would allow people to retire with dignity, avoid hardship and potentially free up jobs for younger workers entering the labour market. It has attracted 112,304 signatures and remains open until March 16, 2027. The campaign comes as the state pension age is gradually increasing from 66 to 67, with the change having started in April 2026 and due to be completed by March 2028. However, the Government has already rejected the call to bring the pension age back down to 65, saying it has no plans to make the change. The petition says: "Reduce the state pension age to 65. We believe this could mean people can retire with dignity and avoid hardship. We also think it could free up jobs for younger workers. "Many aged 65–67 face poor health, caring pressures, and limited work options, which we think is unfair." The campaign passed the 100,000-signature threshold, meaning the Petitions Committee will consider it for debate in Parliament. An update published on October 24 confirmed that the petition would be considered for debate. It does not mean a debate has been scheduled or that the Government has agreed to change the rules. In its response, published on October 13, the Government said: "The Government has no plans to lower the State Pension age. "There are no plans to reduce State Pension age to 65." Ministers pointed to rising life expectancy and said pension age policy takes account of the fact that people are living longer and society is ageing. The Government cited Office for National Statistics projections showing that men aged 66 in the UK could expect to live a further 19.3 years on average in 2026, while women of the same age could expect to live another 21.9 years. By 2046, those figures are projected to increase by a further 1.6 years. The response also said increases to the state pension age had been in legislation since the Pensions Act 1995 and were intended to maintain fairness between generations and protect public finances. The Government confirmed that its Third State Pension Age Review is underway. The review will consider what state pension age is appropriate for future decades, taking into account a range of evidence, including life expectancy projections, findings from the Government Actuary, independent reports from Dr Suzy Morrissey and the Pensions Commission, and lessons from previous increases. The Government also acknowledged that people aged 50 and over can face barriers to staying in work or finding a new job. These include ill health, disability, caring responsibilities, menopause and outdated skills or qualifications. Ministers said support for older workers includes dedicated 50PLUS Champions, additional time with work coaches for new Universal Credit claimants aged over 50, and Midlife MOTs delivered in Jobcentres. The petition, which can still be signed here, argues that lowering the state pension age could free up jobs for younger people. In its response, the Government said it was investing an additional £2.5 billion by 2029 into the Youth Guarantee and Growth and Skills Levy. It said the investment would support almost one million young people and create up to 500,000 opportunities to earn and learn. The measures include expanded Youth Hubs, additional work experience and training, a £3,000 Youth Jobs Grant and a £2,000 apprenticeship hiring payment for employers. The Government also said it would provide a fully funded six-month job for long-term unemployed people aged 18 to 24. The petition remains open for signatures until March 16, 2027.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire firefighters tackle smoke-filled soft play rescue exercise

New firefighters at Ely practised safely pitching a large ladder, a task that requires a four-person team. At Thorney, crews tackled a mock incident involving hazardous materials and heavy smoke, wearing breathing apparatus to search for casualties and extinguish a simulated fire. A spokesperson for Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service said: "The soft play structure provided an excellent setting to test firefighters' ability to work through tight, restricted spaces while remaining calm under pressure. "Thank you to Play2Day Wisbech for hosting us." Training doesn’t always take place at stations, however. Thorney firefighters recently completed a confined space exercise at Play2Day Wisbech, a children’s soft play centre. Wearing full breathing apparatus and with vision deliberately obscured to simulate smoke, firefighters navigated the play structure to find and rescue training casualties. Paul Oliver, group commander and head of on-call for the service, said: "Being an on-call firefighter is a very exciting role. "Our crews take part in all kinds of training to help maintain their skills to keep them ready to respond to emergencies, whether its station based drills or larger exercises with other stations involving more complex scenarios. "It’s a great way to learn new skills and take on a challenge. "We are always looking to recruit more local people that can join stations as on-call firefighters. "We’d urge anyone living close to one of our on-call stations and can respond to emergencies around other commitments to visit our website to find out more about joining." More information is available on the Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service website.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Godmanchester Rovers’ winless run continues as Knowle strike late in fog
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Godmanchester Rovers’ winless league run continued as Knowle FC struck late to claim a hard-earned victory in worsening fog. The league fixture took place on Saturday at the Peter Hodson Community Ground, in misty, gloomy conditions. Rovers had collected only one point from their previous six matches, while Knowle had taken two points from three after winning their opening eight games. The visitors began the afternoon second in the table, but neither side looked capable of imposing itself during a largely uneventful first half. Chances were scarce, although Zane Campbell cut inside from the left and forced a good save from Knowle goalkeeper Matt Horton. Just before the interval, referee Michael Dunkley dismissed the away side’s appeal for a penalty after a challenge involving Hayden Purves. The match changed shortly before the hour when Rovers full-back Alfie-Ray Turner stayed down following a challenge. Both benches called for play to be stopped, but the referee allowed the game to continue until the ball eventually went out. Matty Allan then received a ten-minute sin-bin punishment after voicing the home side’s frustration at the decision. Rather than pushing the visitors back, Rovers attempted to manage the game from deep and invited increasing pressure. Jack Mason produced an excellent save to keep the hosts level, but Knowle continued to threaten before taking the lead after 70 minutes. Captain Jack Duggan’s effort appeared to be heading wide, only for two deflections to send the ball looping over Mason and into the opposite corner. Rovers’ task became harder five minutes later when Tim Momodu, recently cautioned, committed another rash challenge and was shown a second yellow card. Seb Hayes introduced Declan Rogers and Micael Goncalves in a desperate attempt to rescue the contest, but Knowle saw out the remaining minutes as the fog thickened. Rovers now face successive away games against Lutterworth and Highgate United before hosting fellow strugglers FC Stratford on November 21.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Memorial appeal for heroic World War II 'Ghost Patrol' soldiers
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The families of men who served in one of the Second World War’s most remarkable special forces units are launching a £150,000 appeal to create a permanent memorial to their courage and achievements. The Long Range Desert Group (LRDG), nicknamed ‘Ghost Patrol’ by opposing Italian forces, was formed in Cairo in 1940 and often operated in secret behind enemy lines. The appeal follows the death in August of Jack Mann, the last surviving veteran of the LRDG, at the age of 100. Born Zacharia Zuckerman in Cairo in 1925, he altered his age to enlist while still a teenager and was recruited by the LRDG as a radio operator. A talented linguist and wireless operator, he was recruited into the LRDG and subsequently served with other wartime special forces units.  He later served with 21 SAS. The LDRG were founded after explorer and British Army officer Major Ralph Bagnold proposed the creation of a small, fast-moving reconnaissance force capable of travelling vast distances behind enemy lines in the deserts of Egypt and Libya. The unit became renowned for its ability to navigate across apparently featureless desert and operate hundreds of miles from conventional forces, gathering vital intelligence on enemy movements and carrying out raids and other operations. Its expertise also made the LRDG an important partner to the newly formed SAS, transporting and guiding its men across the desert on some of their early operations. After the North African campaign, the LRDG continued to operate across the Aegean, Adriatic, Albania, Italy, Greece and Yugoslavia. The cost was considerable. Fifty-one LRDG men are known to have died during the war and at least 182 were captured. The LRDG Memorial Fund, a registered charity established by people with family connections to members of the unit, plans to erect a spectacular 5.8-metre-high sculpture of a scorpion — the LRDG’s emblem — at the Royal British Legion National Remembrance Gardens in Staffordshire. While many Second World War units are represented at the Gardens, the Long Range Desert Group is not currently among them. The memorial has been designed by internationally recognised British sculptor James Doran-Webb, renowned for his monumental animal sculptures.  At its centre will be a giant driftwood scorpion, surrounded by a three-metre stainless-steel ring with compass-style markings reflecting the LRDG’s navigational skills. The sculpture will stand on a plinth designed to trace the unit’s wartime journey from North Africa to the Aegean, Italy and the Balkans. The LRDG Memorial Fund is seeking donations from the public, military community and organisations towards its £150,000 fundraising target. Donations can be made at www.lrdgmemorialfund.org where there is a link to JustGiving. Meg Kennedy Shaw, daughter of Bill Kennedy Shaw, the LRDG’s intelligence officer, said: “Jack Mann's death this summer marked the passing of the last surviving member of the Long Range Desert Group. "With him, the final living link to this extraordinary group of men has gone. For those of us whose fathers and grandfathers served with the LRDG, it makes it all the more important that their story is not lost with their generation. “These men operated for almost five years across deserts, islands, mountains and coastlines, frequently deep behind enemy lines and in extraordinarily difficult conditions. "They showed exceptional courage, ingenuity and resourcefulness, yet their story remains relatively little known. “We believe the time has come to give the LRDG the permanent public recognition it deserves. The scorpion memorial will be a striking and lasting tribute to them, and a place where their families and future generations can remember what they did.” Sculptor James Doran-Webb added: “The scorpion gave us a powerful starting point because it comes directly from the LRDG’s own insignia. "I wanted the memorial to reflect the incredible ingenuity, endurance and navigational skill of the men who served, while creating something dramatic enough to stop people in their tracks and make them curious to discover who the LRDG were and what they achieved.”

Cllr Patrick Kadewere, Mayor of Huntingdon, said: "Remembrance is an important opportunity for our community to come together and honour those who have served, sacrificed and given their lives in defence of the freedoms we enjoy today. 2Poppy drop during the Remembrance Sunday Service 2025 (Image: RAF Wyton) "Whether attending in person, listening from elsewhere in the town centre or joining us online, I encourage residents of all ages to take a moment to reflect on the service and sacrifice of generations past and present.
