The ceremony will include the Act of Remembrance, the two-minute silence, the Reveille, and the laying of wreaths by civic representatives, military organisations, and community groups. Remembrance Sunday Service 2025 (Image: RAF Wyton) A designated viewing area will be available for wheelchair users and those with mobility requirements, and British Sign Language interpretation will be provided. The Armistice Day service will take place at the War Memorial in Market Square on Wednesday, November 11, starting at 10.55am. It will include prayers, the Act of Remembrance, and the laying of wreaths. More details are available at www.huntingdontown.gov.uk/remembrance.

Agricultural land on the edge of Warboys could become an eight-home housing development (Image: Google Maps) Plans to build four homes at a former kennels and cattery between Hilton and Fenstanton have been refused after a national planning policy change. The application sought permission to demolish the existing buildings at Fields View, Fenstanton Road, Hilton, and replace them with four detached single-storey homes. Plans to build four homes on the site of a former kennels and cattery between Hilton and Fenstanton have been refused after a change in national planning policy (Image: HDC) A popular discount retailer with sites across the UK could be opening a store in Huntingdon under fresh plans. If approved, the "comprehensive development" would also provide customer and service access, car parking and landscaping. The nearest Home Bargains store to Huntingdon is on Smithy Way, Great Cambourne (Image: Street View) Fresh plans have been submitted to turn a former RAF Association club into new homes after a previous application was refused. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: ATM stolen from petrol station in ANOTHER Cambridgeshire ramraid
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An ATM was stolen from a petrol station in the second Cambridgeshire ram raid this week. Police were called to the BP garage on Wisbech Road, Littleport, at 5.06am this morning (Friday November 6) after reports of a ram raid. Officers arrived 12 minutes later to find the cash machine gone and the telehandler used in the raid abandoned nearby. Police searched the area but found no suspects. Yesterday (Thursday November 5), the force were called at around 3am with reports of an attempted ram raid at the Nationwide building on Ramsey Road in Whittlesey. Police have not confirmed if the two incidents are related. Detective Chief Inspector Chris O’Brien said: "Ram-raids are likely to take place between September and January when the nights are darker. A search of the area was carried out but no suspects were found (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) "Our patrols have increased across the county. "We are committed to making it harder for ATM thieves to target our local shops and ATM machines and will be targeting areas we believe are at increased risk – but we can’t do it alone. "We need the public’s help to report anything suspicious or anything they see that might not seem quite right, no matter how small or insignificant it may seem. "One call could make all the difference and potentially stop a store or petrol station being targeted." Police want anyone with information, including dashcam or video doorbell footage, to contact them. They are also reminding the public to take extra precautions, including ensuring vehicles have working trackers, especially high-performance cars and heavy vehicles like transits and flatbeds that could be used in similar crimes. Other advice includes installing CCTV or video doorbells, and reporting any suspicious behaviour such as people tampering with number plates, appearing to study ATMs, or attaching fake "out of order" signs to machines. Concerns should also be raised about unfamiliar high-performance or heavy vehicles parked in the area, especially if they have been left for several days. Anyone with information about the Littleport incident is asked to contact police online quoting incident 52 of 6 November or Op ATMosphere. Those without internet access can call 101.

Ambitious ideas to transform St Ives with new riverside moorings, pedestrianised streets, an enhanced market area and a regenerated bus station have been unveiled. The St Ives Town Team has published an updated 'A Vision of St Ives', setting out ideas to boost the town while protecting its historic character. Town Team spokesman John Souter said the document is a starting point for discussion, with businesses, organisations and other interested parties due to meet next month. MP Ben Obese-Jecty (centre) with John Souter and Sheila Stones of the St Ives Town Team, which has created an updated Vision for St Ives document. (Image: Ben Obese-Jecty) The meeting will be closed to the public, but people will have a chance to give their views later, he said. "We want to discuss what is feasible, and come up with some sort of plan that we can take to the public for people to discuss and then add their views on," said John. "The plan will include some short-term goals that are easily achievable because they won't require a lot of funding. "Longer-term projects where we would need to find funding, and then schemes that we know will take some time to realise, such as regenerating Hyperion corner, alongside the bus station, making them more attractive." Hyperion corner could be completely transformed with new buildings. (Image: Town Team) He said the owners of the buildings were on board with the idea. Among the most striking suggestions are additional mooring pontoons at The Quay, designed to encourage more people travelling on the Great Ouse to stop and spend time in the town. The Town Team says extra visitor berths could bring more people to shops and other amenities, accommodate more boats and create opportunities for river events. It believes pontoons could also improve safety along the water's edge. The bus station could be given a makeover to make it more appealing to look at. (Image: Town Team) Another major idea would see part of Market Hill pedestrianised, particularly around the Oliver Cromwell statue, Town Hall, Free Church and Corn Exchange, and local MP Ben Obese-Jecty has launched a poll on the St Ives Serious Discussion Facebook page asking people for their views on potential pedestrianisation. John said: "This project is about far more than pedestrianisation; we want a vision for St Ives that will make it more attractive, while helping it to prosper." He said he has been pushing for various improvements in the town since 1996, when he was a town councillor. He believes the time is now right for progress. The Octagon could become a venue for daily farmers' markets. (Image: Town Team) "There has not been the political will before, but I believe it is there now, and so this is our chance to do something good for St Ives, and it's probably my last chance to see my ambitions for the town realised in my lifetime," said John. The Town Team's vision suggests reducing parking in Market Hill to create more community space, potentially featuring trees for shade and a covered area inspired by traditional market halls. Changes could also be made to Crown Street, Bridge Street and Merryland, with the Town Team suggesting pedestrianisation while retaining access for residents and delivery vehicles. Public transport is another key part of the vision. One idea is to reroute Cambridge buses through The Broadway, Crown Street and Market Hill, bringing passengers closer to shops and boosting footfall. The document also suggests the existing bus stop in Station Road could be relocated to the Sheep Market. Meanwhile, the area around the bus station is identified as a potential regeneration opportunity, including the historic Octagon. The document envisages a development featuring shops, an improved antiques centre, flats and an historic auction room. The Octagon itself could potentially become a daily indoor produce or farmers' market, while also being used for antique auctions and as a tourist information point because of its proximity to the bus station and main car park. The vision also calls for efforts to revive the town's markets, improve cleanliness, tackle commercial waste and wheelie bins in sensitive historic areas, and boost tourism. It also suggests creating an innovation hub, using vacant properties for pop-up businesses and conference facilities. The Town Team says the updated document aims to spark debate about what could be achieved and inform the Town Council's Neighbourhood Plan. It says St Ives should build on its independent shops, historic streets and riverside setting rather than copy other town centres. The document says some major projects will take time, while others could improve the town quickly. It says: "We understand that no town can stand still and rest on its laurels, and every community needs to assess and reassess itself to ensure it is taking advantage of all the opportunities that exist."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Six passenger planes across Europe, including two UK departures, are being inspected following suspected bomb threats. Elsewhere in Europe, a Ryanair flight from Manchester to Murcia in southern Spain was also subject to a bomb threat, while Bulgarian media reported a flight from Israel to Sofia received a threat via email before landing. The diverted flight, operated by Polish carrier LOT, was carrying 118 people and led to a partial closure of the airport. Francisco Lucas, the Spanish government’s delegate in the Murcia region, said 121 people were on board the Ryanair flight. He added that the plane was being inspected and security protocol was underway. Murcia-Corvera Airport’s fire brigade was also mobilised. In Bulgaria, Lyubomir Nikolov, chief secretary of the Ministry of Interior, said counter-terrorism teams were examining the aircraft for explosives. These incidents follow a separate event on Monday involving a Wizz Air flight from London Luton to Budapest, which was forced to make an emergency landing after a bomb threat. Flight cancellations can quickly turn travel plans upside down, but passengers are not without rights when journeys are disrupted. Under UK law, airlines are required to provide care and assistance in the event of a cancelled flight, regardless of the reason for the disruption. The UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) has clarified what travellers are entitled to, including accommodation, meals, and transport between the airport and hotel if re-routed to the following day. The CAA said: "The airline must provide you with these items until it is able to fly you to your destination, no matter how long the delay lasts or what has caused it." If airlines are unable to arrange assistance due to large-scale disruption, passengers are advised to organise their own accommodation and transport and reclaim the costs later. The CAA said: "If you end up paying for things yourself, keep every receipt and do not spend more than is reasonable. "Airlines are unlikely to refund you for things like luxury hotels or alcohol. "Some will provide guidance on reasonable costs." Travellers must also be given the choice between a full refund for unused parts of their ticket or an alternative flight. Compensation may be available depending on the cause of the cancellation. The CAA said: "Disruptions caused by things like extreme weather, airport or air traffic control employee strikes or other ‘extraordinary circumstances’ are not eligible for compensation." Compensation is also dependent on the notice given and the timing of the replacement flight. The CAA said: "If you received less than seven days’ notice of the cancellation, you can claim compensation based on the timings of the alternative flight. "If your new flight departs no more than one hour before the scheduled time of your original flight and your new flight arrives less than two hours after the scheduled time of your original flight, you are not entitled to financial compensation." More detailed information on entitlements and compensation can be found on the CAA website. Have you ever claimed compensation from a flight being cancelled or delayed? Let us know in the comments.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: £50,000 earners face major tax change this week HMRC explains what happens next
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Sole traders and landlords earning more than £50,000 have just days left to submit their second Making Tax Digital update, with HMRC clearing up five common mistakes ahead of the deadline. Thousands of sole traders and landlords face another important tax deadline this week, as HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) reminds people to submit their second Making Tax Digital (MTD) quarterly update by Saturday, November 7. The requirement applies to sole traders and landlords earning more than £50,000, with the new digital reporting system becoming mandatory for them from April 6, 2026. But after the first quarterly update was submitted in August, HMRC says it has been answering a number of common questions and misconceptions about what people need to do next. HMRC has now highlighted five things customers should know before submitting their latest figures - including whether they need to pay tax, what happens if they make a mistake and whether they can leave their submission until Saturday. One of the biggest misconceptions is that a quarterly update is effectively another tax return. HMRC has stressed that this is not the case. An MTD quarterly update is simply a summary of income and expenses from self-employment and property, which must be submitted using compatible software. There is no tax calculation involved and, importantly, no payment is due when the update is sent. Customers' overall tax position will only be calculated when they submit their tax return for the 2026 to 2027 tax year. Anyone who successfully submitted their first quarterly update in August does not need to contact HMRC again for reassurance that it has been received. Instead, customers can check their submission history whenever they want by logging into their HMRC online account or checking through their Making Tax Digital software. HMRC says there is no need to call or use webchat simply to confirm that an update has gone through. Another concern is that Making Tax Digital means customers must purchase complicated or expensive accounting packages. HMRC says there are several recognised software options available to suit different circumstances. These include: Customers can find guidance on choosing Making Tax Digital-compatible software on GOV.UK . Making Tax Digital is designed to allow customers to keep their financial records up to date throughout the year. If someone spots a mistake in a digital record, they should correct it as soon as possible. The correction will then be reflected in their next quarterly update. This means customers do not need to resend an earlier quarterly update simply because they have discovered an error. With less than a week to go until the second quarterly update deadline for Making Tax Digital, make sure you're prepared. ⏰ If you’re a sole trader or landlord with a combined turnover of over £50,000, you need to send your second quarterly update by 7 November. Act now. ⬇️ https://t.co/ZK0DK3dB8I — HM Revenue & Customs (@HMRCgovuk) November 1, 2026 The second quarterly update deadline falls on a Saturday this year, but HMRC has confirmed customers can submit their figures either before or on November 7. The tax authority is encouraging people to get their updates sent as early as possible following the end of the reporting period. Anyone who needs help is encouraged to contact HMRC during the week, when its full phone service is available. However, phone support will also be available through the Self Assessment helpline on Saturday, November 7, between 9am and 3pm, for customers who need assistance with submitting their quarterly update. Business-as-usual webchat services will be available from 8am to 4pm. The Agent Dedicated Line will not be available on the Saturday. Tax agents can instead contact the Self Assessment helpline on 0300 200 3310. Recommended reading: Craig Ogilvie, HMRC's Director of Making Tax Digital, said: "Thousands of sole traders and landlords have already successfully sent their first quarterly update, and we want the second to be just as straightforward. “As the next deadline approaches, we’re helping customers prepare with confidence by answering common questions about MTD and highlighting the support available. "Customers can send their update any time before 7 November and I would encourage them to do so as early as possible to ensure they have everything in place before the deadline." Customers can check whether they qualify on GOV.UK. More information about the requirements, deadlines and support available can be found in HMRC's Making Tax Digital for Income Tax guidance . Making Tax Digital for Income Tax became mandatory for sole traders and landlords with qualifying income above £50,000 from April 6, 2026. However, the rules are being extended to more people over the next two years. The planned timetable is: There are some exemptions, including for people who are digitally excluded.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Holidaymaker's horror as 'refund' from Ryanair turned out to be £900 scam
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A holidaymaker was scammed out of £900 after complaining online about soaking wet seats on a flight. Sharon Morrell thought she was receiving a £400 compensation payout from Ryanair after rain poured into the cabin before takeoff. The 48-year-old bus driver had booked a four-night package holiday flight from Bristol to Palma, Majorca, alongside her husband and two children on Saturday, October 24. Mrs Morrell said 11 seats near the open aircraft door were left sitting in puddles following heavy downpours. A holidaymaker who complained online about rain-soaked seats on a Ryanair flight was scammed out of £900 after fraudsters offered fake compensation. (Image: Kennedy News and Media) Cabin crew handed passengers paper towels from the toilet to mop up the water themselves before departure, she claimed. Mrs Morrell said: "We were waiting on the stairs for everyone to board the plane, so we were getting soaked then as well. "Obviously Ryanair can't help if there's downpours. "So we got inside the plane and the seats on the left and right side were soaking wet. "Even the seats behind were soaking too. "There were 11 overall that were soaked. "This was all our family's seats and the people behind us. "They weren't just a little bit wet - there were puddles." She said passengers were expected to sit on wet chairs for a two-hour flight, adding: "There was definitely an inch of water. "I said to the staff 'are we expected to just sit on this? This is ridiculous.' "They said 'we'll sort it out in a minute, just get seated so we can get everyone boarded.'" After arriving in Majorca, the mother-of-two shared her frustration on social media. She was shocked when an unknown caller rang her shortly afterwards claiming to represent the airline's compensation team. The caller offered £200 each for her and her husband, and instructed her to download two mobile phone apps to transfer the money safely. Mrs Morrell said: "He said 'no problem, and we can compensate you £200 each for me and my husband for what's happened.' "He sounded genuine." She followed the instructions, only to see funds flowing out of her account instead of coming in. Mrs Morrell said: "I said 'why are there payments leaving my account when it should be the other way around?' "He said 'it's normal process and it's actually payments we're putting into your account.' "He was so clever." The scammer asked for her account balance when payments were declined, prompting her to hang up as transactions totalling £900 went through to Kenya. Mrs Morrell is now disputing the transactions with her bank and warned others against falling for similar traps. She said: "It's so easy to be sucked in and I just can't believe how easy it is to get scammed. "Anybody can fall for these scams. It's my own fault, I got sucked into this." Ryanair said rainwater entered the cabin during boarding due to Storm Boelo. A spokesperson for the airline said: "Due to adverse weather conditions (Storm Boelo) during boarding at Bristol on 24 Oct, a small number of seats near the aircraft door became damp from rainwater entering the cabin. "Crew assisted affected passengers by wiping down the seats and this flight operated normally from Bristol to Palma de Mallorca."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The man accused of a knife attack on board an LNER train in Huntingdon last year "spat at" a police officer on a train travelling to Peterborough, a court has heard. Multiple people were injured on the service travelling to London King's Cross on November 1, 2025 which was forced to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon. Anthony Williams, 33, denies 14 counts of attempted murder: ten of them in relation to the LNER train, three said to have happened in Peterborough and one at Pontoon Dock DLR station in London. Earlier this month, Williams pleaded guilty to 10 counts of wounding with intent relating to the incident on the LNER train, the wounding with intent of a man at Pontoon Dock DLR station in the early hours of November 1 and to the wounding with intent of a 14-year-old boy in Peterborough on October 31, as well as a number of other offences. At Cambridge Crown Court on November 3, Prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC told jurors that a man, agreed by the prosecution and defence to be Williams, 'spat at' a passenger, Jordan Morley, on a train travelling to Peterborough at around 8am on November 1, 2025. Mr Morley, a police detention officer at Islington Custody, was on his way home from work and had boarded the 7.16am service at King's Cross St Pancras, the court heard in a statement read out by the prosecution. He "felt what I would describe as a spray of spittle" as he sat on the train which had just stopped at Hitchin, the court heard. The court heard how Mr Morley was "almost in disbelief that he had spat at him". He had no previous interaction with the male who spat at him, the court was told. Mr Morley exited the train at Biggleswade and sent a text message to British Transport Police at 8.18am on November 1, 2025, the court heard. Williams has pleaded guilty to common assault on a Thameslink train travelling between London and Biggleswade on November 1. The trial continues.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Further details behind closure of much-loved village pub emerge
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary:
For months now mystery has shrouded the fate of a popular village pub in Huntingdonshire which closed its doors without explanation. The Black Bull, on Church Road, in Brampton, announced it had closed "for the foreseeable future" in August. The 16th century venue was run by Malcolm Beswick and is operated by the UK's largest pub company, Stonegate. Now, ex-staff have come forward to reveal further details surrounding the watering hole's sudden closure. They claim "things took a turn for the worst" in February when the pub began "running out of stock", including soft drinks and kitchen supplies. "The place wasn't really managed, if I'm honest, it was all over the place," one ex-employee, who asked to remain anonymous, told The Hunts Post. However, stock would turn out to be the least of the pub's worries as a subsequent Food Standard's Agency inspection revealed. The premises was slapped with a zero food hygiene rating by the independent government body following a review of the site on May 6. It said "major improvement" was necessary in areas including "management of food safety" as well as "cleanliness and conditions of facilities and building". "The kitchen hasn't had a deep clean in a number of years and we were finding food that was out of date," a former employee said. "We once served a whole table with mouldy Yorkshire puddings which had been prepped the week before. "The hygiene was really bad, staff would go outside, smoke a cigarette, go back in and not wash their hands." Read more Eaton Socon home with one-bedroom annexe on sale for £500,000

    Hunts dog lover's event sees 300 labradors gather at Jeremy Clarkson’s pub Former staff said the hygiene rating forced the closure of the kitchen, but claim that despite this it was still not professionally deep-cleaned. "It was quite uncertain and a lot of us were message each other about the future of the pub," they added. "We didn't know if the pub was going to be open and if we were going to have our jobs back which caused a lot of stress." Describing the culture at The Black Bull, one ex-employee even claims they often had no designated break unless they requested one. Mr Beswick revealed the pub would close "permanently" in a WhatsApp message sent to staff on August 13. The correspondence, seen by this newspaper and verified by two sources, confirmed the reason behind the closure in a bid to "avoid speculation". "Thank you all for your patience, I'm afraid we have to close permanently. "To avoid speculation I found out today that the brewery filed a bankruptcy petition over a £21,000 debt for buying out of tie. "I'm afraid I dropped the ball on that and it has cost everything including sadly your jobs," it added. According to The Gazette, a petition to declare Mr Beswick bankrupt was filed at Cambridge County Court on March 16. The application was lodged by the creditor Unique Pub Property Limited, which is a subsidiary of Stonegate. A bankruptcy order has since come into effect and will automatically discharge on June 10 next year, the Individual Insolvency Registers shows. In a statement, Stonegate said it is unable to comment on "any alleged legal or financial matters concerning individual third parties". A spokesperson said: "We are actively seeking a new tenant to take on the Black Bull, Brampton. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire joins major UK trial testing new Alzheimer’s treatments
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire and Peterborough have enrolled their first participants in a major UK trial for Alzheimer’s treatments. The study, supported by Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS Foundation Trust (CPFT), is part of the AD-SMART trial—a national effort to accelerate the search for effective therapies. Dr Ben Underwood, director of research and development at CPFT and the trial’s local principal investigator, said: "We are delighted to welcome Angela and Steve to join the trial with us at CPFT and hope this research will directly benefit them and countless others living with Alzheimer’s disease. "Our research would not be possible without people like them coming forward to help us. "We will support them throughout their research journey and hope that many others will join to help test promising dementia treatments and ensure the most successful ones can be brought to NHS clinics as soon as possible." The AD-SMART trial is the first of its kind to test multiple drugs at the same time, beginning with two medicines already used to treat type 2 diabetes and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Angela and Steve Bucksey, residents from Cambridgeshire who joined the study, said: "Following Angela’s diagnosis, we decided to take part in a study at a local friendly research unit without having to travel into London, and it feels good to be doing something about it." The trial will involve up to 20 NHS sites over the next 12 to 18 months, with more than 30 planned in total. Researchers aim to recruit 1,200 participants across the UK. Researchers expect to finish evaluating the first drugs in 2030. Individuals with a confirmed diagnosis of Alzheimer’s who wish to take part can contact the CPFT Research team at RandD@cpft.nhs.uk or call 01223 219753. For more information on dementia research and other clinical trial opportunities, visit Join Dementia Research.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Walkers recalls crisps over health concerns as shoppers warned 'do not eat'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Walkers snack sharing box is being recalled over undeclared wheat. PepsiCo is recalling its Walkers Variety Snacks Sharing Box after wheat was left off the outer packaging, creating a possible risk for some people with allergies or coeliac disease. The Food Standards Agency (FSA) says the affected boxes have best-before dates of November 21, 2026, or January 16, 2027. The alert applies to crisps sold in England, Scotland and Wales. The problem concerns an 85g packet of Monster Munch Giants Roast Beef inside the box, which contains wheat and gluten not declared on the outside of the sharing box. The FSA said: "This product contains gluten making it a possible health risk for anyone with an allergy or intolerance to wheat or gluten, or with coeliac disease." Affected boxes weigh 655g and contain six packs of snacks. The batch code to look for on the affected boxes is 107543. Anyone who has bought an affected box and has an allergy or intolerance to wheat or gluten, or has coeliac disease, is advised not to eat it. Instead, the FSA says customers can call the PepsiCo Consumer Care Line on 0800 274 777 or visit contact.pepsico.com/walkers to receive a full refund. PepsiCo has issued a point-of-sale notice explaining the recall and what customers should do. The NHS says a food allergy is different from a food intolerance and that allergic reactions can be serious for some people. It advises calling 999 if, for example, someone's lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, or they are struggling to breathe. If someone having a serious allergic reaction has an adrenaline auto-injector or nasal spray, the NHS says to use it immediately and call 999 even if they seem to be feeling better. Coeliac disease is an autoimmune condition in which eating gluten causes the immune system to attack the body's own tissues, damaging the small intestine, the NHS says. Symptoms can include diarrhoea, abdominal pain and bloating, and a gluten-free diet helps control symptoms and prevent long-term complications. The FSA explains that a food may be withdrawn from sale when there is a problem that means it should not be sold. A recall is when customers are asked to return the product, rather than it simply being taken off shelves. Food can be withdrawn or recalled because allergy information is missing or incorrect, or because there is another food allergy risk. When there is a food allergy risk, the agency issues an allergy alert.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Government to proceed with plans for asylum seeker housing in village
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The government has confirmed it intends to proceed with plans to use a former sheltered living complex to house asylum seekers. In a letter, the Home Office confirmed its decision to use Roman Court, in Leverington, near Wisbech, to house mothers and babies. It comes less than two weeks after a fire ripped through a disused building at the site, which police are investigating as arson. Fenland District Council said the decision "demonstrates a complete disregard for the serious risks the plans pose to public safety, community cohesion and civil unrest." Concerns have been raised about the site which was earmarked as part of government plans to move asylum seekers out of hotels and into longer-term homes. Police continue to investigate a fire which ripped through a disused building at the site (Image: Colin Martin) Cllr Sam Hoy, Fenland District Council portfolio holder for housing, said: "We are extremely alarmed by the Home Office’s decision which has been taken despite extensive evidence from the Council and our partners highlighting serious concerns about the suitability of Roman Court and the risks associated with this proposal. "What is particularly troubling is that the Home Office has chosen to proceed at a time when there has already been significant unrest linked to these plans, including public protests and the fire at the site, which remains the subject of an ongoing police investigation. "These events have demonstrated the strength of local concern and the heightened tensions that exist within the community. "We do not believe those circumstances can simply be dismissed as issues that can be managed through routine arrangements. "Our position remains unchanged. Roman Court is the wrong location for this proposal, and we remain deeply concerned about the impact on both future residents and the wider community. "We will continue to make our objections known to the Home Office and work with our partners to ensure local concerns are heard and appropriately addressed." As the contracted accommodation provider, Serco will be required to demonstrate the site meets legal, regulator and property requirements before occupation. "This will include the relevant safeguarding, welfare, security, fire safety and operational arrangements," the letter reads. "Where site-specific action or mitigation is required, this will be taken forward with Serco and the relevant partners as the site progresses. "The accommodation will not become operational until the applicable requirements have been met, with input from relevant partners sought through the appropriate channels where required." summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: No trains between Peterborough or Letchworth and London due to weekend works
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: No trains will run between Peterborough or Letchworth and London later this month due to engineering works. The disruption will take place on Saturday, November 28 and Sunday, November 29, as part of the £1.4 billion East Coast Digital Programme (ECDP), which will replace traditional signals with real-time, in-cab digital signalling. Passengers are advised to check their journeys and expect rail replacement services on affected routes. No Thameslink or Great Northern trains will run between Moorgate, London St Pancras or London King's Cross and Letchworth Garden City or Peterborough all weekend. Rail replacement buses will be operating on the following routes: Most LNER services will start and terminate at Peterborough, with rail replacement coaches connecting customers to Bedford where Thameslink trains will operate to London St Pancras. Ricky Barsby, head of access integration (ECDP) for Network Rail, said: "We have begun to introduce digital in-cab signalling to the East Coast Main Line and we’re getting ready to extend its use to more services. "When all trains operate with digital signalling there will be reliability benefits through less reliance on trackside equipment and better ability to recover from disruption. "We are also taking the opportunity to do other vital engineering work on the track and lineside to improve the reliability of day-to-day services. "We’re sorry to anyone whose journey will be affected. "Those customers who have choice about when they can travel may want to consider travelling on days before or after, which are unaffected by work. "For those who need to travel on the affected weekend, we have plans in place to keep passengers moving." A spokesperson for the train operators said: "We’re working with Network Rail to help passengers plan their journeys while these important upgrades take place. "No trains will be able to run on the East Coast Main Line between Peterborough or Letchworth Garden City and London on November 28 and 29. "Passengers should check before they travel and allow extra time, as services will be significantly altered and rail replacement services will be in operation for many journeys."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire police officers added to barred list doubled in last year
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The number of Cambridgeshire police officers who were added to the barred list doubled in the last year, according to new data. College of Policing figures show 20 Cambridgeshire officers were barred in 2025/26, up from 10 the previous year and three in 2023/24. The College of Policing is an independent body for everyone working in policing. Introduced in 2017, the barred list names officers, special constables and staff dismissed from policing after investigations. Nine Cambridgeshire officers were barred in 2022/23, compared with two in 2021/22 and three in 2020/21. This means more Cambridgeshire Police officers were added to the barred list in 2025/26 than in any other year since 2020. Nationally, 757 police officers were banned from serving after they were sacked for breaching professional standards in the year to the end of March 2026, up from 735 in 2024/25 and 594 in 2023/24. The College of Policing said on November 3 that it was the highest annual total since the barred list began. Assistant Chief Constable Arman Mathieson, director of operational standards at the College of Policing, said: “Policing is built on trust and these figures show we will not hesitate to act when that trust is broken. “757 officers have been removed and barred from ever serving again, including those who retired or resigned while under investigation. “This represents 0.5% of all serving officers, with the vast majority of officers serving with courage, professionalism and integrity. “We all deserve a service that roots out those who fall short. "Where standards are breached, we will find out and we will act. “Since the barred list was introduced in December 2017, 3,591 regular officers have been added in total, with the pace of dismissals accelerating markedly: 757 officers were barred last year alone, more than in any single year since the list began and over twice the annual average of the preceding four years.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: £120,000 conservation project launched to protect historic Houghton Mill
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Conservation work is underway to protect a historic watermill in Huntingdonshire. The project aims to safeguard Houghton Mill, one of the country’s few surviving watermills, from the pressures of age, weather, and seasonal flooding. Funding has come from the Wolfson Foundation, contributing to the estimated £120,000 cost of the scheme. Isabel Sedgwick, visitor operations manager at Houghton Mill, said: "Houghton Mill is a remarkable place, and we’re incredibly fortunate to be able to care for a building with such a rich history while keeping it working for visitors today. "This project is about making sure we can continue to share the sights, sounds and stories of the mill for many years to come. "The support from the Wolfson Foundation is helping us tackle some really important repairs and protect the mill’s character for future generations." External Repairs - Houghton Mill (Image: National Trust Images Mike Selby) The first phase of work will address the north and east sides of the mill, following detailed surveys that identified urgent repairs. A key focus will be the conservation of the north lucam, the overhanging timber hoist once used to lift grain into the mill. Specialist craftspeople will stabilise and repair the historic structure using traditional methods. The project will also include roof repairs, replacement of lead flashings, and restoration of weatherboarding, windows, and dormers. A Cambridgeshire-based firm, Brown and Ralph Ltd, is carrying out the work. The conservation is expected to be completed by January 2027, with the mill due to reopen to the public at Easter. Paul Ramsbottom, chief executive at the Wolfson Foundation, said: "Houghton Mill is an important part of our industrial heritage – there has been an active mill on this site for over 1,000 years. "We are pleased that our long-standing partnership with the National Trust can help support this essential restoration."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Eight sieges for every battle: new exhibition reveals Civil War reality
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Sieges, not battles, take centre stage in a new exhibition in Huntingdon. The Cromwell Museum's latest display, Besieged: Sieges of the Civil War, reveals the overlooked reality of the English Civil Wars. While just 28 major battles took place in England between 1642 and 1648, 189 locations were besieged, and more than 1,000 fortified sites could be found across the British Isles. Stuart Orme, curator of the Cromwell Museum, said: "When people think of the Civil Wars they tend to think of the great battles like Edgehill, Naseby, or Worcester, but there were eight sieges for every one of these. "Places all over Britain and Ireland were fortified and then besieged as part of this brutal conflict, dragging many thousands of ordinary people into the front line of the conflict and leaving scars on the landscape and many of our historic buildings that can still be seen today." The exhibition, which runs from November 3, 2026, to April 4, 2027, explores why so many towns and castles were fortified, how earthwork defences were constructed, and how siege tactics developed throughout the conflict. It also examines the roles of those involved, from engineers and soldiers to civilians and women who defended their homes. Visitors can view original artefacts including siege plans, musket balls, a cannonball from the siege of Sheffield Castle, and a scale model of Earith Bulwark. The only surviving Civil War siege helmet in the UK is also on display. Case studies of key locations feature throughout the exhibition, including Oxford, Bristol, Leicester, Skipton Castle, Pontefract, and Hull. Entry is free, though donations are welcome. The museum is open Tuesday to Sunday from 10am to 3.30pm. More information is available at cromwellmuseum.org.

Mr Obese-Jecty praised the work of Rotary St Ives, which has raised more than £2,000 to fund the rollout of the scheme across seven primary schools. He said: "Arriving at school cold or wet is an immediate barrier to a child's readiness to learn. Of the 10 schools currently participating in the scheme across the Huntingdon constituency, seven are supported through the club’s fundraising. Nationally, Coats4Kids has delivered more than 11,000 brand-new winter coats to children in need. The charity works with school safeguarding and pastoral staff, who identify pupils requiring support. Children are then given a digital voucher to select a new coat online, which is delivered directly to their home. This approach removes the stigma of second-hand clothing and avoids the need for schools to store or distribute items. Mr Obese-Jecty encouraged wider participation. He said: "By raising over £2,000 and backing seven of our primary schools, St Ives Rotary has shown what community spirit looks like in action. The 27-year-old hid behind a nearby van, leaving his front-seat passenger trapped in the vehicle with serious injuries. Members of the public who witnessed the collision chased Ionescu and detained him, before officers arrived and arrested him. Ionescu’s 27-year-old passenger suffered a brain injury, multiple fractures and was in a medically induced coma for two weeks as a result of the crash. At Cambridge Crown Court on Wednesday (October 28), Ionescu, of Granville Street, Peterborough, was jailed for two years. He admitting to causing serious injury by dangerous driving, using a motor vehicle without insurance, and using a motor vehicle without a valid license. Sentencing, Judge Andrew Hurst, commented on the fact that the victim is now unable to work and is "confined by his own fragile mental health". Detective Constable Lauren Byrne, from the force’s Serious Collision Investigation Unit, said: "Firstly my thoughts go out to the victim and his family. "This crash has had an extensive impact on them all and I wish the victim a speedy recovery. "This was a serious, but completely preventable crash, caused by Ionescu’s careless and reckless driving. "The impact of the collision goes far beyond the victim’s physical injuries - he will likely suffer from the ongoing emotional and psychological impact, especially as he is unable to work or continue his life as it was prior to the crash. "The fact Ionescu tried to flee the scene is cowardly and shows his lack of remorse and compassion for the victim, so I am pleased he is now behind bars and will be held accountable for his actions."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: If you're looking for a "traditional" pub serving "sensational" food in Cambridgeshire, then look no further. With its exposed beams, varied furnishings and large inglenook fireplace, The White Horse, in Eaton Socon, has been described as "nice and cosy". On its website, the venue proudly describes how it "pairs centuries-old character with a relaxed, modern pub experience". The former coaching inn was given a new lease of life thanks to its new owners Kerry and Simon Smith. They worked around the clock for more than five weeks to renovate The White Horse in time for its grand reopening in October last year. According to Mrs Smith, the pair had spent "12-hour days" trying to get the pub up to standard, including work to the kitchen and interior. The couple hoped to create a pub that is part of the community, turning their attention to the pub's exterior and garden. Naturally, The White Horse has received raving reviews on Trip Advisor, with visitors praising its "excellent, accommodating staff". One visitor said: "Real value for money and my husband had the Korean crispy chicken burger which he thought was absolutely sensational." The White Horse dates back to the 1700s and the new owners are bringing it back to life as a “true village pub". Whether you're dropping in for a pint, meeting friends or enjoying a roast, "you'll find honest food and genuine hospitality," its website reads. Centred around fresh ingredients, the menu boasts classic British favourites and "hearty plates". It adds: "From Sunday roasts to seasonal dishes and pub staples, everything is prepared with the care you’d expect from a family-run kitchen." "We’re creating a community-focused pub where everyone feels at home." "Expect good food, friendly faces, and regular events — all in a space that celebrates the history and heart of Eaton Socon." Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Centrepoint resident welcomes minister to mark new changes to Housing Benefit
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Following Centrepoint’s yearlong Make Work Pay campaign, young people in supported housing accommodation will no longer be penalised for working more. For years, a flaw in the benefits system meant that those who tried to work more hours, take on extra shifts or do better paid work were often left financially worse off. Now, new changes to Housing Benefit rules mean residents aged 16-25 will keep more of what they earn.  Around 30,000 young people living in supported housing receive Housing Benefit. Centrepoint welcomed the new changes by hosting a visit from Department for Work and Pensions Minister Stephen Timms MP to one of its East London supported accommodation services.  There, the Minister met Sadaf, a 19-year-old resident who talked about her hopes for the future. Throughout her time with Centrepoint, Sadaf has overcome difficulties but remains committed to her long-term aspiration to study medicine and build a better future for herself. Like many young people transitioning towards independence, Sadaf viewed employment as a positive step towards self-sufficiency. Her intention in seeking work was not only to gain financial independence but also to fund her education and create future opportunities. Sadaf said: "Working made me feel like I was moving forward. I finally felt like I was doing something productive and taking responsibility for my future." However, gaining employment triggered a significant reduction in Sadaf’s Housing Benefit entitlement. The reduction created a substantial gap between her accommodation costs and available income, resulting in rent arrears that eventually approached £5,000. Rather than creating greater financial stability, employment created financial uncertainty.  The impact extended far beyond finances alone. Housing uncertainty affected her future plans, educational opportunities, relationships and overall wellbeing. Now that the system is working better, Sadaf is actively seeking employment again.  She said: "There were times when it felt like working made everything harder, but I still believe education and employment are the way forward for me. I want to build a future where I can support myself, help other people and become the person I've always wanted to be.” Seyi Obakin OBE, Chief Executive Officer at Centrepoint, said: “This is a landmark win for young people, and we commend the government for getting this change over the line.  For too long, young people in supported housing, particularly those at the start of their careers, have had their ambitions blocked by a system that punished them for working harder. "This is what it looks like when the system works for young people, and we hope it creates a smoother transition from benefits into work for them.” An incredible evening was had on Tuesday 13th October at London's Bloomsbury Ballroom for the annual Centrepoint Awards. (Image: devantayj) The event, hosted by broadcaster and long-time Centrepoint supporter Gaby Roslin, celebrated the achievements of inspirational young people who have been supported by Centrepoint and, with the foundation of a safe and stable home, have gone on to establish themselves in their careers, interests and relationships. The night was opened by the London Cabaret Club's resident singer Sofia Klimovsky, who got the crowd in the celebratory mood before the award winners were announced. Videos showcasing the young people's stories brought tears to the eyes of many attendees. The awards included categories like Rising Star, won by a young person whose aim is to build the next unicorn and feature on the Forbes 30 Under 30 list, and the Arts and Educational Excellence Award, won by a young care leaver who has just started his first year at Oxford University studying Philosophy, Politics and Economics. Centrepoint were joined on the evening by some of their longstanding partners, including award sponsors the cardfactory Foundation, ASOS Foundation and Clarksons. Seyi Obakin OBE, Chief Executive at Centrepoint, said: "These awards are a poignant reminder that we are surrounded by talented young people, but the opportunities are not always there or equal. The success of the winners shows what happens when young people are given not just an opportunity to shine, but the support to do it." Following World Homelessness Day last month, contemporary artist Hugh Miller has dedicated his latest oil-on-canvas painting to Centrepoint. (Image: Anne-Marie Doohan) As a young aspiring artist, Hugh did a lot of chalk drawings on pavements near London’s famous landmarks and met inspiring young homeless people along the way. His early years led him to take an interest in the charity’s work. Miller’s Houses of Parliament oil-on-canvas painting is the latest in a series designed to "celebrate the aesthetic beauty of cities in the United Kingdom". The artist was given a rare chance to access the Speaker's Terrace in Parliament last month to complete a section of his painting. The visit attracted the attention of cross-party MPs and raised the profile of Centrepoint and youth homelessness in Parliament. His latest painting - which will take another eight months to finish - will form part of his Centrepoint series collection, with all proceeds from the artwork going to the charity to help end youth homelessness. To find out more about Hugh Miller and his work, visit www.hughmillerart.co.uk Last year, over 118,000 young people faced homelessness. That’s one young person every four minutes. At a time of life when most of their peers are trying new things and taking their first steps into adulthood, these young people found themselves alone and afraid, and unsure where to turn. It doesn’t have to be like this.  With the right support at the right time, these young people can escape homelessness or avoid it altogether. At Centrepoint, we provide more than a bed for the night. We provide a safe place to rebuild, support into education and work, and the confidence to believe in a better future. Youth homelessness is not inevitable. With the right help at the right time, it can be prevented and it can be ended. Our mission is to end youth homelessness – and you can help us. Whether it’s running a marathon or holding a sleep out, you, your friends, family and co-workers can join our movement to end youth homelessness and give vulnerable young people a brighter future. To find out more, donate or get involved, please visit our website http://www.centrepoint.org.uk/newspaper Thirty-seven young people experiencing homelessness had their deaths registered in England and Wales last year, according to the latest figures released by the Office for National Statistics. Of the 37 deaths of young people aged between 16-24 years old, 29 were male and eight were female.  This marks a 2.8% rise from the year before. Overall, 974 people died while experiencing homelessness in England and Wales in 2025.  This marks a 77% increase compared to when the figures were first collated in 2013, rising from 550 to 974.  London had the highest estimated number of deaths in English regions, followed by the North-West and the South-East. Matt Bawden, Director of Progression Housing at Centrepoint said: "Even one death of someone experiencing homelessness is too many. These sobering figures represent countless individual tragedies but are also indicative of a system that is failing. The need to work collaboratively to fix that system and to deliver high-quality housing and support is more urgent than ever.  We believe that every young person should be given the opportunity to lead a fulfilling, healthy life where they can realise their potential."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Andy Burnham hails local news as 'critical' as PM backs Journalism Matters campaign
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Journalism is a vital part of our national infrastructure. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has spoken out in support of the Journalism Matters campaign, emphasising the crucial role of news media in democracy, accountability, and community life. The campaign, coordinated by the News Media Association, highlights the value of journalism and will run from November 2 to 8. Mr Burnham said: "I am proud to support this year's Journalism Matters campaign, which is about recognising journalism not as a nice-to-have, but as part of the national infrastructure of a healthy country and democracy. "It holds power to account, strengthens our resilience and connects people to the places they call home." He stressed the importance of local journalism in the Government’s devolution plans, saying that returning power to communities must go hand in hand with local accountability. Mr Burnham said: "Local reporters are the people sitting in council chambers, courts and planning meetings, asking the questions that need to be asked. "They shine a light on decisions made in people’s name and give communities a voice." He also highlighted the vital role of trusted journalism during times of crisis. Mr Burnham said: "At moments when communities are at their most vulnerable, good local journalism can bring people together and separate fact from fiction. "We saw that after Southport and, more recently, in Belfast, when trusted reporters challenged lies and misinformation being spread online." This year’s Journalism Matters campaign will see the news industry come together to celebrate the role journalism plays underpinning national infrastructure. A recent global report by UNESCO found that countries with a strong, independent press enjoy significant economic and security benefits. News Media Association Chief Executive Theo Bamber (Image: NMA) Theo Bamber, chief executive of the News Media Association, welcomed Mr Burnham’s support but called for practical action. Mr Bamber said: "The Prime Minister is absolutely right to point to the critical role that independent journalism plays in our society and particularly how important local news will be to the success of his own sprawling devolution agenda. "Now, the support shown by the Prime Minister must turn into real action that demonstrates the government understands the changed environment that journalists and news publishers are operating in and strengthens their ability to do more of what they’re brilliant at—chasing stories, uncovering the truth and holding power to account." He called on the Government to protect and promote a diverse media ecosystem. The Journalism Matters campaign runs from November 2 to 8, 2026.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Andy Burnham - 'Journalism is a vital part of our national infrastructure'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Too much power in this country has flowed one way: towards Westminster and away from the places where people actually live their lives. This government is changing that. We are putting power and resources back into the hands of communities. Because I want people in local communities to have a bigger say over the decisions that shape their area. But with greater local power must come local accountability. And that is why local journalism matters. Local reporters are the people sitting in council chambers, courts and planning meetings, asking the questions that need to be asked. They shine a light on decisions made in people’s name and give communities a voice. But their role goes much further than holding power to account. At moments when communities are at their most vulnerable, good local journalism can bring people together and separate fact from fiction. We saw that after Southport and, more recently, in Belfast, when trusted reporters challenged lies and misinformation being spread online. And I saw its power myself as Mayor of Greater Manchester. When the Manchester Evening News campaigned for free bus travel for homeless children living in temporary accommodation, it didn't just report what was wrong, it brought people together to get behind the change that was needed. That is exactly what this year's Journalism Matters campaign is about: recognising journalism not as a nice-to-have, but as part of the national infrastructure of a healthy country and democracy. It holds power to account, strengthens our resilience and connects people to the places they call home. And yet access to good local journalism is becoming increasingly unequal. Ninety-five per cent of adults access local news, but the market alone will not sustain it everywhere. Up to 37 local authority districts now have no dedicated outlet of their own, leaving as many as 4.4 million people in local "news deserts", disproportionately in some of our most deprived urban communities. I've spent my career arguing that where you live should not determine the opportunities you get. I believe exactly the same principle applies to information. People in every part of the country deserve trusted local news, scrutiny of those in power and a strong voice for their community. Through our Local Media Action Plan, the new Local News Fund will provide up to £12 million over two years. This is part of a wider package of measures we're delivering to support local journalism. This year, local newspapers, websites and independent television and radio stations in England and Wales have been able to bid for up to £125,000 to invest in their future, whether that's new technology, multimedia journalism, reaching younger audiences or finding new ways to bring in revenue. We have also made up to £275,000 available for projects that strengthen the wider industry. And in the second year, £1 million will help communities bring local journalism back where it has disappeared, whether by reviving a dormant title, expanding a neighbouring publication or establishing a community-owned outlet. We’re doing this because devolution cannot simply mean moving power from one set of politicians to another. It has to mean giving people more of a say. For that to work, they need to know what is being done in their name. They need journalists willing to ask difficult questions, expose wrongdoing, challenge misinformation and champion their communities. That is why I am proud to support this year's Journalism Matters campaign, and why this government will work to ensure trusted local journalism remains at the heart of communities across our country.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Why the UK government must act to protect trusted local journalism
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Where does a news story come from? A scandal exposed, a failure revealed, a decision brought into the open that someone would rather have kept private. Behind each is work we rarely see. We read the story, take it in and move on. In short, we take journalism for granted. Someone had to find that story, check it, check it again, and then tell it. That takes skill, experience and painstaking work, sometimes over hours, sometimes over days, weeks, months or years. The published story is the bit we all see, and if we want that to continue, we must protect the people and the industry that makes it possible. This year’s Journalism Matters campaign is a chance for us to reflect carefully on what journalism does for all of us, and what we would lose if we didn’t have it. In an article launching this year’s campaign, Prime Minister Andy Burnham cites the enormous benefits that independent journalism delivers for our society and the critical importance of local news media to the devolution agenda. He is absolutely right to do so. Journalism is part of the national infrastructure we all rely on, and the benefits it delivers go far beyond the stories themselves. A global report published by UNESCO earlier this year found a raft of economic and security benefits connected to journalism in countries with an ecosystem which supports an independent free press. So how do we make sure more journalism can happen? It’s clear that there is plenty the government can do to strengthen the conditions that the industry operates in and it must use this opportunity to affect real change. In an article launching this year’s campaign, Prime Minister Andy Burnham cites the enormous benefits that independent journalism delivers for our society and the critical importance of local news media to the devolution agenda (Image: Carlos Jasso/Press Association) This should start with digital markets, and creating an ecosystem which can support and maintain a plural and diverse range of media outlets. This increases user choice and allows publishers that invest in reporting to get a fair return for their work. Meta, always ready and willing to play the role of the tech giant bully, recently launched an assault on journalism with its attempt to force publishers and other businesses to hand over all their content to train its AI products. It was a move right out of the tech platform playbook - bury the crucial detail in a ton of paperwork and then feign disbelief and surprise at the horrified reaction from the business community. This can’t continue and, if the government supports journalism in the way the Prime Minister has outlined, it must back the Competition and Markets Authority to the hilt. The CMA is tasked with making the tech platforms play fair, and to do this job effectively it needs full-throated political support. Nothing else will do. But getting the platforms to play fair is just the start. Government must also make sure that its own policies support journalism, not undermine it. The news prominence regime, as proposed in the Media Green Paper, will have a damaging and distortive effect on the news media landscape if implemented in its current form. Inevitably, local news will be hit particularly hard and the lack of clarity on how platform compliance will be enforced does little to boost our confidence that the policy won’t deliver myriad dangerous, unintended consequences. Ministers must also ensure that the BBC Charter Renewal results in a BBC which partners with the commercial sector rather than competing aggressively against it. And, at a local level, transparency must be maintained as power is shifted out of Westminster to the regions, including by keeping public notices in highly trusted local news media. As the noise around us gets louder and more complex, we still need people intent on establishing the truth. The real, actual truth. This is what journalism does, and this is why bold government support for the industry should be non-negotiable. Without it, we’ll lose our ability to understand the world around us and be consigned to a world where decisions that happen behind closed doors never see the light of day and stories that change lives are never told. That is not an acceptable future for a modern-day democracy such as ours. The Journalism Matters campaign runs from November 2 to 8, 2026.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Leading' UK sports supplement brand falls into administration after 15 years
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A "leading" UK sports supplement brand has entered administration after 15 years of business. Promuscle Products is based in Fleetwood, Lancashire and was set up in May 2011. It specialises in creating formulas for the sports supplement market for blending, tableting and encapsulation. The company's website states: "Promuscle Products has been leading the way in the sports supplement market for years contract manufacturing some of the biggest brands that have dominated the UK and EU market. "We specialise in creative, innovative formulas and pride ourselves in creating products that a quality assured and taste superb." Promuscle Products also ships out to the USA, Australia and the UAE alongside the UK market. It has 400 ingredients in-house plus over 30 trademarked ingredients they hold the licensees to manufacture. Administrators Philip Lawrence and Gareth Howarth of AMS Business Recovery were appointed on Tuesday, October 27, The Gazette reports. Promuscle Products has been contacted by Newsquest for comment. It has been a tough year for the UK high street, with several retailers entering administration or liquidation and others announcing widespread store closures. TG Jones and the British Heart Foundation will also be closing around 150 stores each across the UK. Wynsors World of Shoes is shutting 17 stores across the UK, with closing down sales already underway at several affected branches. UK entertainment retailer Zavvi has ceased trading after nearly 20 years, having collapsed into administration for a second time. Australian stationery retailer Typo is also set to pull out of the UK in 2027, closing all its stores and ending online trading. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: One million people warned to act before major UK landline change
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: One million people risk losing landline phone access unless they upgrade to digital lines The warning comes as the UK prepares to retire its old analogue phone network and complete the switch to digital lines. BT-owned Openreach are phasing out the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN), a system in place since the 1870s, with a full shutdown planned for January 31, 2027. James Lilley, director of customer migrations at Openreach, said: "It’s very hard to get [customers] to read and react and do something." Moving to digital lines is expected to provide a more reliable service, better-quality calls and improved blocking of unwanted calls. Despite these benefits, around one million residents and businesses remain on the old network. Those who do not upgrade in time could lose service or be transferred to a basic emergency phone system without features like voicemail. The UK government says the transition is necessary due to the declining reliability of the copper-based PSTN, and Ofcom has said most users are unlikely to experience significant disruption. The original switch-off date was set for December 31, 2025, but concerns about the impact on vulnerable and rural users, particularly those relying on telecare alarms, led to a revised timeline. Under the PSTN Charter, providers have agreed not to migrate customers using telecare devices unless their equipment is confirmed to be compatible with digital lines. Telecom companies, including BT, are supplying vulnerable customers with free back-up battery packs to ensure phones remain operational during power outages. Read More Unlike the digital system, the traditional PSTN does not depend on mains electricity and will continue to function during a power cut. Openreach has stated that there will not be a single day when all customers lose service. Tens of thousands of customers are reportedly switching to the new system each week, Lilley said a rise in scams had made it harder to get consumers to respond to letters about the change. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Huntingdon tutoring business celebrates 10 years after 100,000 hours of tuition
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A tutoring business in Huntingdon is celebrating 10 years of supporting students. Tutor Doctor Peterborough Huntingdon Stamford, founded by Piyush Gupta in 2016, has overseen more than 100,000 hours of tuition and helped more than 1,000 young people. Piyush said: "Before this, I worked as an accountant, where success was measured in financial figures. "Now, those numbers are replaced by student outcomes and the difference we’re making to young people’s lives." The business supports children who struggle with mainstream education, including those with special educational needs and mental health difficulties. Piyush recalled the progress of one student who was selective mute, particularly in educational settings. He said: "At the start, they found it a challenge communicating with their tutor. "After several months, they gradually began talking to their peers and became more comfortable around our team and even volunteered to welcome new students." His wife Smita joined the business five years later, bringing more than 20 years of primary education experience. She said: "I’ve never seen Piyush happier in his work, and I’ve learnt so much from him too. "It’s been lovely to bring my expertise into the business in order for us to support even more local students." The couple’s two sons have also been involved, with their eldest now working full-time, making it a true family business. Smita said: "All the relationships we’ve built over the years have been amazing. "Our staff and tutors have been especially important for us, and we couldn’t have achieved what we have done without them." Piyush said he is proud of how far the business has come. He said: "To see where we started, the thought of not being involved anymore is difficult to imagine. "The journey over the past 10 years has been truly amazing."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Knifeman had ‘eyes wide open like he was on something’, court told
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A knifeman who stabbed 10 people on a London-bound train was described by a boy he stabbed the day before as having ‘his eyes wide open like he was on something’, a court heard. Several people were injured on an LNER train from Doncaster to London King's Cross on November 1, 2025 which was forced to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon, where CCTV of the knife attack was shown in court. Anthony Williams, 33, denies ten counts of attempted murder relating to the incident. He also denies the attempted murders of three people in Peterborough on October 31, and of a 17-year-old boy at Pontoon Dock DLR station in London in the early hours of November 1. His trial opened at Cambridge Crown Court on Wednesday, October 28. Judge Mr Justice Calver earlier told jurors at Cambridge Crown Court that whether Williams carried out the attacks is not in question but they must consider whether he intended to kill those individuals when he carried out the attacks. Cambridge Crown Court (Image: LDR) A 14-year-old boy, who cannot be identified for legal reasons, told police in a video-recorded interview played in court on Friday that he was stabbed on Halloween last year. He said he was going to go trick or treating with friends and was walking over a bridge behind an Asda store in Peterborough when a man ‘just pulled out a knife and stabbed me’. He described the person as "this random guy" and said it happened shortly after 7pm as he was walking with a friend, along a footbridge near Henry Penn Walk. "We’ve pretty much got right up close to him as we’re walking past him and he’s pulled out a knife and just stabbed me," the boy said. He added: "I didn’t feel like he was mentally sane. "His eyes were wide open like he was on something." He said the man "shouted something, I don’t know what he said". "I jumped back a little when I saw he was reaching for something and I started running," the boy said. He continued: "He was screaming something. "My friend said he was shouting something like 'are you involved?'." He said he and his friend ran and hid in bushes and called the police. Asked what force the man had used, the boy said: "It was strong, like it pushed me back a little bit. "He was using his full force, his arm was fully stretched out." He said the man was dressed in black and he believed the knife was around 10 inches long. A group of police officers stand close to the emergency equipment left behind after an incident at Huntingdon train station (Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire) The boy’s friend, who also cannot be identified for legal reasons, said the man who he described as a black male had shouted "are you two involved?". In a statement read in court, he said the man "pulled out a large knife" from a rucksack, describing the knife as a "type of zombie knife or Rambo-style knife". Williams is accused of the attempted murders of two others in Peterborough on October 31, Dawid Taborski and William Ogelby. Mr Taborski said in a video interview that he had been on his way to a rave when a man he had never seen before "kept saying are you involved, are you involved?" He said he "didn’t know what he (Williams) was on about, I was really confused" and he initially thought it may have been "a Halloween thing". "As soon as he took that knife out I ran," he added. "It happened so quickly." The scene at Huntingdon train station after the incident last year (Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire) Detective Constable Ryan Burke said he was on high-visibility foot patrols when Mr Taborski approached him by Charters bar in Peterborough and told him "someone had attempted to stab him but they hadn’t been able to do so". The officer said in a statement that Mr Taborski told him the man had "brandished a long silver blade" and "lunged attempting to stab him". Mr Ogelby told police he had been walking to a cashpoint to get money out when a man walking towards him said "wagwan" to him, which he understood to be a greeting. "I’ve said (it) back and he’s pulled a knife out and tried to stab me three times in my stomach and once in my chest," he said in a video interview played to jurors. He said he ran home "as fast as my legs would carry me" and "checked myself to see if I was bleeding – I wasn’t bleeding". "I thought he was going to kill me," he said. Jurors were shown a photo of Mr Ogelby wearing a jacket which had what prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC described as a "knife cut" to it. The trial continues, with jurors asked to return to court on Monday, November 2.
